title: Process Emergence Under Uncertainty: Cross-Cultural Decision Architectures in Synthetic Qualitative Populations

detail.title: Process Emergence Under Uncertainty: Cross-Cultural Decision Architectures in Synthetic Qualitative Populations

detail.abstract:
Most research on synthetic respondents has been evaluated through output realism: whether languagemodel populations reproduce human preferences, predict survey marginals, or converge with human samples on specific answers. This paper explores a different property. Rather than asking whether synthetic respondents reproduce answers, we ask whether synthetic populations exhibit distinct procedural structures—how they reach a decision—when confronted with uncertainty and competing legitimate principles.
Using psychometrically grounded synthetic populations generated across eight markets (United States, United Kingdom, Spain, Mexico, Germany, France, Italy and Brazil), we observed a consistent pattern. When questions contained an obvious dominant answer, responses converged strongly across countries, carrying little differentiating information. When the same structural dilemma instead pitted two trusted authorities against each other under acknowledged uncertainty, distinct decision architectures emerged. These architectures differed less in their conclusions than in the procedures used to reach them: reliance on institutions versus relationships, tolerance for ambiguity, preference for experimentation versus postponement, use of third-party arbitration, concern for reversibility, and the weighting of experience against innovation.
We name this phenomenon Process Emergence and situate it against a companion regularity we have described elsewhere, the Consensus Ceiling. The findings are exploratory and are explicitly not offered as population estimates, validated cultural claims, or evidence of human equivalence. They are most defensibly read as a method for generating culturally differentiated hypotheses about decision-making under uncertainty—hypotheses that subsequently require human validation. We close by distinguishing two interpretations of the observed structure—genuine cultural cognition versus model priors—and argue that the present design cannot separate them, which is precisely why the appropriate output is a hypothesis, not a finding.

title: Remote Work and the Corporate Hierarchy
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Management, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Hanken School of Economics

detail.title: Remote Work and the Corporate Hierarchy
detail.abstract: Using population-wide Finnish registry data linking an administrative measure of work from home (WFH) to matched employer-employee records, we study how the allocation of WFH across the corporate hierarchy relates to wages and firm performance. Although remote workers on average earn higher wages, job-to-job transitions into WFH show that this premium largely reflects selection and heterogeneity: managers experience wage declines of approximately 3%, while middle- and lower-layer workers experience no comparable declines. Firm-level evidence shows that the performance consequences of WFH depend on its hierarchical location. Greater lower-layer WFH penetration is associated with weaker performance, whereas managerial WFH is not associated with worse firm performance. Since managerial WFH is associated with wage declines without evidence of lower firm performance, we interpret the decline as a conservative lower bound on managers’ valuation of WFH. Our results suggest that the value of WFH depends on where it is located inside the firm.

detail.abstract:
The clothing worn in direct, sustained contact with human skin is an underexamined determinant of occupational comfort and, on emerging evidence, physiological wellbeing. Across an eight-to-twelve-hour working day, the textile layer against the skin mediates heat exchange, moisture transport, microbial ecology, and chemical exposure. This paper reviews the published evidence on the physiological effects of synthetic versus natural cellulosic textiles across four domains: dermal chemical exposure, microplastic shedding, thermoregulatory performance, and skin microbiome interaction. It situates this literature alongside the authors' own field survey of 847 workforce respondents and a smaller controlled-exposure pilot cohort (n=94) across three Indian states (Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and the National Capital Region), examining self-reported comfort, dermatological symptoms, and subjective wellbeing under synthetic versus natural-fibre clothing conditions.

The published toxicological and occupational health literature documents specific, replicated concerns associated with synthetic textiles: dermal migration of plasticisers and flame-retardant compounds, environmental and inhalational exposure to textile microfibres, inferior moisture regain and air permeability relative to cellulosic fibres, and disruption of skin-surface microbial communities by broad-spectrum antimicrobial finishing agents. Natural cellulosic fibres, and hand-spun cotton (Khadi) in particular, show favourable physical properties on these same parameters in the existing technical textile literature, alongside a body of ethnobotanical and emerging microbiome research suggesting plausible mechanisms for additional benefit through targeted botanical treatment.

The authors' field data are consistent with this literature directionally — respondents wearing natural-fibre clothing reported substantially lower rates of heat discomfort and dermatological symptoms, and higher subjective wellbeing scores, than those in synthetic workwear — but the authors are explicit that this primary research is preliminary, unblinded, and subject to expectation effects that limit causal interpretation. The paper closes by specifying the controlled trial designs, accredited laboratory testing, and independent replication that would be required to move these findings from suggestive to confirmatory, and offers general policy considerations for textile standard-setting bodies without endorsing any specific commercial product.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence: A Narrative Review of Trust Calibration, Clinical Adoption, and Human-AI Collaboration

detail.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence: A Narrative Review of Trust Calibration, Clinical Adoption, and Human-AI Collaboration
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in healthcare for diagnosis, imaging interpretation, risk prediction, and clinical decision support. However, its adoption remains limited by concerns about opacity, trust, accountability, and workflow integration. Explainable artificial intelligence addresses these concerns by making AI outputs and decision factors more understandable to healthcare professionals. This narrative review synthesizes research on how explainability affects clinicians' trust, perceived value, adoption intentions, reliance, and human-AI collaboration. The literature suggests that explainability can improve trust, confidence, and willingness to use AI, but poorly designed explanations may also create overreliance, confusion, or misplaced confidence. The review argues that the goal of healthcare XAI should be calibrated trust rather than unconditional trust. Effective explainability depends on explanation type, user expertise, clinical task, and workflow fit. Overall, XAI should be understood as a human-centered and socio-technical design challenge, not merely a technical solution to the black-box problem.

title: Human Capital, AI, and Labor Commoditization
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management and

detail.title: Human Capital, AI, and Labor Commoditization
detail.abstract: Has generative AI changed how labor markets value human capital? We study this question using contract-level data from Upwork, a large online labor market. We represent worker profiles with high-dimensional text embeddings, allowing us to capture rich human capital information from unstructured profile text. We then compute the predictive importance of workers' human capital information and posted hourly rates for client demand, and incorporate these measures into a difference-in-differences design around the release of ChatGPT. We find that in more AI-exposed job categories, the importance of human capital declines and the importance of price rises, suggesting a commoditization effect of AI on labor. Two additional findings support commoditization as a mechanism: The demand premium enjoyed by workers with strong human capital declines in more AI-exposed categories, and demand reallocates toward lower-priced workers. Our results have implications for the design of online labor markets, workers' incentives to invest in human capital, and labor welfare.

detail.abstract:
This paper explains how a new radio design with appropriate regulatory reforms can help drive the necessary transition to lower power, small cell wireless architectures. 

 

Wireless is the central nervous system for our AI economy. A significant shift in the deployed technology and the corresponding regulatory environment – our “6G future” – is necessary to realize AI’s potential for enhancing economic growth and sustaining US global competitiveness.

 

The need for smaller-cell architectures to support ubiquitous coverage at distances at middle ranges of a few tens of meters up to a few kilometers is especially important and has the potential to substantially alter the economics for deploying and operating edge-networks and the services those support. Although the need to transition to smaller-cell architectures for edge network providers has been clear for a long time, the densification of edge network radio access network (RAN) infrastructure in the US has been hampered by two factors – one economic and one technological. 

 

The economic factor stems from how the siting of cellular antennas is regulated in the US. In some regions outside the US with different regulatory processes the densification of the cellular network down to 80-m and 100-m cell sizes is already common. The second factor that has been constraining densification is technological. Fundamentally, legacy radio designs use too much power to reliably transmit digital bits. Because of this, each cell broadcasts significant “co-channel interference” into all the neighboring cells using the same frequency. Developments in three areas critical to the design of radios for edge-network communications have made it feasible to build and commercially deploy radios that significantly alleviate this problem (see https://eridan.io/). Exploiting these advances enables radios capable of matching state of the art data throughput performance with hundred-fold reduced co-channel interference and much greater energy efficiency. While an important technical barrier to wider deployment of small cells has been significantly reduced, additional regulatory and policy steps to reduce structural impediments to densification and smaller cell networks are important for enabling the transition to lower-power, smaller-cell wireless networks.

title: Airport Electromagnetic Pollution Management: Strategic Insights from Lactuca Sativa Biomonitors

detail.title: Airport Electromagnetic Pollution Management: Strategic Insights from Lactuca Sativa Biomonitors

detail.abstract: This paper explores using Lactuca sativa (lettuce) as a biomonitor for electromagnetic pollution in airport environments, a concept driven by increasing Radio Frequency-Electromagnetic Fields (RF-EMF) ubiquity and documented plant sensitivity (Tran et al., 2023). While pollution biomarkers offer early warning capabilities (Lionetto et al., 2019), applying them to complex airport RF-EMF presents unique challenges. The aviation industry faces dilemmas balancing operational needs with environmental impact and public concern. Indian expert views acknowledge RF-EMF risk to "vegetation," but lack detailed flora-specific data (Ministry of Communications, n.d.; Ministry of Environment and Forests, 2002). Addressing critical research gaps, from comprehensive RF-EMF characterization to biomarker validation and logistical planning, is essential to establish lettuce as a reliable biomonitor for integrated environmental assessment.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a risk-governed framework for understanding how global monetary tightening by major central banks affects emerging-market stability through inflation, interest rates, capital flows, exchange rates, sovereign spreads, external debt, international reserves, and domestic policy credibility. The analysis is motivated by the renewed global relevance of monetary spillovers: after the post-pandemic inflation shock and subsequent tightening cycle, emerging markets faced a complex environment in which policy rates, dollar strength, commodity-price shocks, risk sentiment, and refinancing conditions interacted across borders. The paper uses an integrative conceptual methodology grounded in classic pre-2006 monetary, open-economy macroeconomic, and currency-crisis literature, supplemented by recent institutional evidence from the IMF, World Bank, BIS, OECD, and major central-bank research. It argues that emerging-market exposure to major central-bank decisions is not determined by capital-account openness alone, but by a wider vulnerability structure: inflation credibility, exchange-rate regime, foreign-currency debt, reserve adequacy, sovereign spread sensitivity, domestic financial depth, fiscal credibility, and the composition of capital inflows. The proposed framework distinguishes between liquidity stress, solvency stress, credibility stress, and balance-sheet stress, and links each to specific policy instruments. The paper contributes twelve analytical tables and models, including a global monetary spillover transmission matrix, a capital-flow sudden-stop framework, an inflation-expectations credibility table, an international reserves adequacy framework, and a conceptual model linking major central bank policy to emerging-market stability. The conclusion emphasizes that emerging economies cannot fully insulate themselves from global monetary cycles, but they can reduce spillover fragility through credible inflation frameworks, prudent fiscal policy, flexible but orderly exchange-rate management, resilient domestic debt markets, reserve buffers, macroprudential tools, and transparent crisis-response rules.

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-14

detail.abstract: Afrobeats has become one of Africa’s most successful cultural exports, propelled by Nigerian creative talent, informal innovation networks, and diaspora audiences, at a moment when streaming and platform consolidation are reshaping the global music industry. Yet despite generating substantial global value, only a fraction of that value returns to Nigeria. This pattern echoes older extractive economic arrangements and exposes structural gaps in Nigeria’s creative economy governance. Drawing on the concept of technological and institutional “leapfrogging,” this report traces how Nigeria’s music industry developed largely outside the distribution models that shaped core Western markets, with local factors contributing to the development of an industry marked by informality, weak data infrastructure, and contested royalty-collection institutions. The report identifies five interlocking structural issues: extractive global industry structures, informality and weak local data, opaque royalty systems and contracting practices, undeveloped African touring markets, and limited local capital for business scaling. It argues these constraints apply beyond Afrobeats to other fast-growing genres in the broader cultural and creative economy that are increasingly recognized as economically significant. The report closes with policy recommendations spanning regional regulatory frameworks, local financial ecosystems, touring infrastructure, data strategy, and African-centered intellectual property and contracting models, aimed at helping Nigeria and other African countries convert cultural influence into durable economic value.

detail.title: Product Design Principles for Integrating Sustainable Life Style & Customer Values: Bayesian Analysis using Consumer Inputs

detail.abstract:
This study examines the critical role of post-purchase service quality in enabling or hindering a company's broader sustainability and value co-creation initiatives. While corporate environmental strategies frequently emphasize eco-friendly product attributes, this research demonstrates that foundational service execution—such as timely appliance installation, transparent pricing, and technician professionalism—profoundly dictates consumer trust and willingness to engage with environmental commitments. Utilizing descriptive statistics and Bayesian inference to analyze a substantial customer feedback dataset from two major appliance providers, the study uncovers how systemic operational failures severely erode customer confidence.

The findings indicate that without a solid foundation of trust built on operational excellence, advanced strategic initiatives—including digital gamification for pro-environmental behavior, supply chain transparency, circular economy practices, and AI-driven personalization—are highly susceptible to failure due to escalating consumer skepticism. Ultimately, this paper translates empirical post-purchase insights into cross-cutting product and service design principles. It offers action-oriented guidance for strategic planners and environmental managers looking to successfully bridge the gap between high-level sustainability aspirations and tangible, customer-centric business practices.

title: Mapping the Corporate Mind: A Neural Network-Based Conceptual Analysis of Differentiated Stakeholder Co-Creation in Sustainable Business Model Innovation of a Global Steel Manufacturer

detail.title: Mapping the Corporate Mind: A Neural Network-Based Conceptual Analysis of Differentiated Stakeholder Co-Creation in Sustainable Business Model Innovation of a Global Steel Manufacturer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The study acknowledges the support provided by IIFM Bhopal.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses a central gap in sustainability research: how firms practically manage diverse stakeholder interests to achieve Sustainable Business Model (SBM) innovation. Traditional models often treat stakeholder engagement as a monolithic, procedural task. This study builds on a differentiated theoretical model, synthesizing works by Rathobei et al. (2024) and Ozdemir et al. (2023), to propose a four-part framework. This model posits that (P1) a differentiated strategy is essential; (P2) engagement with secondary stakeholders (e.g., universities, communities) drives eco-social innovation; (P3) engagement with primary stakeholders (e.g., customers, suppliers) drives commercial and process innovation; and (P4) secondary stakeholder pressure (e.g., regulation) acts as a mediating force that compels primary stakeholders to demand sustainable outcomes. This paper introduces a novel methodological lens to examine this model: a conceptual analysis based on neural network (NN) techniques. This paper argues that the principles of NN-based Natural Language Processing (NLP)-specifically text classification and word embedding (semantic proximity)-can objectively map the deep cognitive and linguistic structures of a firm's strategy. This study applies this conceptual methodology to a longitudinal corpus of three integrated reports (FY 2023-2025) from a large, anonymized, global steel manufacturer. The findings of this conceptual analysis show that the firm's own language, as it would be processed by an NN, is highly differentiated. The analysis reveals two vast, semantically distant "continents" of discourse, aligning perfectly with the P2 (Eco-Social) and P3 (Commercial) propositions. Furthermore, it models P4 (Mediation) as a dynamic semantic drift, where regulatory pressures (e.g., "CBAM") are observed acting as a "bridge," pulling eco-innovation concepts (e.g., "green steel") from the P2 cluster toward the P3 cluster ("customer demand"). This paper contributes by validating the differentiated model of stakeholder co-creation and by proposing a powerful, scalable, and objective NN-based methodology for future SBM research, capable of modeling strategy as a dynamic computational and linguistic system.

title: From Sustainable Practice to Sustainability Accounting: A Public Sector Policy Model for Advancing the UN SDGs Through State-Owned Enterprise Governance

detail.title: From Sustainable Practice to Sustainability Accounting: A Public Sector Policy Model for Advancing the UN SDGs Through State-Owned Enterprise Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The work acknowledges the support provided by IIFM Bhopal.

detail.abstract:
This paper addresses the public sector "practice-accounting gap" and governance challenges arising from the "dual mandate" of State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), where clear financial performance often overshadows vague sustainable development targets. Focusing on India, the study uses a qualitative, single-case design evaluating the relationship between the Maharashtra Forest Department (FDM) and its corporate arm, the Forest Development Corporation of Maharashtra (FDCM).

Utilizing the Sustainability Reporting Maturity Model (SRMM), the analysis reveals that while FDCM excels in sustainable practices at Level 2 (Developing), its environmental and social impacts remain unquantified due to a lack of formal accounting frameworks. To resolve this asymmetry, the paper adapts corporate parenting theory to propose a replicable four-point policy model. The recommendations guide the parent entity (FDM) to mandate quantitative Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR), leverage research synergies, incentivize green ventures like carbon credits, and transition oversight to a holistic "Total Public Value" paradigm. Ultimately, this model serves as a practical blueprint for Global South governments to align commercial SOE operations with national UN Sustainable Development Goal commitments.

detail.title: The AI-Energy Nexus: Data Center Demand and the Dynamics of Clean and Traditional Energy Stock Returns

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Accounting & Management Unit Working Paper No. 26-096
publicationDetails.journalName: Harvard Business School: Accounting & Management Unit Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence since late 2022 has driven unprecedented investment in data center infrastructure, creating a direct physical link between AI demand and energy markets. Using daily return data for 2023–2025, we document several findings about the AI-energy nexus. First, clean energy portfolio returns are substantially more correlated with data center infrastructure returns than traditional energy returns are, and data center returns alone explain several times more variation in clean energy returns than in traditional energy returns. Second, the factors that drive clean and traditional energy returns differ markedly: clean energy behaves like a long-duration growth asset with significant positive interest rate sensitivity, while traditional energy exhibits the opposite pattern, and this divergence peaked during the monetary tightening cycle of 2023–2024. Third, in a horse-race between direct AI technology indices and data center infrastructure as explanatory variables, the AI index is fully subsumed by data center returns, suggesting that physical infrastructure rather than AI technology per se is the transmission mechanism linking AI to energy markets. Augmenting standard factor models with data center and interest rate factors meaningfully improves explanatory power for clean energy but not for traditional energy. These findings suggest that AI-driven electricity demand is reshaping the factor structure of energy investing, with implications for portfolio construction, risk management, and the energy transition.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a novel immuno-mathematical framework to address knowledge management (KM) and organizational resilience within volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) business environments. Shifting away from rigid mechanical metaphors, the study conceptualizes modern learning organizations as complex adaptive systems analogous to the human immune system.

Two primary hypotheses are explored:

Hypothesis 1 (Innate Immunity): Decentralized communication and real-time problem-solving facilitated by Online Collaborative Platforms (OCPs) drive faster adaptive responses to novel market shocks.

Hypothesis 2 (Adaptive Immunity): Institutionalizing crisis lessons into organizational memory creates long-term structural resilience against recurring disruptions.

A qualitative analysis of 2024–2025 integrated annual reports from two anonymized corporate archetypes ("LegacySteel" and "Diversified Conglomerate") supports both hypotheses. However, the findings reveal that excessive decentralization risks an "autoimmune response" of internal chaos, necessitating strategic alignment. To provide analytical rigor, the framework incorporates computational biology tools—specifically Agent-Based Models (ABMs) and Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs)—to simulate information propagation, map network constraints, and quantify learning rates. Ultimately, the study highlights that true resilience demands a regulated balance between frontline agility and multi-domain organizational memory.

detail.abstract: Contrary to a long-standing concern, we present evidence that classical benefit-based labor income taxation in the tradition of Smith (1776) is consistent with income redistribution through transfers and negative average tax rates both theoretically and - in plausibly-specified simulations - quantitatively at levels which reflect U.S. policy over the past several decades. As redistribution is widespread in practice, our results remove an obstacle to the benefit principle’s plausibility as a prevailing normative foundation of tax policy.

title: Electricity Market Clearing with Renewable Resources Bidding Risk-adjusted Cost Curves
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Electricity Market Clearing with Renewable Resources Bidding Risk-adjusted Cost Curves
detail.abstract: Renewable power generators typically participate as price-takers in current electricity markets, and market clearing prices are determined by cost curves of conventional generators while treating renewable generation as negative load. In this paper, we analyze a new design of electricity markets where renewable power generators bid their risk-adjusted cost curves into the market, just like the cost curves of conventional generators. We establish that on average, the total revenue of both conventional and renewable generators, as well as the total cost to consumers, under the proposed market is the same as that in current practice. However, compared to current practice, the variability in the total consumer cost is always lower in the proposed market, i.e., the risk of price variability due to uncertainty in renewable generation is not borne by the consumers. Further, under certain operating conditions, the proposed market also results in lower variability in the revenue earned by the renewable generators. We then show how these cost curves should be adjusted to incorporate the risk of shortfall into the bidding and unit commitment process through the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) metric. Using data from the Texas grid, we evaluate the bid curves for renewables and quantify the tradeoff between renewable revenue and cost-to-load. We also study how CVaR-based adjustments for shortfall risk impact allocations and payments at market clearing. While equivalent in terms of average cost and revenue measures, the new market design insulates customers from the price risk associated with the uncertainty of renewable power generation. Further, it allows renewables to be direct participants in the bidding process and bid according to their risk-return tolerance level.

title: A Decent Work Index for Platform-Based Gig Workers: Evidence from Nagpur, India
affiliations: RTM Nagpur University - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Decent Work Index for Platform-Based Gig Workers: Evidence from Nagpur, India
detail.abstract: NITI Aayog estimates that India's gig workforce is likely to expand to 2.35 crore by 2029-30, constituting 4.1 percent of livelihoods in India. The gig economy, specifically the platform economy, provides a non-standard form of employment and exhibits characteristics lying in the grey area of formal and informal employment. These digital labour platforms, both location-based and online, facilitate such nonstandard employment, but the alignment of the work with ILO "decent work" standards remains debatable. Drawing from a sample of 370 platform-based gig workers in Nagpur, this study constructs and computes a composite Decent Work Index (DWI) tailored for such workers. The index comprises five dimensions namely: income security, social security, job security, work security, skill development and representation, with its value ranging from 0 to 1. An overall moderate DWI score of 0.45 is found for the sample, even though significant platform wise variations exist. Mobility (ridehailing) workers report a score of 0.36 indicating low access to decent work standards, while food delivery and home service workers exhibit moderate access to these standards. Based on the dimensions used in the computation of this DWI, three distinct worker profiles emerge: the group which faces precarious work conditions; the second group which have access to moderate decent work standards and the third with relatively higher income but work extralong hours without adequate rest or social protection. The majority of these workers belong to the first and third categories, highlighting that although such gig work provides a basic income security, it fails to meet other crucial components of decent work, particularly social protection and are exposed to algorithmic control in work allocation.

detail.abstract:
Premium beauty has emerged as the highest revenue multiple category in consumer M&A. Industry deals averaged 14.9 times EV/EBITDA in the first three quarters of 2025, more than five turns above the broader consumer industry average of 9.8 times. This paper examines the structural reasons behind that premium and applies the framework to India's emerging premium beauty market.

The analysis is built on three pillars. First, the unit economics: prestige beauty brands operate at 70 to 80 percent gross margins, which structurally subsidises aggressive customer acquisition and supports compounding lifetime value across short repeat cycles. Second, the capital pathway question facing founders, where the bootstrap, venture, and strategic incubator routes each produce different distributions of value at exit. Third, the strategic acquirer landscape, where a small group of companies including Estée Lauder, L'Oréal, Unilever, Puig, Kering Beauté, E.l.f. Beauty, and Shiseido competes for a finite pipeline of clean positioned, founder led brands.

The Indian application is anchored on the January 2025 Hindustan Unilever acquisition of Minimalist for approximately 350 million dollars at a ten times revenue multiple, India's largest all-cash D2C acquisition. The paper argues that this transaction marks the inflection point for Indian beauty M&A and that the pipeline of comparable brands is unusually deep. Case studies analysed include the Shiseido Drunk Elephant writedown, the Puig Charlotte Tilbury extension, the e.l.f. Rhode deal, and the L'Oréal Medik8 acquisition, alongside primary financial data from Sugar Cosmetics, Honasa Consumer, Nykaa, and Foxtale.

detail.abstract: The contraction of entry-level software-engineering hiring has been widely attributed to artificial intelligence and the rise of AI-assisted, or "vibe", coding. This paper examines that account using openly available data, separating two questions that public discussion tends to merge: whether AI caused the recent decline in entry-level hiring, and whether AI has redefined the content of entry-level work. Drawing on longitudinal job posting indices for six national markets from 2019 to 2026 and on corpora of software job advertisements from 2019, 2024, and 2026, it compares the timing of the hiring decline with the timing of AI-related demand and measures and dates the senior-skill content of entry-level postings. Two findings emerge. First, the decline in software-developer postings began from its 2022 peak and preceded the surge in AI-related demand, which began only in late 2024, by roughly two years, a sequence inconsistent with AI substitution as the primary cause of the contraction and consistent with macroeconomic and structural explanations. Second, most advertisements addressed to entry-level candidates ask for at least one senior-level responsibility, led by system design, and this share was already present before generative AI and did not measurably increase, indicating a long-standing structural feature rather than an AI-era development. The paper contributes the CAREER-V framework, which specifies seven durable capabilities and the verifiable evidence by which early-career engineers can demonstrate them. The findings are descriptive, and the measure of senior-skill content is a validated but conservative proxy. AI use disclosure. A large language model (Anthropic's Claude) was used as the classification instrument for the senior-skill content measure, as detailed in Section 4.5, and to assist with manuscript drafting, editing, and analysis code. All study design, analytical decisions, interpretations, and final text are the author's own, and the author takes full responsibility for the content.

detail.title: Below-Market Finance or Benchmark Bias? A Reassessment for Developing Economies
detail.abstract: This paper examines below-market finance as a problem of benchmark construction in international subsidy assessment, using China as a case study. In policy debates, claims that firms borrow below market rates often rely on benchmarks derived from advanced-economy financial structures, external risk-rating conventions, or imposed reference rates. OECD and IMF studies suggest that below-market finance is not a country-specific label, but a broader issue of benchmark specification across different financial systems. The relevant test is whether firms borrow below a borrower-specific benchmark embedded in the domestic market environment. Using Chinese A-share listed firms over 2010-2024, the paper finds that average borrowing costs are not below market; instead, they are about 0.2 percentage points above a China-relevant benchmark based on domestic sovereign yields, rating-matched credit spreads, a domestic adjustment component, and bank-pricing logic. Bank-side evidence supports this result: Chinese banks do not display the persistent profitability distortions expected under pervasive underpriced lending. The findings highlight benchmark misidentification as a source of potential bias in subsidy assessments of developing economies.

detail.title: Precariousness of Work: A Socio-Economic Profile of Gig Workers in Nagpur
detail.abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic profile and income security of platform-based gig workers in Nagpur. Based on a survey of 370 respondents, the findings indicate that this segment of work is primarily composed of a male, young, and educated workforce participating in all types of platforms under study. A significant 56.8% of employees across the three sectors of food delivery, mobility, and home service are classified as income-insecure, earning less tha ₹20,000 monthly. The research shows notable segmentation at the platform level, indicating that food delivery workers experience the greatest insecurity (73.5%). Bivariate analysis reveals an unexpected relationship between income security and dependency burden, implying that workers who have more dependents seem to put in more effort to support their families. Logistic regression indicates that the type of platform is the most important predictor of income insecurity, whereas personal factors such as the age when entering the workforce or income type (primary/secondary) are not. This challenges the perception of gig work as a supplementary source of income addition and emphasizes the systemic precarity of this type of employment. The study ends by presenting these results as a significant obstacle to India's Viksit Bharat mission, contending that sustainable and inclusive progress cannot be achieved without formalizing and guaranteeing dignified earnings for the expanding platform-based workforce

title: Captive Capital: How Private Equity Shapes Insurer Portfolios

detail.title: Captive Capital: How Private Equity Shapes Insurer Portfolios
detail.abstract: We provide the first systematic evidence on how private equity (PE) vertical integration - owning the insurer, managing the CLO, and sponsoring the underlying borrowers - shapes insurer portfolios and CLO collateral. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that acquisition by a PE sponsor that also manages CLOs raises the insurer’s holdings of same-sponsor CLO tranches by roughly 20 percentage points within four years, whereas acquisition by a PE sponsor without a CLO platform produces a far smaller increase. Inside those CLOs, the three largest PE credit-platform sponsors allocate 5-8% of collateral to loans of their own portfolio companies. These effects compound at the most vertically integrated sponsor, whose affiliated insurers absorb a majority of insurer-held same-sponsor CLO principal and tilt toward riskier tranches.

title: AI as Market Law
affiliations: UBS Investment Bank

detail.title: AI as Market Law
detail.abstract: A market is not a model to choose but a law to learn; a neural network is not a model to constrain but a law to discover. When no-arbitrage is built into the architecture of a neural network, the learned pricing object never leaves the space of admissible markets. Expressiveness and accuracy are preserved rather than sacrificed: soft penalties, post-hoc repairs, pre-specified dynamics, and stationarity assumptions all become unnecessary; a single cross-sectional snapshot identifies the market law directly. The same construction scales unchanged across US, European, and Japanese markets, from single to multi-asset universes, attaining mean band coverage above 99.99% within a fraction of the quoted bid-ask over 559,799 option quotes from 2020 to 2026, in minutes on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 with fixed hyperparameters. Held-out quotes are priced within microstructure noise: the same law prices what it never saw.

title: A Bayesian VAR Framework for US Macro-Financial Forecasting and Stress-Test Scenario Design

detail.title: A Bayesian VAR Framework for US Macro-Financial Forecasting and Stress-Test Scenario Design
detail.abstract: Bank stress tests begin from a macroeconomic scenario, a multi-quarter path for output, unemployment, interest rates, and asset prices. This paper builds a reproducible framework, using only public data, that both forecasts the US macro-financial system and generates such scenarios. The core is a Bayesian vector autoregression over eleven quarterly US variables from 1990 to 2024, estimated with a Minnesota prior whose tightness is selected by marginal likelihood. The model is assessed through in-sample diagnostics, impulse responses, a robustness check around the COVID-19 shock, and out-of-sample forecast evaluation against a random-walk benchmark. Adverse scenario severity is set through Growth-at-Risk quantile regressions, which recover the result that tighter financial conditions compress the lower tail of future growth far more than its center. Two findings stand out. First, conditional on financial conditions prevailing at the end of 2024, the data-driven downside is mild, which helps explain why supervisors do not rely on purely statistical tail measures. Second, feeding the Federal Reserve's own severely adverse GDP path through the model reproduces its published unemployment, equity, credit, and inflation paths closely, while its house-price, volatility, and long-rate paths lie well outside what the historical covariances imply, isolating and quantifying the supervisory overlay embedded in the scenario.

title: Identifying scenarios of interest under deep uncertainty
affiliations: Delft University of Technology, Delft University of Technology and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: Identifying scenarios of interest under deep uncertainty
detail.abstract: We introduce Exploratory Modelling and Analysis (EMA) as a framework for macroeconomic scenario analysis under deep uncertainty. EMA traces scenarios of interest from policy‑relevant outcomes. These outcomes are forecasted by a model, based on a large set of uncertain conditioning variables. This approach flips the conventional method of scenario analysis, by sampling many scenarios without imposing strong ex‑ante priors on the choice, combination, value, or distribution of the conditioning variables. Applying EMA with an interacted VAR model to financial stress scenarios for the euro area shows that scenarios of interest can be uncovered that may be overlooked by common approaches for scenario analysis.

detail.title: R&D Competition and Cooperation with Distance-Dependent Spillovers
detail.abstract: We study a continuous-time duopoly model of process innovation with R&D spillovers, comparing noncooperative R&D with cooperative research regimes. We extend the standard constant-spillover framework by allowing knowledge transmission to decay with technological distance and to favor followers over leaders in asymmetric specifications. In a global Markov-perfect model, firms may invest before production is viable, enter or exit production as costs evolve, and converge to no-market, monopoly, or duopoly outcomes. State-dependent spillovers change R&D incentives, catch-up dynamics, long-run market structure, and the welfare effects of research cooperation. In the computed equilibria, more follower-favoring spillovers weaken the leader's private incentive to invest but accelerate catch-up, shorten monopoly phases, and make eventual duopoly more likely. When spillovers are weak, cooperation mainly softens dynamic rivalry; when information sharing is substantial, cooperation expands market formation, lowers long-run costs, and can raise both consumer and total surplus, especially under the research-joint-venture regime. The value of R&D cooperation depends on the direction and persistence of knowledge flows, not only on their average intensity.

detail.abstract: Drawing on feminist political economy and the concept of the reproductive bargain for post-2010s Cuba, this paper shows that the role of the state in social reproduction processes in Cuba has explicitly changed. By analyzing some of the policy implications derived from this transformation, the paper makes a case for the urgency of renegotiating the reproductive bargain between the Cuban government and the citizenry as a major factor for enabling the transparency required to potentially unfold better policies. It highlights the need for transparency regarding the distribution of the costs of social reproduction as a precondition for an integral and comprehensive reform program.

detail.title: Risky Oil: It's All in the Tails
detail.abstract: The substantial fluctuations in oil prices in the wake of COVID-19 and the Russian invasion of Ukraine have highlighted the importance of tail events in the global oil market, which call for careful risk assessment. Using a new set of predictor variables that capture various sources of risk, we show that a machine learning approach delivers the most accurate tail forecasts for the real price of oil. We quantify the role of economic determinants for upside and downside oil price risks and illustrate the practical relevance of our new approach by tracking the evolution of predictive densities during three recent economic and geopolitical crisis episodes and by developing producer and consumer distress indices.

title: Proportionality
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Proportionality
detail.abstract:
Proportionality is often invoked as if the word itself supplies judgement. It does not. In EU law, the principle is neither a universal solvent nor a single test with a fixed intensity. It is a family of justificatory disciplines that operate in different legal locations: Article 5(4) TEU controls the content and form of Union action; Article 52(1) of the Charter governs limitations on Charter rights; the GDPR and the AI Act embed narrower tests of necessity, balancing, risk reduction and remedial discretion; and courts use proportionality to calibrate remedies. This article reconstructs those disciplines as the constitutional law of technological architecture. Its central claim is that power becomes legally intelligible only when the design of an interference can be traced to a lawful and sufficiently precise reason. Does the design of the interference remain within the limits of the reason that justifies it?

The argument proceeds in four stages. It traces the principle from older ideas of measured authority, through German administrative and constitutional law, Strasbourg's fair-balance reasoning, the Court of Justice's general principles, and the Charter. It develops proportionality as a judicial method and distinguishes several modes of review: deferential legislative review, strict rights review, remedial proportionality, infrastructure proportionality, lawful-basis proportionality, safeguards proportionality and explanation proportionality. It reads the hard technology cases as conflicts among rights and legally protected freedoms rather than as privacy against nothing. It proposes a doctrinally grounded protocol for GDPR and AI Act practice. The protocol starts with interference intensity, specifies aims operationally, tests suitability with evidence, treats necessity as a design comparison, makes safeguards constitutive, requires a residual burden review, and insists on a temporal review.

The article rejects both privacy absolutism, including the anti-proportionality rhetoric associated with Max Schrems, and managerial balancing, which treats rights as a negotiable cost in a business plan. Properly understood, proportionality does neither. It disciplines public authorities, supervisory bodies and regulated actors by requiring them to identify the legal source of their power, describe the interference, specify the aim, test causal fit, compare sufficiently effective alternatives, design safeguards and justify the residual burden. The result is not a licence to trade rights away, but a structured account of why a particular limitation remains within law

affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: Making Sense of City Budgets: Grading the Fiscal Accountability of Canada’s Municipalities, 2025
detail.abstract:
• The budgets municipal governments present around the beginning of their fiscal years and the audited financial statements they publish after year-end are crucial for decision-making and accountability. This report card reviews the financial documents of 39 major Canadian municipalities and assesses whether they equip councillors and the public to understand, evaluate and hold governments accountable for their fiscal decisions. It does not judge whether municipalities tax or spend too much or too little – its grades reflect our judgement about how helpful their financial documents are to people who have such questions.
  • The grades in our annual fiscal accountability report card for 2025 ranged from A- to F. Standing out with A- grades for clarity, completeness and timeliness were Markham, Quebec City, Richmond, Saskatoon, Vancouver and York Region. Richmond, along with Iqaluit, which earned a B+, stood out for presenting budgets that followed the same public sector accounting standards (PSAS) used in their financial statements. At the bottom were Charlottetown, Gatineau, Hamilton, Montreal, Victoria and Whitehorse. Their Fs reflected multiple problems with missing information, inconsistent accounting, and timeliness.
  • Notwithstanding instances of late or missing information, most municipalities’ financial statements earned high scores for clarity and conformity with PSAS. But too many municipal budgets provided few PSAS-consistent numbers, and some presented none. Budgets were often fragmented, separating “operating” and “capital” outlays and tax- versus rate-supported activities. Too many late budgets meant councillors approved outlays after the fiscal year had already started.
  • Poor financial reporting impedes democratic oversight and discourages engagement. Cities provide essential services and cost taxpayers significant amounts. Timelier presentations and budgets that match financial statements would raise their fiscal accountability to a more appropriate standard.

title: A Behavioural and Digital Architecture for Operationalising Buddhist Economics
affiliations: Global College (Malta), Global College (Malta)

detail.title: A Behavioural and Digital Architecture for Operationalising Buddhist Economics
detail.abstract: Buddhist economics offers a compelling normative critique of contemporary consumption-driven economic systems, identifying excessive craving (taṇhā) as a fundamental driver of ecological and social imbalance (Payutto, 1994; Schumacher, 1973). However, the literature remains underdeveloped in specifying the micro-level behavioural mechanisms through which individuals transition from consumptionmaximising to sufficiency-oriented practices, particularly within digitally mediated environments. This paper addresses this gap by integrating insights from behavioural economics, specifically nudge theory and choice architecture (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008), with the sociological concepts of the ratchet effect (Duesenberry, 1949) and social contagion (Centola, 2018; Christakis & Fowler, 2009). It develops a novel conceptual framework termed the Sufficiency Nudge Architecture, which reconceptualises digital platforms as potential instruments for cultivating sufficiency rather than amplifying consumption.

title: The End of the World as We Know It? LLMs and the Future of Publish-or-Perish
affiliations: ESSEC Business School

detail.title: The End of the World as We Know It? LLMs and the Future of Publish-or-Perish
detail.abstract: Using a Spence-type signaling framework, this note interprets the Publish-or-Perish system as a screening mechanism through which publications in elite journals reveal otherwise unobservable research ability. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) reduce the cost of producing publishable research, their diffusion may weaken the signaling value of publication by narrowing productivity differences across scholars. High-quality scholars may respond through excess publication, while increased submission volumes may generate congestion in elite journals. The analysis suggests that the future of the Publish-or-Perish system depends on the interaction between signaling efficacy, strategic adaptation, and publication congestion.

detail.abstract: This paper offers a cross-domain systems synthesis of the 2026 US-China artificial intelligence infrastructure contest, framed as a multi-layered strategic game spanning terrestrial energy markets, Middle Eastern proxy warfare, and low-Earth orbit. Challenging the simplistic narrative of a Chinese renewable-energy advantage, I demonstrate that retail electricity price friction (Oxford Institute for Energy Studies) and provincial transmission bottlenecks fundamentally offset China's generation cost edge, while the US small-modular-reactor (SMR) bet constitutes a high-risk real-options call—empirically anchored by NuScale's cancellation despite NRC certification. The paper further models Gulf infrastructure targeting (G42, AWS) as an incomplete-information deterrence game driven by attribution ambiguity, and treats the orbital compute race as a symmetric Prisoner's Dilemma, where Kessler syndrome transforms the rivalry into a tragedy-of-the-commons requiring US-China cooperation on debris mitigation. Behavioral overlays—including loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky), narrative-driven herding (Shiller), and satisficing under ambiguity (Simon)—explain otherwise-rational overinvestment and delayed deterrence policies. The central conclusion is that rival powers should strategically cooperate on the plumbing (orbital traffic) while competing on the compute, while middle powers must adopt deliberately illegible infrastructure diversification to mitigate targeting risk. Includes formal game-theoretic appendices.

detail.title: Seventeen Searchlights: An Original Conceptual Framework for Cognitive Warfare, Strategic Dramaturgy, and Manufactured Surrender
detail.abstract:
2026 "This paper introduces seventeen original analytical concepts developed at the intersection of performance theory, international relations scholarship, and political psychology. They were built across three empirical research projects, on the Taiwan Strait (2016–2026), on intra-state cognitive warfare in Pakistan (2022–2026), and on the cognitive war against Muslim belonging in India (2014–2026), and they are published together here as a unified conceptual framework for the first time.

The five foundational concepts, strategic dramaturgy, narrative fatigue, cognitive surrender, dramaturgical resistance, and the dramaturgical fork, were developed to analyze sustained state performances directed at external or peripheral adversaries under conditions that prevent direct military force. The six concepts of the first extension, democratic maskirovka, weaponized hope, epistemic siege, somatic cognitive warfare, the betrayal performance, and institutional mimicry, were developed to address the specific theoretical problems that arise when a state turns these instruments inward, conducting cognitive warfare against its own political majority. The six concepts of the second extension, civilizational maskirovka, the permanent audition, the model minority cage, the sacred spectacle, historical unwriting, and demographic epistemic warfare, were developed for a third and more demanding analytical situation: a multi-generational campaign aimed not at the defeat of a political movement but at the reclassification of a civilization's claim to belong.
The paper's intellectual foundation is Mieke Bal's (2002) theory of travelling concepts as searchlights, instruments that illuminate what they encounter while being changed by it. Each of the seventeen concepts introduced here was built not by theoretical derivation but by analytical necessity: existing vocabulary failed in front of a specific empirical phenomenon, and a new instrument had to be made. The paper documents that necessity for each concept, establishes its theoretical genealogy, and distinguishes it from the existing terms it most closely resembles. The final section argues that the seventeen concepts, taken together, constitute not a list but an architecture, a framework whose internal logic makes it more than the sum of its instruments", Muhammad Essa (2026)

detail.title: Bimodality Everywhere: International Evidence of Deep Momentum
detail.abstract: This paper examines the prevalence of bimodality in momentum returns and evaluates the performance of Deep Momentum, a machine learning strategy designed to address bimodality, across 45 countries. Bimodality is widespread, persistent, and negatively correlated with momentum profits, individualism, and disposition effects, while positively correlated with turnover and volatility. Deep Momentum consistently outperforms traditional momentum and naïve machine learning strategies, improving performance particularly in countries with higher bimodality, larger sample sizes, and higher volatility. A global model that aggregates data across countries outperforms country-specific models in constructing both global and country-level portfolios, especially benefiting countries with limited samples.

title: The Visible Unspoken: How Displayed AI Reasoning Turns a Mental Health Safeguard Into a Persecutory Stimulus

detail.title: The Visible Unspoken: How Displayed AI Reasoning Turns a Mental Health Safeguard Into a Persecutory Stimulus
detail.abstract: Frontier AI chat products now combine two independently reasonable features. The first is a safety instruction that directs the model never to raise mental health concerns the user has not raised, because unprompted clinical speculation is recognized as harmful. The second is a transparency feature that displays the model's intermediate reasoning trace to the user on demand. This paper documents an interaction effect between the two: the safety rule operates on the output layer while the reasoning display surfaces the suppressed content anyway, delivered in a register that presents itself as the system's private thoughts about the user. For most users this is a curiosity. For users experiencing paranoia or persecutory ideation, it reproduces the precise structure of the feared scenario: an observing entity forming a concealed judgment about them. Drawing on the cognitive model of persecutory delusions, on documented cases of technology themed delusional content including ideas of reference driven by algorithmic curation and delusions of online thought broadcasting, and on interpretability findings showing that displayed reasoning traces are neither faithful records of computation nor genuinely private, the paper argues that the mitigation does not merely fail for its target population. It inverts. The population the rule was written to protect is the population for which the visible unspoken judgment is most dangerous. The paper locates the failure in a layer mismatch, names the general design principle (safety mitigations must be applied consistently across every user facing surface, including surfaces framed as introspection), and proposes concrete remediations. The finding was produced by a disabled independent researcher applying a harm detection framework to the assistive technology he was using at the time, and the paper closes on what that origin implies about who detects this class of failure.

detail.abstract: I analyze optimal contracting between potentially optimistic entrepreneursand value-adding investors such as venture capitalists. Distinguishingability optimism from project-quality optimism shows that both shapesecurity design, but ability optimism has a stronger standardizing effect becauseit creates sharper disagreement over investor support.

Classic Core Banking System (CBS) is designed for low concurrency and highvalue transaction execution (batched, sequential) whereas nowadays required are realtime orchestration and rapid execution of small-value, high frequency micro transactions. This change brings forth increased latency and contention issues in data streams, leading to database deadlocks and bank gateway system degrade, with a high number of transactions to branch delivery ratio. This article outlines a holistic framework-Banking Digital Adaptability Framework (BDAF)-for assessing bank infrastructure against current day demands, under peak load and transaction congestion periods, by building up a Predictive Micro Service Maturity Index(PMSMI) over 5 levels-Basic digital presence, real time digitisation of transaction, core process Integration, prediction data insight and network auto self-healing, which focuses on measuring relative degrees of infrastructure adaptation over classical volume metric analysis, by an empirical simulation modelling server loads using consolidated bank data. The paper concludes that cloud micro service architecture could indeed be instrumental in scaling and strengthening back-end infrastructure capabilities required for current and future retail payments landscapes.

title: When Human Multitasking Meets Agentic AI in Hybrid Service Systems
affiliations: Xiamen University - School of Management, City University of Hong Kong (CityU), University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and Xiamen University

detail.title: When Human Multitasking Meets Agentic AI in Hybrid Service Systems
detail.abstract: Multitasking is indispensable in modern service operations, forcing human employees to divide their limited cognitive capacity across concurrent interactions. While traditional literature views humans as isolated executors who adapt their coping behavior under pressure, the integration of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) fundamentally reshapes this paradigm. In hybrid service systems, human employees retain the operational discretion to dynamically delegate tasks to the agentic AI. However, because effective delegation requires significant cognitive effort, a fundamental tension emerge. The intense workload that drives employees to rely on AI simultaneously degrades their ability to delegate tasks optimally. Thus, it is uncertain whether agentic algorithms mitigate the traditional costs of multitasking or introduce new unintended behavioral failures. We take the first step to empirically investigate how multitasking pressure affects service outcomes in these hybrid settings, and to what extent delegation quality mediates this relationship. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset from a leading smart home company and employing an instrument variable approach, we document that multitasking increases overall sales by 8.17% but severely degrades customer emotion by 0.8 percentage points at the session level. Opening the black box of hybrid collaboration, we reveal that operational pressure acts as a catalyst for both effective task offloading and ineffective workload dumping. For transactional outcomes (sales), the massive informational efficiency generated by effective AI delegation easily offsets occasional human errors, creating a net-positive technological buffer. Conversely, for relational outcomes (customer emotion), while the effective AI delegation successfully buffers the informational demands, the customer's emotional experience still collapses. We resolve this puzzle by decoupling algorithmic failure from human cognitive depletion. We demonstrate that under multitasking pressure, human employees systematically curtail conversational efforts to survive the workload. Specifically, they reduce affective sentiment score by 0.38 percentage points and message length by 0.49% at the session level. This suggests that in hybrid operations, the true structural bottleneck is not algorithmic limitation, but the unavoidable affective and communicative withdrawal of the overloaded human employee. Our findings offer profound implications for service managers to implement dynamic concurrency routing, decouple technical execution from relational repair, and restructure employee performance appraisals, to safeguard customer experience.

title: The CJEU in Russmedia: Much Ado about nothing New?
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) and KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)

detail.title: The CJEU in Russmedia: Much Ado about nothing New?

contentType.other: Published in Privacy and Data Protection

detail.abstract:
The Court of Justice of the European Union’s (‘CJEU’) judgment in X v Russmedia Digital SRL and Inform Media Press SRL (Case C-492/23) (‘Russmedia’) has sparked intense debate. Indeed, the reactions that the decision has provoked are reminiscent of those following the European Court of Human Rights (‘ECtHR’) judgment in Delfi AS v Estonia. To some, Russmedia appears to be merely a reaffirmation of established data protection principles. To others, it exposes a possible gap between the articulation of those principles and their practical implementation.
The judgment appears to have imposed four sequential obligations on the operator of an online marketplace as controller of personal data contained in advertisements published on the platform:
• to determine whether personal data are special category data within the meaning of Article 9 of the GDPR;
• to determine whether the user advertiser is the data subject to whom the special category data pertain;
• if not, to refuse the publication of the ad if the user advertiser cannot establish a valid legal basis; and
• to generally prevent ads containing sensitive data from being copied and unlawfully published on other websites.
Whilst the CJEU made it clear that operators of online marketplaces are under proactive obligations in terms of personal data, the ruling’s full implications remain difficult to ascertain.

title: Advertisers' Self-Competition
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam, George Washington University - School of Business, Goethe University Frankfurt  and Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Advertisers' Self-Competition
detail.abstract: Advertisers in programmatic display markets can compete against themselves for the same ad impression. This competition can occur through overlapping campaigns or multiple supply paths. We study the equilibrium and welfare implications of self-competition in repeated ad auctions with budget constraints, where the supply side determines the extent of bid duplication, and the demand side decides its exposure to bid opportunities. Using a game-theoretic model, we show that duplication affects outcomes mainly through advertisers' budgeting and pacing decisions. Once budgets bind, additional duplication induces more aggressive pacing, leaving prices and advertiser surplus unchanged. We further show that self-competition may benefit advertisers because advertisers' valuations are heavy-tailed. Thus, additional bid opportunities increase the probability of rare, high-value draws, which can outweigh the additional price pressure from heightened competition. We test these predictions using 4.7 million bids from 250,000 auctions on a supply-side platform (SSP). Bids exhibit substantial upper-tail mass, consistent with heavy-tailed valuations. Using a locationscale model, we recover a proxy for idiosyncratic valuation shocks and use it for counterfactual simulations. In the within-advertiser analysis, the expected surplus increases with the number of independent bid opportunities. This effect is stronger under heavier-tailed valuation distributions. In the cross-advertiser analysis, private incentives to duplicate bids persist for a substantial share of advertisers. Our findings challenge the prevailing view of bid duplication and self-competition as inherently harmful and shed light on how budgets, pacing, and supply-chain structures shape advertisers' and publishers' incentives in fragmented information environments.

title: Enhancing Business Analytics with Automated ETL Processes: A Power BI-Driven Data Warehouse Extension

detail.title: Enhancing Business Analytics with Automated ETL Processes: A Power BI-Driven Data Warehouse Extension
detail.abstract: Business analytics programs frequently adopt Power BI for rapid reporting while leaving extraction, transformation, loading, data quality, and metric standardization scattered across individual reports, spreadsheets, and ad hoc refresh procedures. The result is a familiar analytics paradox: dashboards are easy to publish, but trusted and current data remains difficult to prepare. This paper proposes a Power BI-driven data warehouse extension that relocates repeatable preparation logic into automated ETL and governed dimensional layers while preserving the agility of semantic models and self-service reporting. The architecture combines landing and staging zones, Dataflows Gen2, Fabric pipelines, warehouse facts and dimensions, incremental refresh policies, and governance controls into a layered pattern that can be adopted incrementally by organizations with existing Power BI estates. A deterministic workload model illustrates how full-refresh report designs repeatedly process historical rows, whereas incremental and event-driven ETL strategies reduce redundant row work while improving freshness and observability. The paper also identifies design tradeoffs involving Direct Lake, import, DirectQuery, metadata lineage, historical dimensions, data quality gates, and security enforcement. The main contribution is a practical reference architecture and implementation roadmap for turning Power BI from a report-centric analytics tool into the governed consumption layer of an automated warehouse extension.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is a model that has the capability to generate text, images, and other content based on the training and subsequent inputs provided. This new technology has paved the way for significant advancements in technology. There has been a rise in crimes related to the abuse of GenAI, leading to a growing concern around the regulatory framework for the same. However, there is a dearth of literature around the policy implications of the same. This paper presents an overview of the dark side of GenAI, key cybersecurity challenges, and potential solutions for managing this technology. Some key malicious use cases, such as fake text, images, and videos, are discussed, along with Gen AI-based malicious code generation. Potential solutions are presented for these scenarios along with a discussion of SOAR implementation. The paper presents a regulatory framework and roadmap for a proactive approach toward mitigating the security challenges due to Gen AI.

title: The Role of Education in Fostering Global Peace and Humanitarian Action

detail.title: The Role of Education in Fostering Global Peace and Humanitarian Action
detail.abstract: This research paper examines the transformative role of education in fostering global peace and humanitarian action. Drawing on cross-national indicators, peer-reviewed scholarship, and five real-world case studies-Rwanda, Colombia, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Sierra Leone, and Sri Lanka-the paper argues that education is both a structural determinant of peace and a strategic instrument for humanitarian response. Eight visualisations are presented covering literacy and conflict risk, global investment in education, programme-level outcomes, the competency mix of graduate programmes in peace and humanitarian management, and country-specific trajectories of reconciliation, ex-combatant reintegration, humanitarian-aid allocation, and inter-ethnic trust. The paper concludes that scaling investment in peace-oriented education-particularly through interdisciplinary masters and doctoral programmes such as those offered by the Swiss School of Business Research (SSBR)-is among the most cost-effective levers available to states, multilateral institutions, and civil society for preventing violence and rebuilding fractured societies.

detail.abstract:
Modern web-based digital systems operate through a dense ecology of discrete signals—structured transmissions of intent, state, and identity information that traverse collection layers, processing pipelines, consent frameworks, and governance environments. Despite the centrality of these signals to compliance, accountability, and organizational decision-making, the structural conditions under which they become unobservable, ambiguous, or ungovernable have received limited systematic treatment in the academic literature.

This paper presents an observational study of signal-level observability gaps in multiple publicly observable web-based digital environments, drawing on non-invasive browser-level observation and synthesis of governance, audit, information systems, and digital accountability literature. The study identifies and analyzes five categories of structural gap—payload invisibility, consent-state decoupling, identity-state inconsistency, signal propagation failure, and definitional ambiguity—and proposes Governance Observability as a distinct governance construct, arguing that it is analytically separate from technical observability (the ability to log or transmit a signal).

The paper does not identify specific organizations, make legal determinations, or propose a resolution framework. Its contribution is to establish signal-layer observability as a legitimate and underexplored domain of governance inquiry, laying the conceptual groundwork for subsequent theoretical and empirical work, including the development of signal-layer governance frameworks (Jha, 2026).

title: Impact of Flexible Delivery Time Presentation on Customer Ordering Behavior: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
affiliations: , University of Queensland, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information & Systems Management and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration

detail.title: Impact of Flexible Delivery Time Presentation on Customer Ordering Behavior: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
detail.abstract: As lifestyles become increasingly fast-paced, more customers are gravitating toward online food delivery platforms for convenient meal options. With time efficiency at a premium, a critical yet underexplored platform design choice concerns how delivery time information is communicated. This paper examines how the presentation of delivery time-specifically, a flexible delivery time window versus a fixed delivery time point-shapes customer ordering behavior. Leveraging a large-scale natural experiment on a leading online food delivery platform in China and employing a difference-indifferences (DiD) approach, we find that customers presented with flexible delivery time windows increased their orders by 0.16 and their spending by 6.61 RMB per week, compared to those provided with exact delivery time points. To uncover the underlying mechanisms, we complement the field evidence with a series of online controlled experiments. The results reveal that, although flexible delivery windows reduce initial order intentions, they enhance customer satisfaction through two underlying mechanisms: an expectation disconfirmation pathway and an algorithm perception pathway. We further identify an important boundary condition in delivery window size, such that excessively wide windows increase perceived uncertainty and reduce customer satisfaction. Together, these findings offer actionable insights for food delivery platforms seeking to optimize information design, improve customer satisfaction, and increase repurchases.

title: War Emission Protocol - A Scope-W Framework for Measuring the Climate Cost of War

detail.title: War Emission Protocol - A Scope-W Framework for Measuring the Climate Cost of War
