detail.abstract:
Armed conflict remains a structurally under-accounted driver of greenhouse gas emissions, ecosystem degradation, and climate-transition disruption. Although the international community has developed increasingly sophisticated systems for measuring emissions from energy, industry, agriculture, transport, and land use, no standardized framework exists for classifying and quantifying conflict-related emissions and climate-relevant destruction as a distinct category of climate accountability. 

This paper introduces the War Emission Protocol (WEP), a structural accounting framework for conflict-related climate damage. WEP proposes Scope-W as a parallel emissions and damage-accounting category operating alongside existing Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 inventories. The framework defines seven War Emission Components (WEC₁–WEC₇), covering direct combat emissions, military platform fuel use, forest and vegetation carbon loss, wetland and soil carbon disruption, biodiversity-function loss, infrastructure destruction and reconstruction emissions, and human and economic opportunity loss.

The paper distinguishes between two analytical layers. The first is a direct emissions and carbon-stock layer, covering emissions that can be expressed in tonnes of CO₂ equivalent through established physical or land-use accounting methods. The second is a climate-relevant damage valuation layer, covering biodiversity, human, economic, and institutional losses whose contribution to climate-transition capacity requires valuation rather than direct emissions accounting. Together, these layers form the Total War Emission Equivalent (TWEE) and support calculation of Total Compensation Value (TCV) for post-conflict restoration and climate reparations.
WEP does not determine legal responsibility for initiating armed conflict. Attribution of aggression remains the responsibility of competent international legal and political bodies, including the United Nations Security Council, the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, and the United Nations General Assembly where applicable. WEP is designed to operate after such attribution, providing a standardized method for quantification, monitoring, reporting, verification, and compensation assessment.

By introducing Scope-W, this paper seeks to close a major gap in global climate governance: the absence of a formal method to account for the planetary cost of war. The framework does not treat war solely as a humanitarian or security failure. It treats war as a measurable climate-disruption event whose emissions, ecological losses, and transition damages should no longer remain external to the climate accountability system.
The paper further identifies human capital loss — concentrated among working-age men through the demographic structure of conflict mortality — as a causal antecedent of reconstruction emissions rather than a parallel and independent component. This relationship introduces the Reconstruction Capacity Constraint (RCC) as a methodological development priority for future iterations of the framework, and reframes the dominance of reconstruction emissions in Strict TWEE as a structural consequence of war rather than a methodological artifact.

title: Designing Cyber Threat Intelligence Artifacts Using Darknet Hacker Forums: A Systematic Literature Review & Systems Analysis Working Paper 2025
affiliations: Mississippi State University, Department of Computing and Cyber Security, Texas A&M, San Antonio, TX, USA and Montclair State University

detail.title: Designing Cyber Threat Intelligence Artifacts Using Darknet Hacker Forums: A Systematic Literature Review & Systems Analysis Working Paper 2025
detail.abstract: The need for organizations to combat cyberattacks is more urgent than ever. One emerging research approach that addresses this need builds upon leveraging darknet cybercriminal/hacker forums to design cyberthreat intelligence (CTI) solutions. To investigate this design strategy, we conducted a systematic literature review on the use of darknet hacker forums for designing CTI solutions. We provide a comprehensive synthesis of the literature. Further, we adopt a systems perspective and analyze the system development elements in the identified literature based on the input-process-output framework. Our synthesis offers a valuable resource for both researchers and practitioners, providing them with a detailed understanding of the current state of darknet hacker forums-based CTI development, the methodologies employed, and the diverse outcomes achieved. Our analysis comprised analyzing the input (data extracted from darknet hacker forums), process (methods/techniques used for processing/analyzing the data), and output (CTI solutions). In our analysis of the three components (i.e., input, process, and output), we identified heterogeneous and homogeneous elements within each; this served as the basis for categorizing the studies. By offering a structured overview of the field, this paper underscores the different darknet hacker forum-based CTI design approaches found in existing research and additionally suggests directions for future research.

detail.abstract: The entry into force of the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) in January 2025, the subsequent designation of Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud EMEA as Critical ICT Third-Party Providers, and the January 2026 launch of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud have together created a regulatory and technical landscape that did not exist when most prior cloud sovereignty literature was written. This study extends an earlier comparative architecture analysis of Google Cloud Platform and AWS for financial services sovereignty by examining the two providers' dedicated sovereign offerings specifically: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, operated as a single wholly-owned EU subsidiary, and Google Cloud's federated network of national sovereign partners. The two architectures are mapped onto the European Commission's Cloud Sovereignty Framework and its eight weighted Sovereignty Objectives. Galij, Pawlak and Grzyb benchmarked data-sovereignty tooling overhead on Google Cloud and Azure in 2024, then extended that same benchmark to standard AWS regions in a 2025 follow-up; this study treats their published baseline as the empirical foundation rather than re-running it, and instead develops a documentationbased estimate of the cost and performance overhead, the "sovereignty tax," of the providers' dedicated sovereign infrastructure relative to their standard regions, since neither AWS European Sovereign Cloud nor Google's sovereign partner infrastructure is currently reachable for hands-on benchmarking by an independent researcher. An independent replication of the published baseline and a direct measurement inside the sovereign partitions themselves are proposed as future work. The analysis finds that the two providers have converged on the same regulatory target through structurally opposite means: centralized single-entity ownership versus distributed multi-partner ownership, a contrast with direct implications for how financial institutions and regulators should reason about concentration risk under DORA.

title: Assessing The Effectiveness Of Local Government Disaster Preparedness And Response Strategies: Uncovering Gaps In Coordination And Community Participation

detail.title: Assessing The Effectiveness Of Local Government Disaster Preparedness And Response Strategies: Uncovering Gaps In Coordination And Community Participation
detail.abstract: This study examined the local government's preparedness for and response to disasters, with a focus on identifying areas where coordination and community involvement were lacking. To evaluate the implementation of local disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) systems at the community level, the research employed a qualitative documentary analysis approach, examining disaster-related policies, evaluation reports, and scholarly literature. Results indicate that although the majority of local government entities have set up DRRM structures in accordance with national regulations like RA10121, the degree of implementation is still uneven. Response efficiency is still impacted by coordination issues, especially when it comes to agency communication and role clarity. In the meantime, community involvement is frequently restricted to preparedness planning, post-disaster risk reduction, and relief. The study concludes that disaster resilience necessitates not only the presence of formal disaster management structures but also improved inter-agency coordination and ongoing community engagement.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the empirical linkages between regional infrastructure deficiencies, seaport inefficiencies, manufacturing performance, and export diversification across developing economies, with an emphasis on the Pan-African context. Developing countries face structural bottlenecks, including prolonged customs turnaround times, inadequate multi-modal transportation networks, and unreliable power grids, which combine to act as an implicit tax on domestic manufacturing inputs and final exports. Utilizing a gravity model framework augmented with structural logistics indicators, this study quantifies the elasticity of export diversification measured via the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) and the number of unique HS 6digit product codes relative to port dwell times and regional transport costs. The empirical results demonstrate that a 10% reduction in port clearance delays yields an estimated 3.4% increase in manufacturing output value-add and a 2.1% expansion in the export product space. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that port inefficiencies disproportionately harm complex, high-value-added manufacturing sectors, which are highly time-sensitive, thereby forcing developing economies to rely on primary commodity exports. Strategic frameworks for regional infrastructure integration, digital trade corridors, and public-private logistics collaborations are proposed to overcome these structural constraints.

detail.abstract: Why do pre-election polls underestimate rising outsider candidates in Latin American two-round elections? This paper identifies and evaluates the veda-consolidation mechanism: strategic vote transfer toward the most viable opposition candidate during legally mandated polling blackouts. The mechanism can generate large candidate-level errors while leaving bloc-level electoral structure comparatively well characterized. Using a composite-weighted poll aggregation model, the study tests three hypotheses: composite weighting improves on simple averaging; bloc-level forecasts outperform individual-candidate forecasts under blackout-driven consolidation; and errors for the consolidating candidate are directionally consistent across polling firms. Evidence comes from Colombia's 2026 first round (bloc error: 0.36 percentage points; Espriella individual error: 18.4 points), a retrospective comparison on Colombia 2022 (composite MAE 3.4 pp vs. simple average 4.8 pp), and a pre-specified 2026 runoff forecast (Espriella projected at 53.46%; conservative P(wins)=91.4%; 90% CI [49.3%-57.6%]). A benchmark suite and leave-one-out robustness tests confirm results are robust to modeling choices. The framework is extended to 12 Latin American two-round systems with polling blackouts.

detail.abstract: This brief advocates for the Supreme Court to clarify the limits of patent inducement liability in the pharmaceutical context. Recent Federal Circuit decisions—including GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva, United Therapeutics v. Liquidia, Vanda v. West-Ward, and the decision below—have expanded inducement doctrine by treating FDA-regulated drug labels and routine statements of generic equivalence as sufficient evidence of encouragement of infringement. This approach, which amici have described as “infringement by label,” departs from both the common-law foundations of inducement and this Court’s precedent requiring purposeful conduct intended to bring about infringement. Under established principles, inducement exists only when a party affirmatively encourages, recommends, or promotes infringing acts with the requisite intent. Generic manufacturers, however, generally do not draft their labels; federal law requires them to copy the labeling of the reference listed drug, and both brand and generic labels are heavily constrained by FDA regulation. Moreover, prescribing decisions are driven primarily by physicians rather than label text. By grounding liability in mandatory labeling language rather than voluntary efforts to influence prescribing behavior, the Federal Circuit has transformed inducement into a form of strict liability. The Court should reaffirm that inducement requires evidence of intentional, targeted conduct—not merely the contents of FDA-mandated labels.

title: Three Failures: Willingness to Pay, Willingness to Accept, and the Welfare Economics of Community Destruction

detail.title: Three Failures: Willingness to Pay, Willingness to Accept, and the Welfare Economics of Community Destruction
detail.abstract: The gap between willingness to pay (WTP) and willingness to accept (WTA) is conventionally treated in the welfare economics literature as having two independent sources: income and wealth effects within standard microeconomic theory, and the endowment effect from behavioral economics. This paper identifies a third source-lexicographic categorical commitments-and argues that when all three operate simultaneously, as they do in every significant community destruction event, the standard welfare measure is not merely biased but conceptually misapplied to a domain it cannot enter. The central claim is precise: the standard welfare measure fails the deindustrialized community at three independent and compounding levels-and calls the failure objective science. The first failure is the income and wealth effect: willingness to pay is bounded by budget constraints in ways that willingness to accept is not, systematically underweighting the welfare of the poor and those bearing losses. The second failure is the endowment effect: communities are multigenerational endowments whose loss triggers loss aversion at a scale that makes WTA substantially and predictably higher than any WTP measure captures. The third failure is the deepest: for residents whose community is lexicographically prior-not tradeable at any price, not in the domain of compensable goods-the WTA is not merely high but potentially infinite, placing it outside the domain of the welfare measure entirely. The continuity axiom required for utility representability, identified in prior LawQuant work as the hiding mechanism for Bentham's commensurability assumption, excludes this preference structure by definition. Autor, Dorn, and Hanson's China Shock research provides the primary empirical case study: the deindustrialized communities that bore the costs of trade liberalization were not undervalued by the standard welfare measure. They were invisible to it at three compounding LawQuant Working Paper-1 levels simultaneously. The paper extends the analysis to constitutional just compensation doctrine, which systematically undercompensates community and rights-implicating losses for the same structural reason: it applies a WTP-based continuous welfare measure to losses that are WTA-infinite. Patrick Henry's formulation-give me liberty or death-is not rhetorical hyperbole but the precise formal statement of a lexicographic preference that the continuity axiom excludes and just compensation doctrine is constitutionally required to compensate but structurally prevented from measuring. This paper is the operational complement to the LawQuant working paper "The Concealed Axiom," which took down the positive science pretense at the foundational level. This paper takes it down at the level of specific communities, specific people, and empirically documented consequences.

title: Balance of Payments and Capital Flows

detail.title: Balance of Payments and Capital Flows
detail.abstract: In the era of economic globalization, every country is inevitably interconnected through international trade, investment, and cross-border financial transactions. The balance of payments (BOP) is a comprehensive statistical record that systematically captures all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world over a given period. As an essential domestic savings. However, they also carry significant risks: short-term speculative capital movements can trigger exchange rate volatility, financial crises, and macroeconomic imbalances. This paper examines the conceptual framework of the BOP and capital flows, identifies the main types of international capital movements, analyzes the relationship between BOP components and capital flows, and evaluates the impacts of capital flows on national economic stability. The study underscores the importance of sound macroeconomic policy and prudent capital flow management in sustaining economic growth and financial stability.

detail.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables artificial neural networks to adapt to new information while ideally retaining prior knowledge. Despite progress, most CL methods are still evaluated under idealized, unrealistic conditions that fail to capture the complexity of real-world learning. While previous reviews have surveyed continual learning algorithms and categorized strategies, they have not systematically addressed the disconnect between experimental protocols and real-world deployment requirements. In this work, we critically assess the limitations of current CL benchmarks and propose a structured framework consisting of three interconnected components: (1) benchmark datasets that reflect real-world complexity, (2) training protocols that accommodate non-stationary, task-agnostic data streams, and (3) comprehensive evaluation metrics beyond accuracy. We demonstrate critical flaws in widely-used benchmarks, which we reframe as instances of structural information leakage. Drawing on neuroscience principles-including synaptic plasticity mechanisms, complementary learning systems, and memory consolidation processes-we discuss how biological insights can inform more robust algorithm design. Through this review, we aim to inspire more robust, flexible CL systems and evaluation platforms capable of tackling the challenges of practical learning environments.

detail.abstract: This article examines the impact of ESG policy on the capitalization of American companies. The paper explains the concept of ESG and distinguishes between two principal approaches to its implementation: the integration of ESG standards into the operations of already established companies and the creation of businesses whose models are ESG-oriented from the outset. The study compares the experience of ExxonMobil and Chevron with that of Tesla and NextEra Energy in order to assess whether adherence to ESG principles contributes to market capitalization growth. Particular attention is paid to the role of investor expectations, sector-specific factors, corporate strategy, and public positioning. The analysis shows that for large traditional energy companies ESG compliance does not appear to be a decisive driver of capitalization, whereas for companies associated with environmentally oriented business models capitalization dynamics may depend not only on ESG positioning but also on branding, communication strategy, and broader market sentiment.

title: Learning from Limited History: Recency Bias and Risk Aversion to Bitcoin

detail.title: Learning from Limited History: Recency Bias and Risk Aversion to Bitcoin
detail.abstract: We study how investors form their risk attitudes toward novel assets, such as Bitcoin, when historical information is limited. Our portfolio-choice framework shows that risk aversion evolves endogenously as investors update their perceptions of average returns and adjust their portfolio accordingly. Using Bitcoin option prices, we recover the time series of Bitcoin-specific risk aversion and document that its fluctuations are strongly linked to investors' perceived average returns, which are shaped by past realizations. A key feature of belief formation is recency bias: investors place disproportionate weight on recent returns when forming expectations. This bias is markedly stronger in the Bitcoin market than in the equity market, reflecting its novelty and perceived structural uncertainty.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the effect of trade integration on export sophistication is conditional on the quality of domestic legal institutions. Using a panel of 125 countries over 1998–2023 and a fixed-effects design with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, it finds a robust negative interaction between the rule of law and a policy-based index of international integration: the marginal effect of integration on export complexity is positive where the rule of law is weak and turns negative where it is strong, so that deeper integration reinforces existing specialization rather than promoting diversification in institutionally strong economies. The result holds under both static and dynamic specifications, which differ in magnitude but agree on sign, and it survives a decomposition of the integration index and an independently constructed institutional measure. Its central feature is generality: the conditioning does not weaken when the most resource-dependent economies are excluded, so the pattern is not specific to commodity exporters but a broader feature of how institutional quality mediates the gains from integration.

title: War Risk and Time-Varying Return Predictability of the Dividend-Price Ratio

detail.title: War Risk and Time-Varying Return Predictability of the Dividend-Price Ratio
detail.abstract: This paper documents novel evidence that the ability of the dividend-price ratio (DP) to predict market excess returns is contingent on the level of war. We find that DP predicts future returns primarily in high-war periods, whereas this ratio holds no predictive power in low-war periods. This pattern holds across short and long horizons, survives both in-sample and out-of-sample tests, is supported by both statistical and economic metrics, and extends to other standard valuation ratios. To rationalize these findings, we develop a war-dependent present-value framework that links war regimes to DP persistence and return predictability via a mispricing correction channel. Our model shows that in high-war periods, mispricing corrects rapidly, and DP becomes less persistent and exhibits strong predictive power for stock returns. In low-war periods, mispricing persists and DP becomes more persistent, and its predictive power is substantially weaker.

detail.abstract:
The biggest challenge that Asia is currently facing is to balance environmental responsibility and economic growth. Although many of the countries have introduced various green finance policies and ambitious climate targets, they continue to face various challenges due to how their financial system is structured. This report compares the approaches of China, Japan, Singapore, Indonesia, Bangladesh, and Mongolia towards sustainable finance through a comparative case-study analysis. The information used in this study was collected solely from the publicly available data, regulatory documents, central bank publications, multilateral development bank records, and financial news reports.

Through the three case studies, this report developed a Three-Model Framework that consists of the Capital-Market Model, the Command-Control Model, and the Concentration-Risk Model. The framework suggests that each type of market model has its own unique weaknesses in implementing sustainable finance. Despite these problems, a common promise-to-performance gap exists across all three models, where sustainable finance is not defined by the commitments, but rather by measurable and verifiable environmental outcomes. The report further suggests that countries are unlikely to follow only one of the three models, as financial systems, technologies, regulatory frameworks, and climate policies continue to evolve over time. Instead, improving the verification of environmental outcomes should become the next step in strengthening sustainable finance across Asia.

title: CLEIG: An Institutional Diagnostic Framework for Digital Health Data Governance in Africa

detail.abstract:
Background: Digital public health data systems are expanding rapidly across Africa, yet governance frameworks have not evolved at the same pace. Existing approaches emphasise normative principles such as privacy, consent, equity, and sovereignty but provide limited specification of enforceable institutional mechanisms. This gap creates risks of asymmetric decision-making authority, disproportionate value capture by external actors, weak enforcement across jurisdictions, and systematic exclusion of data-origin communities from governance decisions.

Methods: We developed CLEIG (Custodianship, Legal accountability, Equitable benefit-sharing, Inclusive participation, and Governance capacity) through structured conceptual policy analysis informed by institutional governance theory. The framework draws on narrative synthesis of governance literature, African policy frameworks (including the African Union Data Policy Framework and Africa CDC digital health strategies), and applied governance cases from H3Africa, DS-I Africa, Rwanda COVID-19 mobility data governance, and South African national digital health systems. The synthesis followed four iterative stages: open conceptual extraction, mechanism clustering, abductive synthesis to identify stabilised structural governance challenges, and institutional mapping using mechanism-interruption logic. 

Framework: CLEIG translates existing governance principles into five measurable institutional conditions: Custodianship (decision authority in data-origin institutions), Legal accountability (enforceable oversight and redress), Equitable benefit-sharing (fair distribution of value), Inclusive participation (binding inclusion in governance decisions), and Governance capacity (implementation infrastructure). Each domain is operationalised through a 4-point ordinal diagnostic rubric generating a governance profile vector (CLEIG-V) for identifying institutional gaps and supporting policy prioritisation. The framework is proposed as a conceptual diagnostic tool requiring empirical validation.

Implications: CLEIG provides a diagnostic tool for policy engagement and institutional design, enabling ministries of health, data protection authorities, research funders, and ethics review boards to assess governance readiness and target reforms. The framework is conceptual and requires empirical validation through inter-rater reliability testing, cross-country calibration, and criterion validity assessment.

title: Writings, Discoveries, and Composite Authors: A Constitutional Argument from James Madison to AI

detail.title: Writings, Discoveries, and Composite Authors: A Constitutional Argument from James Madison to AI
detail.abstract: Creative acts that discover and express existing but unexpressed realities, synthesizing inherited tradition into genuinely new form, are largely unrecognized in Western intellectual property law. This paper examines that gap across three domains: folklore and traditional knowledge, where the Berne Convention's response has failed; music sampling and remix, where case law has foreclosed rather than accommodated composite authorship; and AI-assisted creation, where human engagement with encoded human tradition produces new expression that current doctrine cannot place. The paper argues that the United States Constitution, read according to its original public meaning, has always had room for these acts. The copyright/patent split is a statutory artifact of the First Congress, not a constitutional command. Authors can have Discoveries. The IP Clause grants Congress authority to protect distributed and composite creative acts through a unified statutory framework, one that recognizes the human synthesis and accounts for the tradition that made it possible. I. A Persistent Failure Across Three Domains The question of who owns a creative synthesis, a work that emerges from human engagement with an inherited tradition, is not a problem the digital age invented. It has recurred across at least three distinct domains of American and Western cultural production, in each case producing legal outcomes that serve neither creators nor the public interest the intellectual property clause was designed to promote.

detail.abstract:
Background: Magnetic resonance imaging is central to assessing axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), but expert SPARCC scoring of sacroiliac inflammation is labour-intensive and difficult to standardise. We developed SPARC-Net (Structured Prediction of axSpA inflammation consistent with SPARCC Network), an automated deep learning framework that operationalises SPARCC scoring as an interpretable, component-resolved measurement of inflammatory burden.

Methods: In this single-centre model development and internal validation study based on a prospectively assembled cohort, 282 patients with axSpA underwent sacroiliac joint MRI. SPARC-Net sequentially performed sacrum and ilium segmentation, SPARCC-defined quadrant partitioning, and component-wise prediction of bone marrow oedema extent, signal intensity, and depth, which were integrated into final SPARCC-consistent scores. Reference standards comprised expert-consensus SPARCC assessments. Performance was evaluated using segmentation metrics, component-level classification metrics, agreement with expert scoring, associations with clinical disease activity, and GE MAGiC-derived quantitative T2 mapping.

Findings: SPARC-Net achieved high anatomical segmentation performance and strong component-level prediction of SPARCC-defined inflammatory features, with overall accuracy of 0·91 and AUC of 0·86 across bone marrow oedema extent, intensity, and depth tasks. Model-derived SPARCC scores showed good agreement with expert scoring. In the held-out test set, model-derived scores were associated with ASDAS-CRP (Spearman r=0·43, p=0·04) and showed concordance with MAGiC-derived quantitative T2 values (r=0·41, p=0·06), with numerically higher correlations with clinical variables than expert-assigned SPARCC scores.

Interpretation: SPARC-Net provides a clinically aligned framework for automated, reproducible, and SPARCC-consistent assessment of sacroiliac joint inflammation in axSpA. By harmonising anatomical localisation with multidimensional lesion characterisation, SPARC-Net delivers clinically actionable, interpretable outputs concordant with expert consensus and quantitative MRI biomarkers. As a scalable digital tool, it has the potential to streamline large-scale screening, reduce inter-reader variability, and support evidence-based clinical decision-making, objective outcome monitoring, and multicentre clinical trials.

title: Overcoming the Transaction Cost Trap: Cross-Sectional Conviction Ranking in Machine Learning Equity Prediction

detail.title: Overcoming the Transaction Cost Trap: Cross-Sectional Conviction Ranking in Machine Learning Equity Prediction
detail.abstract: Machine learning classifiers applied to equity return prediction routinely achieve statistically significant directional accuracy whilst failing to generate positive returns in live execution environments. This divergence, termed here the transaction cost trap, arises because naive threshold-based execution generates excessive portfolio turnover that mechanically destroys gross alpha under realistic transaction costs. Existing literature evaluates most models on gross returns or static probability thresholds, neglecting relative cross-sectional conviction and the structural relationship between execution frequency and net profitability. This paper proposes a Cross-Sectional Conviction Ranking framework that treats calibrated ensemble probabilities as ordinal conviction scores, allocating capital exclusively to the Top-K highest-ranked assets within the universe on each trading day. An expanding walk-forward validation protocol with a two-day embargo governs all estimation, combining gradient boosting, random forests, and a deep neural network into an equal-weight ensemble with isotonic probability calibration. The cross-sectional ranking signal demonstrates statistically significant predictive content (Information Coefficient = 0.0197, t = 1.834, p = 0.034, N = 1,512 trading days). A permutation test of 1,000 randomised cross-sectional probability assignments formally rejects the null hypothesis of random selection (p = 0.001, 99.9th percentile), confirming that ranking skill is attributable to the ML signal and not to portfolio concentration alone. The Top-1 strategy achieves an annualised return of 45.8% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.183, compared to 6.9% and 0.162 for a random selection baseline, with a break-even transaction cost of 24.2 basis points representing a 4.8× safety margin above assumed institutional execution costs. These results establish cross-sectional conviction ranking as a viable and empirically rigorous framework for deploying ML equity signals under realistic market frictions.

title: Who Bears the Burden? Heterogeneous Racial Approval Differentials in U.S. Mortgage Lending: Evidence from Causal Forest Double Machine Learning on 42 Million HMDA Applications, 2020–2024

detail.title: Who Bears the Burden? Heterogeneous Racial Approval Differentials in U.S. Mortgage Lending: Evidence from Causal Forest Double Machine Learning on 42 Million HMDA Applications, 2020–2024
detail.abstract: This paper studies racial differences in U.S. mortgage approval using 42.3 million conventional HMDA applications from 2020 to 2024. Its main contribution is to map how the conditional Black-White approval differential varies across applicants and lending channels, rather than reducing it to a single national number. The gap is largest in the manual-underwriting channel (14.79 pp versus 6.17 pp under automated systems)-a lender-controlled routing decision; this channel contrast is the paper's primary finding. A Causal Forest reveals wide heterogeneity: the estimated CATE distribution has a standard deviation of 8.47 pp. Comparing Black and White applicants at the same lender in the same year still leaves a gap of 7.13 pp (300K subsample), so between-lender sorting does not explain it. The pooled conditional differential, estimated with Partially Linear Double Machine Learning, is 9.39 pp (HC0 SE = 0.07; lender-clustered t =-16.3). Because HMDA does not contain individual credit scores, assets, or reserves, I treat this figure as an upper bound on the conditional differential. The channel contrast does not depend on the absolute level and is robust to this limitation. Standardizing and monitoring manual review may therefore be a more targeted policy lever than broad restrictions on algorithmic underwriting.

title: Flight-to-Safety and Term Spread-Targeted Bond Operations in China

detail.title: Flight-to-Safety and Term Spread-Targeted Bond Operations in China
detail.abstract: In financially segmented economies, declining risk-free rates may fail to stimulate corporate credit. Documenting a severed transmission mechanism in China, this analysis shows that flight-to-safety shocks paradoxically tighten corporate credit. A multi-sector DSGE model with safe-asset scarcity and institutional segmentation demonstrates that safe-asset demand induces deposit outflows, forcing constrained intermediaries to contract corporate lending. This financial crowding-out channel explains the coexistence of record-low Treasury yields and elevated corporate spreads. Targeted "buy-short, sell-long" operations effectively accommodate safety demand and stabilize credit, whereas conventional longbond purchases during scarcity traps exacerbate intermediary stress, thereby inducing a suspension of such operations.

detail.abstract: Energy transition economics asks whether credible climate policy can reduce petroleum dependence before regulations become legally binding. This paper examines anticipatory responses to California's Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) regulation, adopted across 14 U.S. states during 2022-2023, with binding requirements beginning only in model years 2026-2027. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design on a balanced panel of 51 states from 2016 to 2023, we find no significant average anticipatory effect on electric vehicle adoption overall. However, later-adopting states exhibit a 3.9% increase in electric vehicle stock, consistent with a policy credibility mechanism. We calibrate the estimated policy effects into a GTAP-E-Power framework to evaluate global welfare and energy-security implications. Credible electric vehicle mandates reduce petroleum dependence and redistribute welfare primarily through terms-of-trade adjustments, operating through the same transmission channels as major oil supply disruptions, but in the opposite direction. The findings have direct implications for energy security policy in petroleum-importing economies seeking to reduce geopolitical exposure to global fossil fuel supply chains.

detail.abstract:
Background: Out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure (OOPHE) drives health inequities for Australian First Nations Peoples, particularly in rural and remote areas. While financial barriers are well documented, less is known about the cultural, social and emotional consequences of travelling away from Country for healthcare.

Methods: Aboriginal yarning methodologies informed by Knowledge-Interface approaches were used across eleven yarning sessions with 22 Aboriginal participants living on Kokatha, Mirning and Wirangu Country in the Far West of South Australia. Data were analysed thematically through deep listening and iterative coding, guided by Aboriginal researchers and an Aboriginal Governance Group. Findings were presented through three consolidated stories to maintain relational meaning, cultural integrity, and participant voices.

Results: Participant stories revealed how repeated travel for healthcare creates cumulative financial, cultural, and emotional consequences. Leaving Country disrupted kinship networks, reduced cultural safety, and exposed participants to unfamiliar and culturally unsafe environments, contributing to distress and erosion of identity during periods of vulnerability. For many, these impacts led to delayed, rationed, or forgone care.

Discussion: This study extends existing OOPHE literature by foregrounding cultural disconnection as a central mechanism shaping healthcare access. These impacts are fundamental, shaping decisions about when, how and if care is sought, contributing to ongoing inequities and extended periods off Country.

Conclusion: Travelling for healthcare is not simply a logistical or financial challenge but a deeply personal and culturally disruptive experience. Addressing OOPHE requires system-level reform that prioritises culturally safe and locally delivered care and supports on Country.

title: Signaling Vice: Why Looking Bad Wins Votes
affiliations: Maastricht University and

detail.title: Signaling Vice: Why Looking Bad Wins Votes
detail.abstract: We use a formal model to analyze why politicians engage in vice signaling - a deliberate display of bad behavior, transgressive views, or lack of moral integrity. We show that it is possible even when voters prefer candidates with moral character, as long as they are also wary of the candidates who they believe are inauthentic or capable of concealing their immorality. Vice signaling allows an immoral candidate to present oneself as a "bad but authentic" type, implying that the competition is both immoral and inauthentic. This tactic is especially effective with politically cynical voters who are prone to drawing sweeping conclusions about the self-serving nature of political actors. Raising the reputational cost of signaling vice has an ambiguous effect-improving voter welfare, while leading to more low-integrity candidates getting elected.

detail.abstract:
Background: The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region carries the highest diabetes prevalence globally, at 17·6%, with an estimated 1·4 million individuals living with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D). Large-scale characterization of cardiometabolic risk, Steatotic liver disease, and microvascular complications in T1D from this region has not been reported.

Methods: This is a cohort study of 1,233 patients with T1D attending multi-center government endocrinology facilities in the UAE (EHR data: October 2025–February 2026). Comorbidities were ascertained from ICD-10 electronic records. Three pre-specified multivariable logistic regression models addressed three distinct clinical outcomes. Model-level goodness-of-fit (Nagelkerke R2, Hosmer–Lemeshow) and bootstrap-corrected AUROC for the composite cardiovascular score were additionally reported. Reporting follows the STROBE checklist.

Findings: Median age was 23 years (IQR 14–38); 51·6% were male; 38·1% were pediatric (<18 years). Median HbA1c was 9·1% (IQR 7·3–11·1); Approximately 76% of pediatric patients failed to achieve the ISPAD-recommended HbA1c target (≤7.0%), highlighting a substantial gap in glycemic control. ICD-coded MASLD was present in 3·5% of the cohort. Among adults with calculable FIB-4 (n=554), 10·5% had FIB-4 > 1·3 the AASLD threshold, warranting hepatological evaluation, including 2·9% with probable advanced fibrosis (FIB-4 >2·67). The composite cardiovascular risk score based on the multivariable logistic regression models yielded an AUROC of 0·883 (95% CI 0·849–0·917),which indicates good predictive performance of the cardiovascular risk score. Age (OR 1·06, 95% CI 1·039–1·082) and CKD/proteinuria (OR 4·15, 95% CI 1·898–9·068) were the dominant predictors of CVD. Dyslipidemia was the strongest predictor of microvascular complications (OR 2·50, 95% CI 1·712–3·643). CSII uptake was 6·9%.

Interpretation: This is the largest T1D cohort from the MENA region. The findings expose three clinically actionable service gaps: critically suboptimal glycemic control, undetected hepatic fibrosis in adults with T1D, and substantially under-recognized cardiovascular risk in adults under 45 years. National T1D registries, integrated hepato-endocrine care pathways, and expanded access to diabetes technology are warranted.

title: People make One Health. A rapid review of reviews and a global survey for the identification of personal drivers for meaningful action
affiliations: University of Padua, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and World Health Organization (WHO)

detail.title: People make One Health. A rapid review of reviews and a global survey for the identification of personal drivers for meaningful action
detail.abstract: Although One Health is gaining increasing global attention, concerns remain about its limited translation from concept to practice. Several studies have investigated operational barriers, focusing on what hinders the ”how” of One Health action. Less attention has been paid to the ”who” component, that is the people who adopt this approach: what deeply motivates them to shift from appreciating One Health theory to truly doing it in practice? To answer this question, this research combines a rapid scoping review of existing reviews on implementation challenges, with findings from a global qualitative and quantitative survey involving 341 participants working in One Health, who shared their experiences and thoughts about the most effective personal motivations for achieving meaningful impact. First, respondents assessed the 62 potential challenges that had emerged from the literature, and found the most substantial ones in the monitoring and evaluation phase (especially in the area of evaluation), followed by the preparation phase (mostly in relation to funding, evidence, and policy). Then, they identified impact-related motivations as the most powerful ones, especially the wish to make a sustainable impact. Career-related drivers ranked second, while social and professional recognition was not considered relevant. Overall, findings highlight that One Health implementation is fundamentally people-driven. Individual motivations, values, and attitudes play a central role not only at the operational level, but also in shaping broader cultural, systemic, and institutional change. This study highlights the need to place human factors at the core of One Health strategies to achieve a lasting and transformative impact.

title: Visionaries at the Gate: Unlocking Dynamic Merger Efficiencies Through the Market for Corporate Control

detail.abstract: This article addresses how a well-functioning market for corporate control may create efficiencies benefiting the overall economy. We assess how mergers and acquisitions may be manifestations of a market for corporate control, what the performance of private equity investments tells us about the benefits that such a market can unlock, and the implications for merger control. In doing so, we hope to add nuance to the understanding of the role of mergers in promoting dynamic economies.

title: The World in Three  - Cognition and the Uneven Rise of Economic Progress
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The World in Three  - Cognition and the Uneven Rise of Economic Progress
detail.abstract: Long-run GDP per capita data reveal striking discontinuities in the economic history of the world. Western Europe and the Western Offshoots experienced a dramatic acceleration around the turn of the twentieth century, East Asia underwent a similarly remarkable transformation during the late twentieth century, while Africa has yet to experience a comparable economic turn. This paper argues that these trajectories cannot be adequately explained by capital accumulation, technology transfer or geography alone. Rather, they reflect differences in the conditions under which cognition acquires economic force. The Western jolt emerged when centuries of scientific inquiry culminated in thermodynamics, electromagnetism and the embodiment of abstract mathematics within infrastructure and industrial production. Asia's turn reflected a different process. Deep traditions that attached prestige to learning, combined with institutions capable of recursive adaptation, enabled East Asia to absorb and exploit the informational energies of the late twentieth century. India followed a distinct path, investing heavily in theoretical inquiry and fundamental science as civilisational ends in themselves. Africa presents a contrasting historical experience. Postcolonial Africa inherited substantial state machinery but confronted simultaneous challenges of identity formation, nationbuilding and economic transformation under the disruptive conditions of the Cold War and compressed historical time. The paper proposes that Africa's economic trajectory is best understood as one of interrupted adaptation rather than simple underdevelopment. More generally, it argues that economic progress depends upon the capacity of societies to transform knowing into capability, adaptation and collective purpose. The uneven rise of economic progress is therefore interpreted as the visible trace of a deeper phenomenon: the uneven capacity of human ecosystems to convert cognition into historical force.

title: From Hash to Hosting: The Structural Transformation of Bitcoin Mining in the AI Era
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: From Hash to Hosting: The Structural Transformation of Bitcoin Mining in the AI Era
detail.abstract: The Bitcoin mining industry is undergoing a fundamental structural transformation as miners diversify their operations toward artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. This paper provides an empirical analysis of this transition by examining the price-hashrate relationship over a 12-year period (2014-2026) using weekly data from the Coin Metrics CMBIHASH Index and Yahoo Finance. We employ cointegration analysis, Granger causality tests, and structural break detection to evaluate whether the traditional economic relationship between Bitcoin price and network hashrate has been altered by the emergence of AI as an alternative use for mining infrastructure. Our findings reveal a significant strengthening of the price-hashrate correlation from 0.731 to 0.875 across periods, but more importantly, we document a fundamental reversal in the causal direction: hashrate now Granger-causes price at all tested lags (p < 0.05), whereas price does not Granger-cause hashrate (p > 0.26 for all lags). This suggests that miners have transitioned from passive price-takers to strategic price-influencers, with implications for Bitcoin's security model and the sustainability of proof-of-work networks.

title: The Activist-Private Equity Rollover Nexus in Japan: Documented Cases and the Limits of Public Disclosure

detail.title: The Activist-Private Equity Rollover Nexus in Japan: Documented Cases and the Limits of Public Disclosure
detail.abstract: A recurring policy concern in Japan is that activist shareholders may coordinate with private equity (PE) acquirers in take-private transactions—proposing a buyout, then re-investing in the very vehicle that executes it, thereby securing returns that diverge from those of the ordinary shareholders they purport to represent. In June 2026, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's study group on fair acquisitions formally raised this "rollover investment" concern, and a ruling-party project team announced a parallel review. We provide the first systematic empirical assessment of how far this phenomenon can be traced in public disclosure. Screening all 600 tender offer (TOB) filings on EDINET from 2021 to 2026, and identifying acquirers from the structured filer field rather than from full-text mentions, we find that among 68 PE-led take-private transactions, activist re-investment ("rollover") is explicitly documented in four: Trancom (Bain / Dalton), T&K TOKA (Bain / Dalton-NAVF), Topcon (KKR-JIC / ValueAct), and Hogy Medical (Carlyle / Dalton-NAVF). In each, the activist had held a stake above five percent for at least one and a half years—and in one case about four years—before the buyout and then re-invested—twice into the acquisition vehicle (14.40% and 15%) and twice as a limited-partner commitment to the acquirer's fund (up to JPY 28.05 billion in one case, and an indirect interest of up to roughly 20% in the other). These four correspond directly to the two forms the policy debate identifies, each represented twice. We emphasize what the data cannot show: a time-series pattern of "activist holds, then PE acquires" does not identify coordination—we document would-be matches that dissolve on inspection, where the activist was simply a co-investor in the same undervalued target, or where a full tender obscured a separately documented re-investment—and rollover through limited-partner commitments or fund-of-fund structures is largely outside the disclosure perimeter. The documented rate (four of sixty-eight, or 5.9%) is therefore a lower bound on a phenomenon that is, by construction, only partially observable. Documented rollover is, moreover, only one form of activist–PE coordination—the capital form that disclosure happens to record; coordination effected through deal structuring or through information-sharing below the disclosure threshold lies outside what our method can observe. Our contribution is to delineate precisely what public disclosure can and cannot reveal about activist–PE capital ties, at the moment Japanese policymakers are deciding how to regulate them.

title: Breaking the 'Pink Ceiling': Does Digital Financial Literacy Moderate the Impact of Government Schemes on Women's Entrepreneurial Perception?

detail.title: Breaking the 'Pink Ceiling': Does Digital Financial Literacy Moderate the Impact of Government Schemes on Women's Entrepreneurial Perception?
detail.abstract: India's flagship women's entrepreneurship schemes-Stand-Up India and Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana-have collectively sanctioned hundreds of millions of loans, yet only one percent of women entrepreneurs have successfully accessed them. This study investigates whether digital financial literacy explains the gap between policy design and ground-level reach by testing its moderating role in the relationship between government scheme awareness and women's entrepreneurial engagement. Using primary cross-sectional survey data from 580 women across five National Capital Region districts and hierarchical logistic regression, the study finds that digital financial literacy positively and significantly moderates the awareness-entrepreneurship relationship: scheme awareness substantially amplifies entrepreneurial outcomes among digitally literate women but has minimal effect among those without digital skills. A complementary mechanism test confirms that higher digital literacy reduces reliance on personal connections with bank officials by 30 percent-empirical support for a 'digital bypass' of traditional social capital gatekeeping. The findings operationalize Sen's Capability Approach: digital financial literacy is the conversion factor that transforms scheme awareness from a latent resource into actionable entrepreneurial capability. Policy implications point toward mandatory co-delivery of digital literacy training within scheme rollout, rather than treating the two as separate interventions.

title: E-GEO: A Testbed for Generative Engine Optimization in E-Commerce
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Decision Risk and Operations

detail.title: E-GEO: A Testbed for Generative Engine Optimization in E-Commerce
detail.abstract: With the rise of large language models (LLMs), generative engines have become powerful alternatives to traditional search, reshaping retrieval tasks. In e-commerce, for instance, conversational shopping agents now guide consumers to relevant products. This shift has created the need for generative engine optimization (GEO)---improving content visibility and relevance for generative engines. Despite its growing importance, current GEO practices are largely ad hoc, and their impacts remain poorly understood, especially in the e-commerce setting. We address this gap by introducing E-GEO, the first dataset built specifically for e-commerce GEO. E-GEO contains 13,747 realistic, multi-sentence consumer product queries, each paired with 10 retrieved Amazon listings, capturing rich intent, constraints, preferences, and shopping contexts that existing datasets miss. Using this dataset, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of e-commerce GEO across five representative generative engines, seven popular LLM rewriters, and fifteen hand-crafted rewriting heuristics. We further formulate GEO as an optimization problem and develop a lightweight prompt meta-optimization algorithm that significantly improves over heuristic baselines. Notably, the optimized prompts reveal a stable, domain-agnostic pattern, suggesting the existence of a "universally effective" GEO strategy. Finally, we red-team the GEO system through both heuristic and optimization-based attacks and show that, under a simple in-prompt defense, gains from GEO reflect genuine content improvement rather than manipulation, anchoring GEO as a substantive and well-defined optimization problem.

title: The Boardroom Link: Board Composition and Stock Performance Evidence from NSE-listed Companies

detail.title: The Boardroom Link: Board Composition and Stock Performance Evidence from NSE-listed Companies
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether board size is associated with stock-market performance among firms listed on the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE). Using a cross-section of 50 NSElisted companies, stock performance is measured as the mean daily closing price over the 2023 calendar year and related to board size, defined as the number of directors on the board. Pearson correlation analysis is conducted for the full sample and separately for three board-size bands: small (fewer than 10 directors), medium (10 to 12 directors), and large (more than 12 directors). For the full sample, board size and the mean stock price exhibit a positive correlation (r = 0.275). The relationship is not uniform across bands: small boards show a weak positive correlation (r = 0.162), large boards show the strongest positive correlation (r = 0.369), while medium-sized boards show a near-zero correlation (r =-0.026). This near-zero association in the medium band, here termed a "dead zone" in which incremental board size bears no linear relationship with valuation, is the paper's principal contribution. It is consistent with a nonmonotonic link between board size and market performance in an emerging-market setting and suggests that, within the most common board-size range, composition characteristics beyond headcount dominate. None of the correlations is statistically significant at the 5% level on a two-tailed test, and the full-sample coefficient is marginal (p = 0.053); the patterns are therefore presented as descriptive associations rather than established effects. The findings inform the corporate-governance debate on optimal board structure in India and motivate multivariate and longitudinal extensions.

title: Regulating intelligence: Shareholder value effects of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
affiliations: , The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School, The University of Manchester - Manchester Business School and The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School

detail.title: Regulating intelligence: Shareholder value effects of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
detail.abstract: We examine the shareholder value implications of the European Union (EU) Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act, the world’s first comprehensive AI regulation. Using a global sample of AI-intensive firms, we document negative stock price reactions around key legislative events. Consistent with expectations, firms with stronger financial health, lower information asymmetry, and first-mover AI advantages experience less adverse stock returns. However, contrary to expectations, we find no evidence that the Act generates legitimacy benefits by reassuring stakeholders about the responsible development and use of AI. Instead, firms with larger pre-existing legitimacy deficits react more negatively, consistent with investor concerns that the regulation may expose unethical AI practices. Overall, our findings suggest that comprehensive technology regulation may unintentionally concentrate innovation rents among incumbent firms by raising barriers to entry and reinforcing market power in emerging industries, without generating offsetting legitimacy gains.

title: Regulating AI Procurement in the Public Sector: Lessons from Defence, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice

detail.title: Regulating AI Procurement in the Public Sector: Lessons from Defence, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice
detail.abstract: Governments are among the largest buyers of artificial intelligence systems, yet public sector AI procurement remains ad hoc, poorly standardized, and frequently captured by vendor marketing narratives that promise transformation while obscuring risk. This paper examines AI procurement practices across three high-stakes government domainsdefence, healthcare, and criminal justice-identifying four systematic failures that collectively constitute what this paper terms the Public Sector AI Procurement Gap: evaluation criteria optimized for cost and delivery speed rather than for fairness, transparency, and long-term performance; vendor evaluation frameworks that lack the technical depth to assess model quality, bias, and robustness; contracts that fail to specify performance degradation thresholds, retraining obligations, or liability allocation for algorithmic harm; and accountability vacuums when deployed AI systems produce harmful outcomes with no clear institutional owner of responsibility. Drawing on procurement case studies from the US Department of Defense's AI acquisition programs, the UK National Health Service's AI deployment initiatives, and Indian criminal justice and social welfare AI pilot programs, the paper proposes the Public Sector AI Procurement Standard (PSAPS)-a five-component framework that includes mandatory algorithmic impact assessments, independent technical evaluation, AI-specific contract clauses, continuous performance monitoring, and structured accountability allocation. The paper argues that procurement reform is the most effective and politically feasible lever for improving public sector AI governance-more impactful than broad AI legislation (which takes years to enact), more specific than ethical guidelines (which lack enforcement), and more actionable than regulatory frameworks (which require institutional infrastructure most governments lack). The paper concludes with implications for government procurement officers, public policy researchers, AI vendors selling to government, and civic technology advocates.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces the organizational skeleton as a structural framework for understanding how organizational systems simultaneously enable stability and generate conditions that progressively constrain adaptation. While dominant explanations of organizational decline often emphasize managerial inefficiencies-commonly framed as "big company disease"-this paper argues that such symptoms are better understood as surface manifestations of deeper structural mechanisms embedded within organizations. The organizational skeleton is defined as the relatively durable configuration of structures, routines, governance arrangements, and institutional mechanisms that provide coherence, scalability, and continuity in complex organizations. Although essential for organizational functioning, these structures tend to accumulate structural rigidity over time. Rather than treating rigidity as a managerial failure, the paper conceptualizes it as an emergent property of organizational evolutionarising from the very mechanisms that produce organizational success. Building on this structural perspective, the paper introduces organizational self-renewal as the capacity to periodically reassess and reconfigure internal architectures in response to accumulated rigidity and environmental change. Self-renewal is therefore not an exceptional organizational event, but a recurring systemic requirement for maintaining adaptive capacity in complex environments. Through comparative conceptual illustrations from global enterprises including Nokia, Kodak, Boeing, Toyota, Haier, BHP, Fonterra, and General Motors, the paper demonstrates how structural success may paradoxically generate long-term adaptive constraints, and how different organizations vary in their capacity to manage this structural tension. The paper argues that long-term organizational sustainability depends not on the elimination of structural rigidity, but on the continuous management and periodic renewal of the organizational skeleton itself. This reframes organizational change not as episodic reform, but as an ongoing structural recalibration embedded within organizational evolution. The paper thus reframes organizational decline not as a failure of management, but as a failure of structural diagnosisshifting the question from "who made the wrong decision" to "what has the skeleton become." This reframing positions skeletal rigidity not as an alternative to existing theories, but as the structural condition beneath them.

title: 24-Cell Polytope as an Early Warning System for Market Criticality: cosD Precedes VIX by 211 Days Across Three Financial Crashes

detail.abstract: We apply the Watabe-Claude Method (WCM), a 4D geometric analysis framework based on the 24-cell regular polytope, to financial market data spanning 2005-2024. The 4D feature space encodes log return, realized volatility, TED credit spread, and volume ratio as spatial coordinates. We conduct a retrospective analysis of three major market crises: the 2008 Lehman Brothers collapse, the 2020 COVID-19 crash, and the 2022 Federal Reserve rate hike shock. Our principal finding (Finding FIN-4) is that the cosD indicator, derived from the cosine similarity of the 24-cell shape vector to the uniform distribution, precedes the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) peak by an average of 211 days across all three crashes (+216, +167, and +249 days respectively). This 7month lead time suggests that the geometric concentration of the 4D market state within the 24cell framework captures structural pre-critical dynamics that are not yet reflected in implied volatility. We additionally report that D_eff (effective fractal dimension) behaves as a market chaos diversity index, rising during acute crashes (Lehman: 2.172, COVID: 1.572) while remaining low during chronic downtrends (Fed Hike: 0.155). These results extend WCM's demonstrated applicability from seismic precursor detection and climate attractor analysis to financial market early warning.

title: Flow Control Rewrites Globalization. Implications for Business and Investors

detail.abstract: Today's international order has enabled and has been shaped by the free flow of goods, services, data, and capital and the unrestricted movement of people. These global exchanges have created strategic flows that have advanced prosperity and deepened connectedness. But the fraying international order gives rise to a more skeptical view on connectedness. Rather than emphasizing the benefits and opportunities, a prevailing zero-sum logic underlines and exploits the vulnerabilities of dependence. That is why nations, in particular ambitious emerging status quo challengers, are focusing increasingly on flow control. Flow control describes the will and the capability of an actor to define the framework and the operational conditions for strategic flows. As the paper discusses in detail, flow control is the testing ground on which a new grand systemic competition is emerging.

title: A Framework for Social Order: Empirical Evidence and Conditional Prescriptions

detail.title: A Framework for Social Order: Empirical Evidence and Conditional Prescriptions
detail.abstract: Across every domain of human life — law, politics, economics, culture, and personal behavior — outcomes are driven by the same underlying architecture: belief, power, and behavior. Yet no unified framework exists that explains how these fundamentals operate, what biological forces shape them, or how they produce meaning. This thesis proposes a natural‑law‑based model that identifies the universal variables governing human action. Existing theories of meaning rely on cultural, religious, or philosophical assumptions. None provide a biologically grounded, universally applicable structure that explains how meaning emerges from the interaction of natural law and human fundamentals. This thesis identifies three fundamentals — belief, power, and behavior — and demonstrates how they are shaped by a set of biological derivatives operating under the constraints of natural law. Meaning is not treated as a metaphysical truth, but as an emergent property of this system. A unified behavioral framework has implications for governance, negotiation, legal reasoning, and social stability. By grounding human action in natural law rather than ideology, this model provides a consistent basis for decision‑making across institutions and communities. The purpose of this thesis is to define the fundamentals, identify the biological derivatives that shape them, and demonstrate how meaning emerges as a structural output of the system.

title: Public Order, Morality, and their Religious Foundations in Patent Law

detail.title: Public Order, Morality, and their Religious Foundations in Patent Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: in E. Bonadio, N. Lucchi; B. Khan (eds), IP & Religion (Forthcoming, Hart Publishing, 2026)

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the public order and morality exclusions in patent law, as codified in TRIPS Article 27(2), EPC Article 53(a), and EU Directive 98/44/EC, and develops a genealogical account of their religious foundations. Drawing on Christian natural-law thought, Catholic social teaching, and the role of church organisations in shaping EU biotechnology legislation, it argues that concepts such as human dignity, the sanctity of life, and the non-commodifiability of the human body entered patent law not as neutral secular values, but as translated theological commitments. The chapter traces how those commitments migrated from theological anthropology into European biolaw through instruments such as the Oviedo Convention and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, and how they informed landmark rulings, including Brüstle v Greenpeace. It then examines morality exclusions in practice through disputes over embryos, germline modification, and gene editing, while comparing how different jurisdictions structure morality review. The chapter argues that the religious genealogy of these exclusions is not incidental to their interpretation; it is the condition under which their application to contested biotechnology cases can be both honest about its normative premises and accountable to the plurality of moral perspectives present in contemporary legal orders.

detail.title: The Stability Pivot: Proactive Monetary Policy and Exchange Rate Management in Indonesia (2016-2026)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution of Bank Indonesia's monetary policy framework from a reactive stance to a proactive "Stability Pivot" during the period 2016-2026. Utilizing GARCH(1,1) volatility modeling and cross-asset correlation analysis, we evaluate the effectiveness of yield spread management in anchoring the USD-IDR exchange rate against global interest rate shocks. Our findings reveal a significant inverse correlation (-0.58) between the BI-US 10Y yield spread and Rupiah depreciation, identifying a 1.5% spread floor as a critical threshold for macro-financial stability. While the hike cycles of 2023-2024 necessitated a tactical trade-off in equity performance (IDX Composite), the results demonstrate a marked reduction in conditional volatility compared to the 2020 pandemic era. This study concludes that the proactive maintenance of yield differentials effectively decoupled local market risk from global tightening cycles, providing a strategic blueprint for emerging market resilience in a "higher-for-longer" interest rate environment.

title: Peer Profitability Sentiment and Strategic Earnings Announcement Delay: Evidence from Quarterly Reporting Decisions
affiliations: , IBS Hyderabad (A Constituent of the ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education, a Deemed University) and IBS Hyderabad (A Constituent of the ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education, a Deemed University)

detail.title: Peer Profitability Sentiment and Strategic Earnings Announcement Delay: Evidence from Quarterly Reporting Decisions
detail.abstract: Quarterly earnings announcements unfold sequentially: each peer disclosure reshapes the information environment facing firms yet to report. Prior research documents that delay reflects strategic choices conditioned on firm-specific bad news, but whether the profitability content of sequential peer disclosures conditions reporting timing — distinct from peer occurrence — remains unexamined. This study introduces a dynamic peer-profitability disclosure framework that draws on strategic disclosure, investor attention, peer effects, and governance-monitoring perspectives to examine managerial responses to evolving industry profitability sentiment. Using 82,044 firm-quarter observations from 3,258 Indian listed firms during 2010–2025 — where mandatory quarterly reporting, concentrated promoter ownership, and thin institutional monitoring make peer-profitability signals observable and strategically consequential — the study employs Dynamic Industry ROA, a measure conditioned on already-reporting peers, across delay and governance-moderation specifications. The findings reveal a threshold mechanism: mild adversity generates a differentiation response among favorable-news firms, while severe distress activates a camouflage effect. Earnings-flow vulnerability amplifies delay while balance-sheet leverage does not, indicating that informational commensurability with peer profitability content — not financial structure — activates delay incentives. Institutional investor oversight and audit quality constrain peer-conditioned delay while formal board independence does not, reflecting the divergence between governance form and monitoring capacity in concentrated-ownership markets. Three contributions follow: peer-profitability content is established as a conditioning variable distinct from peer occurrence; a threshold nonlinearity extends avoidance logic from earnings management to disclosure timing; and external market-based monitoring is the operative governance constraint — with implications for regulatory design and investor interpretation of reporting lags.

title: Networked Risk Perception and Behavioral Bubbles: The Case of a Pandemic
affiliations: Northeastern University (USA), Paris School of Economics (PSE), Northwestern University and Northeastern University

detail.title: Networked Risk Perception and Behavioral Bubbles: The Case of a Pandemic

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation under Award No. 2421289 (IHBEM: "No One Lives in a Bubble: Incorporating Group Dynamics into Epidemic Models")

detail.abstract: Risk perception is typically modeled as an individual cognitive readout of objective hazard. Yet during crises what people judge as risky is shaped by what their peers do, making risk perception in part a property of communities, not just individuals. Using weekly mobility data from 313 Massachusetts municipalities over the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic and a pre-pandemic inter-town mobility network that fixes interaction structure before the shock, we estimate twoway fixed-effects panel regressions that separate the response to local case incidence, inter-town behavioral spillover along the mobility network, and within-town behavioral inertia; the preshock network and a lagged peer signal address the standard reflection and endogenous-group concerns. Inter-town behavioral spillovers are substantial and localize almost entirely within mobility-defined communities (the empirical referent of behavioral bubbles), with effectively no propagation across community boundaries. The within-community spillover carries behavioral content beyond what peer-town case information alone would predict: when network-exposureto-cases and network-exposure-to-behavior are raced, the behavioral channel survives and the case-exposure channel goes null. A four-way decomposition by mobility and demographic similarity shows the spillover requires both, concentrating where towns are routinely connected and socioeconomically similar and vanishing between similar towns that are not connected, which points to an observational and normative channel rather than a purely informational one. These results recast risk perception as a networked phenomenon and identify mobility-defined communities, rather than administrative units, as the operative scale of behavioral response. The pattern should generalize wherever exposure is uncertain, evolving, and socially negotiated, including climate adaptation and financial contagion.

detail.title: Integration of Crop, Livestock Farming and Food Security: Evidence from Households in South Kivu ​
detail.abstract: This article assesses the impact of livestock integration on the food security of agricultural households in South Kivu. The data used comes from a cross-sectional database collected through a stratified random survey of 1,498 farming households, conducted by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) between October and December 2014, and is based on a sample of 402 farming households. Using propensity score matching, the results show that households that combine livestock farming with crop production have a dietary diversity score that is 14.3% higher than that of households with similar socio-economic characteristics but without livestock. These results confirm the initial hypothesis that livestock has a positive effect on the food security of households in the study area. The findings of this study suggest strengthening development policies and actions focused on promoting livestock farming to improve the food security and livelihoods of farming households.

title: Phenotypic Characterization, Morphometric Diversity, and Live Weight Prediction of Indigenous Turkeys across Ecological Zones of Ghana
affiliations: Wesley College of Education, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana and Jiangsu University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Phenotypic Characterization, Morphometric Diversity, and Live Weight Prediction of Indigenous Turkeys across Ecological Zones of Ghana
detail.abstract: AbstractIndigenous turkeys are an important component of Ghana’s animal genetic resources, yet information on their phenotypic diversity across ecological zones remains limited. This study characterized qualitative and quantitative traits of indigenous turkeys across five ecological zones: Coastal Savanna, Transitional Zone, High Rainforest, Guinea Savanna, and Semi-Deciduous Rainforest. A total of 350 mature turkeys (200 females and 150 males) were evaluated using FAO phenotypic descriptors and morphometric measurements. Qualitative traits were analyzed using chi-square tests, while quantitative traits were subjected to analysis of variance, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis (PCA), and principal component regression.Significant ecological variation (p < 0.05) was observed in plumage, beak, shank, and eye colour, indicating phenotypic differentiation among populations. Morphometric traits also varied significantly across zones. Turkeys from the High Rainforest and Semi-Deciduous Rainforest exhibited superior growth traits, including higher live weight, larger chest circumference, wider wingspan, and longer shanks, whereas Guinea Savanna birds showed greater body and neck lengths, suggesting environmental adaptation. Pronounced sexual dimorphism was evident, with males generally larger than females. Live weight was positively associated with wingspan length, shank length, and chest circumference (p < 0.01).PCA extracted three components explaining 85.8% of total variation, with body robustness identified as the strongest predictor of live weight (R² = 0.380; p < 0.001). These findings highlight substantial phenotypic diversity and provide a basis for conservation and genetic improvement programmes.

title:
Emerging Threats: Artificial Intelligence and the Potential for Bioterrorism in the Digital Age
