detail.title:
Emerging Threats: Artificial Intelligence and the Potential for Bioterrorism in the Digital Age 
Navigating Risks, Theory, and Countermeasures in the Era of AI-Driven Biowarfare
detail.abstract:
The emergence of large language models and generative AI systems presents a significant and underexplored threat to biosecurity. While bioterrorism has been historically rare in its occurrence and restricted by the high-level expertise required for weapon creation and deployment, AI systems are bridging the knowledge gap between expert competence and general accessibility, fundamentally altering the risk calculus. This paper examines how the integration of artificial intelligence may be exploited by terrorist actors to plan and execute bioterrorist attacks, with a focus on the mechanisms by which AI lowers the barriers that have historically contained such threats.  

 

Drawing on historical analysis of bioterrorism and covert poisoning incidents, a conceptual framework of terrorist learning, emulation, technology adoption, and definition of success, and an assessment of current large language model capabilities, this paper identifies the conditions under which AI-enabled bioterrorism becomes operationally viable. Findings indicate that the rarity of historical bioterrorism attacks relative to covert poisonings is primarily attributable to the absence of high-level expert knowledge in non-state actor networks, a gap that generative AI systems look to fill. Further, contrary to Adoption Capacity Theory’s prediction that demanding technologies are unlikely to be adopted, external pressures including councounterterrorism policyterterrorism competition and inter-group rivalry are shown to drive terrorism technology adoption regardless of complexity. 

 

These findings have direct implications for AI governance and biosecurity policy. This paper argues that open-weight AI systems require specific regulatory attention, including scrutiny of training data sets and identity verification mechanisms for high-risk query categories. The research underscores the pressing need for interdisciplinary collaboration between AI governance, biosecurity, and counterterrorism policy communities to address emerging threats before operational adoption occurs.

detail.title: Rights and Challenges in the Technological Domain: Navigating the Transformations of Digital Property

publicationDetails.detailsText: in C. Bevan (ed), Research Handbook on Property, Law and Theory (Edward Elgar 2024) 394–405.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the challenges that digital technology poses to established frameworks of property and intellectual property law. Starting from the observation that digitization has dissolved the physical anchors of ownership, it traces the conceptual and legal consequences of the shift from possession to access as the dominant mode of engaging with content. The chapter surveys the historical development of copyright law, from Gutenberg through the Berne Convention and the WIPO era, highlighting how intellectual property protection has progressively prioritized private interests over the public domain. It then analyses the regulatory landscape governing digital content, including the roles of Internet intermediaries, graduated response systems, and content-filtering obligations. The chapter concludes that the disruptive impact of the digital revolution requires a fundamentally new perspective on copyright, one that elevates exceptions and limitations to a central rather than peripheral function and embraces regulatory flexibility as the condition for sustaining creative and digital ecosystems.

title: Trends in Income Inequality in India: Evidence from Periodic Labour Force Surveys

detail.title: Trends in Income Inequality in India: Evidence from Periodic Labour Force Surveys
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the mechanisms that sustain the gender wage gap in India's regular salaried labour market. We combine a theoretical model of statistical discrimination, where gender bias and imperfect skill observability create wage disparities, with an empirical analysis of seven rounds of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) from 2017-18 to 2023-24. A Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition reveals that the mean wage gap is not driven by differences in endowments; the explained component is negligible. Instead, over 90% of the gap is unexplained, stemming from differential returns to characteristics. To analyze the gap's structure, we employ a Recentered Influence Function (RIF) decomposition. The results consistently confirm a sticky floor. The wage gap is largest at the 25th percentile, penalizing low-earning women most severely. Conversely, at the 75th percentile, we find high-earning women possess superior observable endowments, yet a massive and discriminatory unexplained component overwhelms this advantage. We pinpoint the primary channel of discrimination as intra-occupational; the gap is not due to occupational segregation but to unequal pay within the same job categories, a penalty that is most highest at the top of the distribution. The major finding of the paper, through the theoretical model validated by the empirical analysis, shows that although the raw income gap keeps falling as we move up the income distribution ladder, the contribution of discrimination sustaining that wage gap keeps on increasing as well. This implies that, although there might be some skill-based differences at the lower end of the income distribution between male and female workers, the gap is mostly sustained by pure discriminatory effects at the top.

title: The Concealed Axiom: Bentham's Normative Choice and the Positive/Normative Distinction in Economics

detail.title: The Concealed Axiom: Bentham's Normative Choice and the Positive/Normative Distinction in Economics
detail.abstract: Introductory economics textbooks present welfare analysis as positive science-a technical description of how markets allocate resources and generate well-being. This paper argues that the foundational welfare measure embedded in that analysis encodes a normative choice made by Jeremy Bentham in the late eighteenth century: that human welfare is reducible to a scalar quantity derived from the satisfaction of preferences, that preferences are commensurable, and that their aggregation across persons is legitimate. The technical development of welfare economics through Pareto and Samuelson did not eliminate this choice; it progressively concealed it under layers of mathematical formalization, relocating the normative commitment from declared philosophy into axiomatic necessity. The continuity axiom required for utility representability is identified as the primary hiding mechanism: it encodes preference commensurability as a technical requirement rather than a philosophical assumption-a point Svensson (1980) noted in passing in the social choice literature but which has not been theorized as a mechanism of concealment. Lexicographic preferences-formally non-representable by any utility function per Debreu's theorem-serve as the mathematical proof of this claim. Prior work in the philosophy of economics-principally Hausman and McPherson (2006) and Putnam (2002)-has established that welfare economics embeds contestable normative commitments through philosophical and linguistic argument. This paper advances three additional lines of challenge. First, the mathematical proof: the structural exclusion of lexicographic preferences is not contestable in the way philosophical claims are-it follows necessarily from Debreu's theorem. Second, the biological and psychological challenge: Bentham's foundational assumption requires not only that preferences be commensurable but that they be stable. The behavioral LawQuant Working Paper-1 biology literature-including Sapolsky's multi-causal framework on hormonal and developmental contingency of preference formation, and Kahneman's documented bewilderment at economics' insulation of its behavioral assumptions from empirical pressure-shows that preference stability is empirically falsified at the mechanistic level. This is categorically different from philosophical contestation: it attacks the framework's positive self-description on its own scientific terms. Third, the genealogy: this paper traces the specific sequence from Bentham's declared commitments through the purification attempts to Mankiw's Chapter 7, assembling a transmission history that prior work has not constructed. The indictment is not Bentham's choice itself, which carried genuine tractability virtues, but the discipline's failure to maintain it as a visible, contestable modeling decision. The stakes are not merely academic. The positive science pretense this concealment produces licenses the authority claims of an enormous downstream institutional apparatus-cost-benefit analysis, regulatory impact assessment, judicial efficiency standards, and the policy architecture of modern governance-all of which present Bentham's normative choice as objective measurement of social value. Taking down the positive science pretense is the prerequisite for an honest accounting of what that apparatus is actually doing.

detail.abstract: Long-distance and covert navigation missions of autonomous vehicles impose stringent requirements on the autonomous perception capability, environmental adaptability, and path decision stability of navigation systems. Traditional geomagnetic navigation methods rely on prior geomagnetic maps, are susceptible to local magnetic anomalies, and suffer from poor heading decision stability in complex environments. To address these problems, this paper proposes an autonomous vehicles geomagnetic perception navigation method based on attention-enhanced long short-term memory (LSTM) network. The proposed method fuses the measurement data of geomagnetic sensor and the motion state information of inertial navigation to construct a time-series sequence for collaborative geomagnetic-motion navigation. The LSTM network is adopted to extract the temporal correlation features between geomagnetic variations and navigation motion states, and an attention mechanism is introduced to weight and enhance key geomagnetic variation features, so as to improve the local geomagnetic environment perception capability.  Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method can realize autonomous geomagnetic navigation without prior geomagnetic maps. It achieves superior convergence performance, path smoothness and robustness in both normal and disturbed geomagnetic environments, which effectively improves the navigation stability and environmental adaptability of autonomous vehicles.

title: The Containment Paradox: U.S. Export Controls on Frontier AI and the Rise of Open-Weight Competitors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial relationship with any party discussed in this paper. The paper was prepared with assistance from AI tools developed by Anthropic, a company whose conduct is discussed in the analysis; the author has no commercial or contractual relationship with Anthropic. The views and conclusions are the author's own.

detail.abstract:
On 9 June 2026, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5, the most capable model the firm had ever made generally available. Three days later, a U.S. export-control directive forced Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and its sibling Mythos 5 for every customer worldwide, because the firm had no way to filter foreign nationals from U.S. users in real time. Within days, the Chinese laboratory Z.ai released GLM-5.2, an open-weight model that, on at least one crowdsourced human-preference coding leaderboard, edged past the very model that had just been pulled by a narrow margin, though the withdrawn model retained an edge at the top of the closed frontier and the gap to the leading open model was narrow on the benchmarks where it could be measured.

This paper treats that sequence as a near-coincidence that renders a structural mechanism visible. Its thesis is structural: access restrictions on closed frontier models impose real costs on competitiveness and goodwill while buying little of the containment they promise. The reason is that what such restrictions target, model capability, is diffusion-prone: it is demonstrable, recoverable through distillation, and substitutable by openly published weights whose distribution, once accomplished, cannot be reversed. The paper draws a distinction the policy debate tends to blur. Some control targets are diffusion-resistant, above all the frontier training compute embodied in advanced semiconductors. Others, such as access to a deployed model and the behaviour it exhibits, are not. Treating the second kind like the first produces self-defeating policy. A sharper version of that claim, advanced here as a conditional argument and not as a settled fact, is that such a measure can convert a national-security rationale into a national-security liability, displacing deployment that sits inside a legal accountability framework in favour of open-weight substitutes that sit outside one. The argument is developed from the vantage point of a non-aligned third country, the swing adopter whose standardization choices help decide whether the open or the closed model becomes the world's default. The paper closes with recommendations for a transparent, technically grounded process for any state intervention in model deployment.

detail.abstract: This study explores whether and how a green technology pool – a centralized mechanism through which technology holders can license relevant patents and know-how – can accelerate climate technology transfer to low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). It first maps the international legal framework governing such transfers, spanning customary duties to cooperate on climate action, treaty-based obligations to promote technology transfer, and flexibilities for governing relevant intellectual property (IP). It then assesses key IP management tools for transferring climate technologies, before analysing the advantages and recurring pitfalls of technology pools in depth. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a practical design framework for a green technology pool specifying: (i) a narrow technological focus aligned with identified IP bottlenecks, market demand, and LMIC absorptive capacity; (ii) calibrated incentives for licensors and licensees combining standardized yet flexible terms, appropriately structured royalties, and complementary public support; (iii) comprehensive transfer that bundles patents with codified and tacit know-how, training, and implementation support; and (iv) governance structures that balance political support with operational autonomy.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether firms strategically adjust environmental performance around initial public offerings (IPOs). Using real-time plant-level data from Chinas Continuous Emission Monitoring System (CEMS), we find that firms significantly reduce excess emissions in the six months before IPOs but relax controls afterward, indicating temporary, strategic abatement. The evidence suggests firms aim to avoid regulatory penalties and improve valuations, as poor environmental records increase both approval risks and underpricing. Our findings highlight environmental performance as a form of IPO window dressing and underscore the need for stronger post-IPO regulatory oversight.

detail.abstract: The Hasbrouck Information Share is the most widely used measure of cross-venue price discovery, but on daily-frequency data the contemporaneous correlation of venue innovations is high, so the Cholesky-ordering bounds are wide and the midpoint is uninformative about leadership. Using three commodity contract pairs that trade on the Moscow Exchange and on the CME group, we show that the Information Share bounds span roughly 0.05 to 0.85 at daily frequency, that the Information Leadership Share inherits this width because it takes the Information Share as an input, and that this combination can produce a leadership ranking that contradicts a known institutional fact: on the pre-2022 Brent pair the Information Leadership Share assigns 0.765 to the Moscow Exchange leg even though that contract settles off the global ICE Brent benchmark. The Gonzalo-Granger Component Share, which depends only on the error-correction loadings and is invariant to the innovation correlation, returns the institutionally correct ranking and is sharply identified. We conclude that on daily or coarser data the Component Share should be reported as the operational single-number measure, the Information Share as a bound, and the Information Leadership Share as a supplementary statistic whose reliability is constrained by the width of the bounds it inherits.

detail.abstract: Using repeated large-scale surveys of US households, we study the cryptocurrency investment decisions and motives of households relative to other financial assets. Cryptocurrency holders tend to be young, male, and more libertarian relative to non-crypto holders. Crypto holders expect much higher rates of return for crypto and perceive it as relatively safer than non-holders do. For those holding cryptocurrencies, changes in Bitcoin prices translate into their purchases of durable goods. Finally, information about historical returns of cryptocurrencies in an information provision experiment embedded in the survey leads individuals to increase their desired crypto holdings and increases their actual cryptocurrency purchases subsequently. We compare these views and behaviors to those of households toward other financial assets and argue that cryptocurrency is unique in many of these respects.

title: From Summly to Claude: A Bayesian Computational Bridge

detail.title: From Summly to Claude: A Bayesian Computational Bridge
detail.abstract: We trace the mathematical lineage from extractive news summarization (Summly, 2013) to modern large language models, making three claims. First, the four-stage Summly pipeline summarizability gate, hand-engineered sentence features, length-dependent scorer, and budgeted greedy selection has a precise descendant in every stage of a transformerbased language model. Second, the central object connecting the two eras is personalized PageRank: softmax self-attention is one step of a generalized personalized random walk with learned transition kernels and vector-valued centralities, with classical PageRank as the damped scalar special case. Third, the computational bottlenecks of both pipelines SVM training, logistic gating, ReLU network optimization, iterative attention all admit conditionally Gaussian latent-variable representations that enable substantial speedups. We develop these in detail: PolsonScott data augmentation for SVMs, PólyaGamma augmentation for logistic and softmax models, WangPolsonSokolov augmentation for ReLU networks, and Generative Bayesian Computation for amortizing iterative inference into a single forward pass. The unifying principle is that conjugate latent representations convert non-conjugate iterative inference into either fast Gibbs sampling or one-shot generative amortization. A worked reformulation of the Summly pipeline achieves a 47× inference speedup at equal or improved ROUGE-L with calibrated uncertainty quantication as a byproduct.

title: The Impact of Bilateral Investment Treaty Termination on India's Outward Foreign Direct Investment

detail.title: The Impact of Bilateral Investment Treaty Termination on India's Outward Foreign Direct Investment
detail.abstract: India adopted a new model Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) regime in 2016, and began a mass termination of BITs that were based on the old model. While the effects of this termination in terms of reduced foreign direct investment inflows into India have been established, the effects on outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) from India are lesser known. This paper adopts an event study design with two-way fixed effects, comparing trends in FDI outflows to countries with which BITs were signed and terminated (treated group), with trends in outflows to countries that have either never signed a BIT with India or hold an active BIT (control group), and thus did not experience the shock. The study finds statistically significant declines in OFDI beginning two years after termination, while finding a general downward trend in OFDI flows from India post BIT termination. This pilot study attempts to draw attention to the importance of BITs for sustained OFDI flows.

detail.abstract: We examine how e-commerce penetration reshapes offline commercial activity across Seoul's 523 commercial clusters using 9.7 million establishment-month observations (2020-2024). Exploiting cross-industry variation in online penetration and a Bartik-style shift-share design, we identify two channels through which digitisation erodes in-person sales: A ten-percentage-point increase in own-industry online penetration is associated with a 26-29 per cent reduction, while rising online intensity among colocated industries creates distinct negative spillovers. Conventional agglomeration benefits are also reshaped: Marshall-type specialisation premiums reverse once online substitutability exceeds an estimated threshold of around 15 percent, whereas Jacobs-type diversity benefits in mixed-industry clusters remain unconditionally positive. These findings reveal how digitisation selectively transforms the mechanisms sustaining urban commercial clusters in a major Asian city.

detail.abstract:
(forthcoming in the Oxford Handbook on Global Corporations and International Law, Oxford University Press, edited by Andrew Sanger, Andreas Kulick and Doreen Lustig (2027))

Both corporations and intellectual property (IP) rights are creatures of and coded by law-and hence in principle subject to the state's rule-making power. Since both commonly relate to activities that cross borders, private and public international law, as well as technologies, infrastructures and institutions are frequently designed to validate and facilitate such acts. Given how essential IP rights are for many intangible assets commercialised globally, it is not surprising that corporate actors aim to shape international legal regimes for the global protection and enforcement of IP. This paper reviews the role of corporate IP owners and users in creating, maintaining and updating the global legal infrastructure relevant for accessing, utilising and exploiting IP. Taking a bird-eye perspective, it shows how, since the advent of the international IP system in the 19 th century, corporations act as global norm drivers, entrepreneurs and creators, as well as norm antipreneurs and private standard-setters.

detail.abstract: This theoretical essay proposes the concept of definitional power: the capacity to fix and sustain the recognition criteria by which a market decides what counts as quality. The concept carries an endogenous property that the literature has not yet articulated. The very mechanism that naturalizes those criteria produces, over time, its holders' blindness to their obsolescence. Engaging the sociology of market categories, I identify a double gap: that literature does not connect the mechanism explaining the policing of categorical boundaries to the mechanism explaining their later erosion, and its canonical cases examine only challengers able to compete within the dominant field's existing grammar of evaluation. In response, I formulate the grammar hypothesis. The fate of a categorical challenger without prior status depends on the kind of admission it demands. When the challenge is legible to existing judgment devices, the lack of status can be overcome; when admission would require redefining the yardstick itself, the lack of status capital and political voice becomes decisive, because redefining a yardstick is a political act, not an act of evaluation. I illustrate the hypothesis through three contrast cases (the 1976 Judgment of Paris, the mezcal denomination of origin, and the position of Brazilian cachaça in the international spirits market) and close with the empirical research agenda designed to test it.

detail.abstract: This article belongs to the field of administrative tax procedure and the public law of artificial intelligence, examining the use of AI tools in the formation of decisions by a tax adjudicatory body. Its objective is to establish the due-process architecture that must be fixed for IARA, the Artificial Intelligence in Administrative Appeals tool of Brazil's Administrative Council of Tax Appeals (CARF), introduced on an experimental basis by Ordinance CARF/MF No. 854/2026 under the governance guidelines of Ordinance CARF/MF No. 142/2026, while the tool is still experimental and before future modules broaden its access to extra-procedural data. The method is doctrinal and legal, without an empirical component, articulating Brazilian normative sources, the international literature on AI and adjudication, and comparative parameters such as CNJ Resolution No. 615/2025. The result is the proposal of five categories, algorithmic procedural transparency, second-order algorithmic reasoning, the Algorithmic Provenance Annex, the evidentiary firewall, and the meaningful human review test, converted into verifiable procedural duties, together with a materiality test for assessing nullities. It concludes that human supervision is necessary but insufficient, and that the experimental character brings forward, rather than postpones, the moment to establish such safeguards.

title: Navigating Urbanization Microeconomic Household Decisions and Predictive Modeling in Slum Formation

detail.title: Navigating Urbanization Microeconomic Household Decisions and Predictive Modeling in Slum Formation
detail.abstract: Slum formation is often described as a planning failure, but it is also the aggregated result of household decisions made under constrained budgets, uncertain employment, incomplete property rights, limited affordable housing supply, and spatially uneven access to jobs and services. This paper develops a synthesis of microeconomic urbanization theory and predictive modeling for slum formation. Building on expected-wage migration models, poverty-trap accounts of slums, tenure-security evidence, agent-based settlement models, and recent remote-sensing and data-centric AI approaches, it frames informal settlement risk as a dynamic choice-and-capacity problem: households choose locations and tenure arrangements, while cities expose them to rationed formal housing, commute costs, service deficits, eviction risk, and hazard gradients. The paper proposes an operational pipeline that combines household surveys, administrative records, transport accessibility, Earth observation, community-generated labels, and calibrated spatial risk models. A small illustrative simulation shows how formal housing supply, serviced land, transit access, and tenure-service upgrading can shift predicted slum formation away from high-deprivation equilibria. The central claim is practical: early-warning models should not be used as instruments of exclusion or eviction; they should identify where affordable housing, infrastructure, tenure security, and labor-market access must arrive before informal deprivation hardens into a durable spatial poverty trap.

title: Creativity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Simulation, the Muse and the Dethronement of the Human Creator
affiliations: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi Christian University Inc.

detail.title: Creativity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Simulation, the Muse and the Dethronement of the Human Creator
detail.abstract:
This article examines what happens to the human self-image when machine-generated forms are culturally received as creative. This question continues the preceding contributions Existential Alignment: When Guidance Appears as Meaning-Making, Freedom in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Why Relief Is Not the Same as Freedom, and Existential Non-Absorption: Freedom after Relief in the Gentle Totality, and it sharpens an aspect that those texts only touched upon.

To this end the contribution distinguishes three levels of creativity, the anthropological, the aesthetic and the functional, in order to show that artificial intelligence touches them unequally. At the anthropological level it lacks the existential bearing that makes the human act of creation what it is. Aesthetically and functionally, by contrast, it can produce effects that in many contexts can no longer be reliably distinguished from human form-giving. The thesis is therefore not that AI ontologically displaces human creativity, but that it undermines its public evidentiary force. Simulation suffices wherever cultural reception no longer examines provenance.

The text links this diagnosis with empirical findings on the reception of AI-generated forms. At the same time it places them within a longer history of theory. The decentring of the author was already prepared in the artistic procedures of the twentieth century and in post-structuralist authorship theory. Against this background artificial intelligence appears not as a rupture but as the escalation of an old contradiction. The author was theoretically decentred yet remained practically liable.

At the end stands the figure of the dethroned creator. The human being does not lose creativity, but can no longer assert it as the unquestioned credential of a special standing. What remains is responsibility for forms that can arise even without a human inner life.

title: Error Bars for the Arrow of Time: A Transferable Coverage Guarantee for Learned Entropy-Production Estimators

detail.title: Error Bars for the Arrow of Time: A Transferable Coverage Guarantee for Learned Entropy-Production Estimators
detail.abstract: Across the sciences (living cells, neural recordings, active matter, financial markets) the arrow of time has become a measurement: neural estimators now read a system's entropy-production rate straight off its trajectories. These estimators return a number with no error bar, and the dominant family maximises a variational lower bound, so the number is biased low by an amount its own dispersion cannot detect. A point estimate of irreversibility, however accurate on average, is not yet a measurement. This paper supplies the missing error bars through a reusable template. We first prove that a classical frequency-domain estimator is coveragevalid, and then transfer that guarantee onto any learned estimator through a dependence-aware conformal step that needs only paired evaluations, with no retraining and no assumption on architecture. The transfer is provably necessary rather than merely convenient: no dispersion functional of a variational estimator's own sampling law can identify its bias, so an external anchor is required. The anchor's only structural requirement is unbiasedness, since a noisy anchor costs interval width but never validity. The classical side is unified as well. Timereversibility, a fluctuation-dissipation identity, and a spectral-efficiency restriction all collapse into a single smooth constraint on the spectral density, the second-order irreversibility spectrum Λ(ω), which carries one central-limit-and-bootstrap theory and frequency-localised bands (Λ resolves linear currents while the scalar rate covers higher orders). The classical machinery is reused and cited as such; the contribution is the object, the transfer, and the impossibility result that forces it. Empirically, three architecturally distinct learned estimators, covering the truth as little as 6% of the time at the nominal 95%, all snap to nominal once wrapped, and they beat strong uncertainty baselines (deep ensembles, last-layer Laplace) that no deployable width fix can rescue. One consequence is physical: under a rotational drive, irreversibility is a first-order signal, whereas the total variance underlying the standard critical-slowing-down early-warning diagnostics moves only at second order, so the spectrum detects an emerging non-equilibrium transition while volatility is still flat. We close on real data, reading broken detailed balance off 25 years of S&P 500 prices (the leverage effect) and off human cardiorespiratory recordings. Calibration is validated on synthetic systems with known ground truth; the real-data studies are genuine applications reported with bootstrap p-values rather than coverage claims.

title:
The Great Indian Illusion: 
Unpacking the Gap between Growth Statistics and Citizen Well-being
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Great Indian Illusion: 
Unpacking the Gap between Growth Statistics and Citizen Well-being
detail.abstract: Headline indicators of the Indian economy in 2025-26-GDP growth, record public capital expenditure, and a multi-decade low in bank non-performing assets-coexist with a parallel set of indicators that are considerably less favourable: persistently elevated youth unemployment, a record annual exodus of foreign portfolio capital, a collapse in fresh retail SIP registrations, a fiscal structure in which two of every five rupees of government revenue service old debt, and a rupee under sustained depreciation pressure from an oil price shock. This paper does not argue that India's growth statistics are fabricated. It argues that several headline aggregates are accurate but incomplete-they describe the upper half of the income and capital distribution while remaining largely silent on the lower half, on first-time market participants, and on the structural composition of bank credit risk. Each of five pillars is examined against the most recent verifiable data available as of June 2026: jobless growth, the asymmetry between foreign-capital incentives and retail participation, a narrow but real pocket of credit stress in unsecured retail and microfinance lending, the fiscal constraint imposed by interest payments, and currency vulnerability to imported energy costs. The paper closes by arguing that this gap between aggregate and distributional indicators is itself a measurable, monitorable signal-one that requires the same kind of real-time, device-level instrumentation that AION Analytics has built for retail algorithmic trading auditability, applied instead to economic-indicator literacy at the citizen level.

title: Stablecoins on Unstable Venues: A MiCA Depeg Episode

detail.abstract: In June 2026 Binance had to leave the European Union after failing to secure a permanent MiCA license, while the issuer of EURI, a euro e-money token, stayed solvent and redeemed at par throughout. EURI traded up to 438 basis points below par on Binance, yet comparable euro stablecoins on licensed venues and dollar stablecoins on Binance stayed near par. On-chain records show redemption cleared at par but too slowly and too gated to bind the intraday price. The dislocation tracked venue concentration, not issuer soundness: the first MiCA enforcement episode where issuer supervision did not secure secondary-market parity.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that comparative legal reasoning fails when foreign law is treated as a detachable example, exotic contrast, or ready-made borrowing for the home legal system. Successful comparison is instead a disciplined encounter between cognitive matrices: the categories through which the comparatist sees, the self-understandings through which the foreign legal order reasons, and the institutional, linguistic, and living-law conditions that give legal materials their force. The argument proceeds in six steps. First, it argues that comparison must subserve edification by exposing the home matrix, so that foreign law can teach rather than be flattened by unexamined domestic categories. Second, it argues that what can travel is not a rule-fragment but a legal reason whose route, speaker, authority, medium, and uptake must be reconstructed. Third, it treats global legal language as the hard case, because terms such as rights, rule of law, governance, dignity, or constitutionalism may circulate widely while silencing the local conditions that make law operative. Fourth, it defends thin borrowing as legitimate only when the claim is graded, bounded, reversible, and kept distinct from thick reconstruction. Fifth, it explains how comparison can expose the home matrix without mastering the foreign one, by preserving alien intelligibility while allowing foreign friction to reconfigure domestic assumptions. Sixth, it translates the account into a proportional protocol: claim discipline asks what work the foreign material is doing; source discipline tracks its route, carrier, authority, translation, and medium; interpretive discipline returns it to legal activity; and normative discipline asks whether its use preserves intelligibility or risks domination, exoticization, or misuse. Comparative reasoning becomes legally judicious when it lets an alien matrix discipline the home argument without allowing the home matrix to seize, flatten, or speak in the other's name.

title:
Corporate Liability in Autonomous Systems: Intersecting Corporate Ethics with Transnational Tech Governance

An Indonesia Perspective on Cross-Border Algorithmic Accountability and Legal Risk Mitigation

detail.title:
Corporate Liability in Autonomous Systems: Intersecting Corporate Ethics with Transnational Tech Governance

An Indonesia Perspective on Cross-Border Algorithmic Accountability and Legal Risk Mitigation
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of high-level Autonomous Systems (AS) has generated unprecedented systemic risks, exposing a profound accountability gap within classical jurisprudence. This study investigates the legal friction arising from borderless algorithmic harms operating within a fragmented transnational tech governance landscape, focusing on the Global South perspective. Utilizing a hybridized methodology rooted in Digital Legal Realism, this paper establishes the "Empirical-Content Nexus" to concurrently confront voluntary corporate ethical commitments against the empirical realities of algorithmic failures documented in the AI Incident Database (AIID). The findings expose a critical asymmetry: while tech conglomerates utilize Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR) frameworks to project a strategic facade of safety, their actual operational architectures systematically externalize severe risks onto human users. When confronted with these automated harms, traditional fault-based liability regimes-specifically Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code-are rendered structurally paralyzed by black-box opacity and probabilistic causation. To rectify this enforcement vacuum, this study argues that through deliberate judicial activism and rechtsvinding, the Indonesian judiciary must convert a corporation's own highly advertised CDR blueprints into an objective, legally binding standard of care within tort litigation. Coupled with a shifted burden of proof (res ipsa loquitur), this framework functionally weaponizes corporate ethics as an immediate interim mechanism to enforce cross-border algorithmic accountability.

title: The Effect of Return Migration on Prices
affiliations: Banco de Mexico and Banco de Mexico

detail.title: The Effect of Return Migration on Prices
detail.abstract: We exploit Secure Communities, a deportation policy, to identify the effect of return migration on prices. Combining deportation records with Mexican migrant-network data, we construct municipalities' deportation exposure and link it to local producer and consumer prices. Agricultural producer prices decline, consistent with increased labor supply lowering production costs. In contrast, consumer price increases are concentrated in housing, where supply does not adjust in the short run. Comparing producer and consumer prices for the same goods, we show consumer prices can attenuate production-cost effects when production and consumption occur in different locations.

title: Comparative Garch Volatility Forecasting of the MSCI World Index and Equities on the Ghana Stock Exchange
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana - , Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana - , Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana -  and Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana -

detail.title: Comparative Garch Volatility Forecasting of the MSCI World Index and Equities on the Ghana Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: Globally, indices like MSCI provide insight into major financial markets while the volatility patterns of smaller, less liquid markets such as the Ghana Stock Exchange remain under-explored. The study investigated the volatility behavior of these markets using GARCH models to inform risk management and investment decisions. Historical daily price data from June 2015 to May 2025 were collected from Alpha Vantage and the official website of the Ghana Stock Exchange. Multiple GARCH models were applied to the data, and the most suitable models were identified using statistical accuracy measures. Model selection was guided by criteria such as the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and log-likelihood values. It was found that the GARCH(1,1) model provided the best volatility forecasts for most equities, with the exception of Tullow Oil, where GARCH(0,1) was more appropriate. While the MSCI World Index exhibited a gradual decline in volatility, Ghanaian equities showed a period of heightened volatility before stabilizing, except for Unilever Ghana, which displayed a persistent increase in volatility over time.

title: Moral Geometry: Endogenous Scaling in Nash-Kantian Games
affiliations: and Higher Colleges of Technology

detail.title: Moral Geometry: Endogenous Scaling in Nash-Kantian Games
detail.abstract: We study the strategic implications of the non-invariance of multiplicative Kantian equilibrium (MKE) under monotone transformations of the strategy space. Before interacting with a standard Nash player, a Kantian player publicly selects a smooth increasing scale that determines how proportional deviations are evaluated. Material payoffs and feasible actions remain unchanged, but the chosen scale alters the Kantian first-order condition through endogenous elasticity weights. The representation of actions therefore becomes a commitment device. We characterize the stationary outcomes implementable by a common monotone scale. A sharp dichotomy emerges. Under strategic substitutes, the Kantian player can approach the Nash payoff arbitrarily closely but cannot exceed player 2's Nash benchmark; scaling is defensive and eliminates the payoff loss associated with naive Kantian behavior. Under strategic complements, scaling becomes offensive: the Kantian player can stationary-implement the Stackelberg leader outcome and obtain a payoff strictly above the Nash benchmark. In the canonical Cournot and differentiated Bertrand examples, we explicitly construct scales satisfying the required local elasticity ratios and verify the secondorder conditions, so the stationary outcomes are local transformed Nash-Kantian equilibria. Allowing player-specific scales would align the Kantian first-order condition with the Stackelberg condition along the entire reaction curve under complements, but would violate monotonicity under substitutes. This reveals a trade-off between universality and strategic flexibility. The results identify endogenous scaling as a commitment mechanism and connect Kantian optimization to strategic leadership and strategic nonequivalence.

detail.abstract: Drawing on sociological phenomenology and more-than-human theory, we explore how synthetic voice reshapes practices of listening, attention, and environmental meaning-making. We argue that AI-mediated speech creates new forms of environmental attunement in which ecological data becomes socially and sensorially available through conversation rather than visual analytics alone. In doing so, the study examines how synthetic voice may alter perceptions of identity, agency, and epistemic legitimacy by positioning nonhuman phenomena within dialogic interaction. The paper contributes to debates within AI & Society concerning anthropomorphism, synthetic identity, AI mediation, and the social construction of knowledge. We position AImediated voice not as a transparent representation of nature, but as a culturally situated form of mediation that reshapes how humans interpret and relate to the more-than-human world.

title: Attempted Administrative Entrenchment in Trump's Second Term
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco

detail.title: Attempted Administrative Entrenchment in Trump's Second Term

publicationDetails.detailsText: 40 Notre Dame Journal of Law, Ethics, and Public Policy __ (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract: Across recent administrations, political polarization has thus yielded a dispiriting cycle of flip-flopping in executive policy.  In this context, the second Trump administration has pursued several unconventional administrative tactics that might reflect efforts to break this cycle and entrench durable policy change through unilateral executive action.  This brief adaptation of symposium remarks discusses three such tactics.  First, by firing staff and impounding funds, the administration has sought to strip capacity from disfavored agencies, thereby impeding their viability as policy tools in future administrations.  Second, by pursuing large penalties from universities and other targets, often on doubtful legal grounds and without following required procedures, the administration has established deterrence with respect to future violations of its legal understandings.  And third, by requiring disclosure of certain information from universities and by pursuing novel readings of the False Claims Act, the administration has activated potential private litigation advancing its policy goals (even as it has sought to limit private litigation in some other respects).  All three of these tactics may succeed to some degree in producing durable change, but insofar as they do so, their very success may simply encourage similar unilateral actions by future administrations, thereby producing yet another escalation in the cycle of partisan flip-flopping and unilateral executive action.

title: Tariffs, production networks, and spillovers: the case of a US-China trade war
affiliations: , , European Central Bank (ECB), , ,  and Bank of Spain

detail.title: Tariffs, production networks, and spillovers: the case of a US-China trade war
detail.abstract: We study the short-run macroeconomic transmission of a US–China tariff war in an open economy multi-sector New Keynesian model with input–output linkages, sectoral nominal rigidities, and heterogeneous currency invoicing. A reciprocal 10 percentage-point tariff increase generates asymmetric incidence: the tariff-imposing country bears more of the inflationary burden, while the targeted country experiences the larger output contraction. Production networks amplify this contraction by propagating the shock beyond the directly tariffed bilateral margin. Currency invoicing further shapes transmission. Under heterogeneous invoicing, dollar-priced border prices weaken the expenditure-switching role of exchange rates, deepening the contraction in China relative to producer-currency pricing and altering third-country spillovers. The EA response is small in the aggregate, but only because positive trade-diversion margins are offset by weaker demand from China and multilateral adjustments. We then exploit the model’s sectoral structure by imposing tariffs on one Chinese sector at a time. Sectoral incidence is highly concentrated, but aggregate effects cannot be inferred from the directly tariffed sector alone: domestic propagation offsets own-sector gains in the US, reinforces own-sector losses in China, and leaves the EA as a net object shaped by opposing trade margins. The results show that tariff incidence depends jointly on where the tariff lands, how the shock propagates through production networks, and how invoicing governs border-price adjustment. A framework that combines these margins delivers a materially different assessment from one built on bilateral trade shares alone.

title: The Bounds of Bounded Rationality: Heuristics, Norms, and the Case for Ecological Rationality

detail.title: The Bounds of Bounded Rationality: Heuristics, Norms, and the Case for Ecological Rationality
detail.abstract: Two influential research programs claim the legacy of Herbert Simon's bounded rationality while drawing nearly opposite conclusions from it. The heuristics-and-biases program of Kahneman and Tversky documents systematic deviations of human judgment from the norms of logic and probability and interprets heuristics primarily as a source of error; the fast-andfrugal heuristics program of Gigerenzer and colleagues argues that such norms are contentblind and that simple heuristics, when matched to the structure of the environment, can equal or outperform information-greedy statistical models. This paper critically reviews both programs and defends a qualified position: the ecological-rationality program is the more constructive and the more faithful development of Simon's vision. The review covers the core bias findings and prospect theory; the evidence that celebrated cognitive illusions attenuate under natural-frequency formats and ecologically motivated problem representations; the formal models and competitive tests of the recognition and take-the-best heuristics, including their critical literature; the bias-variance logic that explains why simple models can outpredict complex ones under uncertainty; and field applications ranging from the 1/N portfolio rule to one-reason election forecasting. The paper also identifies the ecological program's open problems, notably strategy selection, and argues that adversarial collaboration offers the appropriate method for resolving the remaining disputes.

title: Picking Winners or Marking Them? Timing-Based Evaluation of Innovation Certification
affiliations: Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l. and Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l.

detail.title: Picking Winners or Marking Them? Timing-Based Evaluation of Innovation Certification
detail.abstract: Voluntary certification policies-which let firms self-nominate for innovative or privileged status-increasingly channel fiscal, financial, and regulatory support, yet evaluating them is deceptively hard: certified firms may outperform because certification works, or simply because firms apply when already rising. We show that voluntary certification can certify winners precisely because rational firms time entry to moments of transitory expansion: the measured premium largely reflects when firms participate, not what participation does. We formalise this as anticipatory take-up: because the benefits are most valuable while a firm scales, forward-looking firms register at the crest of a growth run-up. The mechanism yields three predictions-a cross-sectional premium, a premium that largely predates certification, and entry driven by recent growth, not profitability. We test them in the Italian innovative-SME regime, linking panel data for roughly 2,900 certified and 1,200 non-certified SMEs to each firm's registration date and sector, and treating performance as a six-dimensional vector. Certified firms grow far faster than balanced peers yet are financially less solid, especially when smaller and capital-intensive. Once registration timing is exploited through event-study and staggered difference-indifferences designs, the premium proves largely selection: about 81 per cent of the revenue advantage predates registration, and the residual merely continues a pre-existing trend. A hazard model confirms it-entry rises with recent growth and smaller size, not profitability. The paper reframes the evaluation of voluntary certification from average effects to observable dynamic selection: such schemes mark firms already on distinctive trajectories rather than create them. The lesson generalises-robustness to omitted variables is not robustness to selection on trends, and cross-sectional evaluations mislead unless they exploit the timing of take-up.

title: Climate Policy, Shadow Banking, and Financial Fragility
affiliations: Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK), Potsdam Institute of Climate Impact Research and Potsdam Institute of Climate Impact Research

detail.title: Climate Policy, Shadow Banking, and Financial Fragility

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR) under grant number 01LA2205C (OVERHANG).

detail.abstract: Carbon-intensive assets are increasingly migrating to the shadow banking sector, shifting transition risk to institutions with limited regulatory oversight that are a well-documented source of financial fragility. This paper embeds carbon pricing and climate-related financial regulation into a model of shadow-bank runs and firesale dynamics, extending the wholesale-bank framework of Gertler et al. (2016) to a two-sector economy with clean and dirty capital and asymmetric management costs. We find that both a carbon tax and higher disclosure costs for dirty assets shift carbonintensive capital to shadow banks, raise leverage, and make run equilibria feasible; under plausible calibrations, a moderate carbon tax or a doubling of management costs generates run probabilities of up to 5%. The two instruments interact nonlinearly, as disclosure-driven reallocation toward dirty assets amplifies the fire-sale discount triggered by carbon pricing. Extending regulation to shadow banks reduces fragility, and anticipated run risk further dampens it, but only at the cost of lower aggregate consumption, implying a shadow cost of financial fragility that constrains climate policy.

title: Law in Books, Law in Action, Law Through Systems
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Law in Books, Law in Action, Law Through Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest.

detail.abstract: Roscoe Pound's distinction between law in books and law in action remains a warning against confusing legal formulation with legal operation. Yet in many institutions the decisive choices occur before an official encounters the individual case. An intake form determines what can be said; a routing rule determines who will see it; a reporting architecture determines what an organisation is capable of disclosing. Such arrangements belong within Pound's law in action, but they warrant separate scrutiny because they preserve earlier judgments and reproduce them across later cases. This essay calls that scrutiny reading law through systems. The expression denotes neither a source of law nor a version of systems theory. It is a method for tracing how a legal requirement is translated into an operating environment, and for testing whether the resulting choices remain visible, reviewable and revisable. Sustainability reporting under the Singapore Exchange Mainboard Rules and recommender-system duties under the European Union's Digital Services Act illustrate two different relations between law and infrastructure. In one setting, infrastructure enables compliance; in the other, it is itself regulated. Both show why the final report or decision may reveal too little. A lawyer must sometimes examine the system that prepared it.

title: A Participation-based Framework of Market Selection under Heterogeneous Demand and Supply

detail.title: A Participation-based Framework of Market Selection under Heterogeneous Demand and Supply
detail.abstract: This paper develops a participation-based framework for market selection under heterogeneous demand and supply. Consumers differ in willingness to pay, while firms differ in marginal costs and production capacities. Market exchange is coordinated through a common price, which functions as a participation boundary determining whether agents are included in decentralized exchange. On the demand side, consumers participate if their willingness to pay exceeds price, while on the supply side firms participate if their marginal cost is below price. Aggregate outcomes are therefore generated through discrete participation sets rather than smooth representative demand and supply functions. Some firms may satisfy cost-based participation conditions but fail to contribute to realized exchange when demand is insufficient to absorb their production. The framework interprets market dynamics as a process of structural selection over heterogeneous populations, in which prices govern the inclusion and exclusion of agents from market activity.

title: The Disaggregation of Authorship: What Copyright Law Can Learn from Bioethics
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley Law School, Kyushu University - Graduate School of Law and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Disaggregation of Authorship: What Copyright Law Can Learn from Bioethics
detail.abstract: In this comment, we address an issue that has remained largely overlooked by law and technology scholars and practitioners: who "owns" content created with the assistance of a person's personal AI twin. We briefly explain the technology underlying personal AI twins and offer three possible answers to this question. We also suggest that copyright law could benefit from developments in bioethics over the past thirty years, particularly the emergence of different concepts of "death." We propose that the concepts of the author and authorship should be disaggregated. Distinguishing among different forms of human-AI collaboration, and thus among different forms of authorship, could facilitate a more nuanced understanding of how creators integrate AI tools into the creative process.

title: Stock Market–Growth Nexus in Nepal: An Empirical ARDL Bounds Testing Analysis of Long-Run and Short-Run Dynamics (1994–2025)

detail.title: Stock Market–Growth Nexus in Nepal: An Empirical ARDL Bounds Testing Analysis of Long-Run and Short-Run Dynamics (1994–2025)
detail.abstract:
Background
This study examines whether Nepal’s developing stock market has measurable long-run and short-run relationships with real economic growth. It focuses on the role of stock market indicators in explaining movements in real gross domestic product (RGDP) during the period 1994–2025.

Method
Annual time-series data were taken from 1994 to 2025. RGDP was modeled as a function of the NEPSE Index, real market capitalization, real paid-up capital, inflation, and the number of listed companies. Since the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test indicated mixed integration order among the variables, the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach was applied to examine long-run equilibrium and short-run dynamics.

Results
The ARDL bounds test confirmed co-integration among the variables, with an F-statistic of 6.8769. The long-run results showed that inflation had a negative statistically significant association with RGDP, while the number of listed companies had a positive statistically significant association with RGDP. However, the NEPSE Index, real market capitalization, and real paid-up capital were not statistically significant in the long-run equation. In the short run, the error-correction results showed a significant negative association between the NEPSE Index and inflation, and a significant positive association between listed companies, paid-up capital, and RGDP growth. The error correction coefficient was negative and significant, indicating that approximately 27.9% of deviations from long-run equilibrium are corrected annually. Diagnostic tests showed no evidence of serial correlation or heteroskedasticity, supporting the model’s reliability and stability.

Conclusion
The findings suggest that Nepal’s stock market contributes to economic growth more through market breadth, listed-company expansion, and productive capital mobilization than through index-level growth alone. Inflation management also appears important for sustaining real economic growth. Therefore, policy attention should be directed toward strengthening listing quality, expanding market participation, improving capital mobilization, and maintaining macroeconomic stability.

Novelty
This study contributes to the literature by providing updated empirical evidence on the stock market–growth nexus in Nepal using annual data from 1994 to 2025. By applying the ARDL bounds testing approach, it captures both long-run and short-run dynamics and distinguishes the effects of multiple stock market indicators, rather than relying only on the NEPSE Index as a measure of stock market development.

title: Sentiment Innovations and International Equity Returns
affiliations: Labcorp,  and University of the Aegean

detail.title: Sentiment Innovations and International Equity Returns
detail.abstract: This paper examines the dynamic effects of sentiment on international equity returns using two complementary empirical approaches. First, we estimate panel Local Projections (LPs) for 31 advanced and emerging economies over the period 1996-2023 to trace the response of real equity returns to sentiment shocks. We define a sentiment shock as the innovation in sentiment that is orthogonal to uncertainty, thereby isolating sentiment from the broader informational environment in which it is formed. Positive sentiment innovations increase real equity returns on impact, but the effect is short-lived and dissipates within two quarters. The estimated responses are larger for emerging markets than for advanced economies, although the confidence intervals overlap. Second, we estimate a global Bayesian Vector Autoregression (BVAR) based on common international factors. The BVAR results indicate that sentiment shocks influence short-run global macrofinancial dynamics; however, forecast error variance decompositions and historical decompositions show that sentiment is not a dominant persistent driver of global equity-return fluctuations. Taken together, the panel LP and global BVAR evidence suggest that sentiment innovations primarily act as short-run amplification shocks rather than as persistent sources of international equity-market movements.

title: Broad-Based Employee Ownership and Earnings Quality

detail.abstract: The paper examines whether broad-based employee ownership (BBEO) improves corporate governance by constraining managerial opportunism through increased monitoring by employees. We investigate this proposition by examining the relationship between BBEO and earnings quality. Using own-company stock in defined contribution pension plans as proxy for BBEO, we find that higher BBEO is associated with lower abnormal accruals, more persistent earnings, and a reduced likelihood of financial restatements and securities class action lawsuits. Several additional tests were performed to rule out alternative explanations. The results thus provide evidence that BBEO encourages monitoring by employees, leading to reduced managerial opportunism and enhanced financial reporting and accountability. Our paper therefore highlights the underappreciated corporate governance role of BBEO.

Other chapters cover jurisdictions representing distinct legal traditions: common law (Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaysia and India), civil law (China, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand), and hybrid systems (Philippines).

title: Fixed Point Empirical Proofs as a Deterministic Resolution to the Scientific Reproducibility Crisis: A Self-Referential Implementation
affiliations: Universal Standard Axiom Corp

detail.title: Fixed Point Empirical Proofs as a Deterministic Resolution to the Scientific Reproducibility Crisis: A Self-Referential Implementation
detail.abstract:
The scientific reproducibility crisis is not a crisis of effort or intent; it is a structural failure arising from the probabilistic accumulation of unexamined assumptions at the foundational layer of experimental design. This paper presents the Fixed Point Empirical Proof (FPEP) framework as a deterministic resolution to this crisis, executing its thesis through a unique self-referential implementation: the method is applied directly to the reproducibility problem as though reproducibility itself is the discovery target.

​By mining the existing body of meta-scientific literature for empirically hardened invariants—propositions so exhaustively validated across independent replications that residual doubt becomes operationally meaningless—we establish immutable boundary conditions from which valid experimental architectures can be deductively synthesized rather than probabilistically guessed. We formalize the core logical architecture of the FPEP framework, outline its three-stage recursive falsification protocol, and apply a Systemic Integrity Assessment (SIA) to establish foundational invariants (R_1–R_4) covering measurement validity, statistical power, construct operationalization, and contextual boundaries.

​Finally, we introduce the Empirical Inheritance Principle, demonstrating how deductive synthesis within constrained bounds allows derived conclusions to directly inherit the empirical legitimacy of their premises. The resulting framework inherits empirical legitimacy from its premises by construction, dissolving the reproducibility problem at its root rather than patching it at the surface.

title: What Reliability Metrics Miss: Evidence from NJ Transit

detail.title: What Reliability Metrics Miss: Evidence from NJ Transit
detail.abstract: NJ Transit routinely attributes service failures to Amtrak, but Amtrak may not explain every dimension of its reliability problems. We test this using monthly data from 2020-2024, estimating separate models for on-time performance (OTP), which captures schedule adherence, and mean distance between failures (MDBF), which captures fleet mechanical condition. Reported Amtrak-related incidents significantly reduce OTP but are not significantly associated with MDBF, which is far below regional peers Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road. MDBF is instead associated with ridership and funding patterns consistent with reactive investment. Amtrak explains why NJT trains run late. It does not explain why NJT trains break down.

title: From Extensional Alignment to Operator-Centric Intelligence: A Unified Framework for Turing-Computable Approximation of Physical Dynamics and Control
affiliations: and Tsinghua University

detail.title: From Extensional Alignment to Operator-Centric Intelligence: A Unified Framework for Turing-Computable Approximation of Physical Dynamics and Control
detail.abstract: Modern deep generative models display a fundamental paradox: while bounded strictly by the limits of Turing computability (T), they routinely provide highly accurate, computationally tractable solutions to physical and biological problems known to be NP-hard or non-computable from first principles. This paper presents a unified two-tier mathematical framework that resolves this paradox, spanning from foundational computability theory to engineering-ready intelligent system paradigms. At the foundational tier, we model physical reality and biological neural systems as an infinitedimensional continuous smooth manifold M governed by a non-computable evolution operator Φ t / ∈ T. Through physical measurement and symbolic recording, continuous states undergo a topological collapse via a dissipative projection operator P drop onto a discrete symbolic space D, leaking fossilized solutions of the continuous operator into empirical datasets. We prove that deep learning architectures do not execute intrinsic hypercomputation; instead, they achieve extensional alignment, minimizing empirical risk over leaked oracle pairs to yield an ϵ-approximation of Φ t 's image over a compact domain. We further formulate and prove the Semiotic Collapse Theorem, showing that recursive training on isolated synthetic data loops leads to monotonic decay of mutual information I(M; D n) and zero-measure support collapse. Building on this foundation, we present Operator-Centric Intelligence (OCI), a post-reinforcement learning paradigm that transcends the limitations of traditional RL via two core insights: (1) neural operators provide a dimensionality reduction advantage by directly learning intrinsic physical dynamics, and (2) the success of intelligent systems stems from computational delegation to external physical systems that solve intractable problems in O(1) physical time. We formalize OCI as a four-layer architecture centered on the Continuous Flow Operator (CFO), with three core mechanisms: symplectic Hamiltonian operator alignment, Pareto-optimal active querying for computational delegation, and reward demotion to a prior hint. We prove that OCI unifies all existing control and intelligence paradigms as special boundary cases, achieving unprecedented sample efficiency and engineering scalability. This framework provides a first-principles explanation for AI4Science success, establishes strict algorithmic boundaries for synthetic data scalability, offers a rigorous foundation for embodied cognition, and opens a new era of post-reinforcement learning artificial intelligence.

title: Mandated Transparency and the Production of Research: Evidence from a Data-and Code-Sharing Policy
affiliations: Yale School of Management and University of Miami - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Mandated Transparency and the Production of Research: Evidence from a Data-and Code-Sharing Policy
detail.abstract: We examine what happens to research when a journal requires authors to document their data and share the code that builds their samples. The Journal of Accounting Research (JAR) imposed such a rule on all empirical submissions in January 2015 while its closest competitors did not. We compare roughly 4,600 articles across six journals before and after the mandate. Consistent with disclosure disciplining authors, post-mandate JAR papers are written more plainly, stake fewer hedged claims, and report more completely. The hedging decline is concentrated in papers with the weakest headline evidence. Consistent with the mandate resorting who submits, JAR shifts toward more novel work by a more elite author pool, and its papers are cited less but by more prominent outlets. The writing effects are absent from exempt theory papers and reappear when a second journal adopts its own mandate. Overall, opening the research pipeline changes not just what can be checked and replicated, but what gets written and who publishes where.

title: Commodity Markets and Environmental Sustainability
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Accounting and Finance, Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Accounting and Finance and

detail.title: Commodity Markets and Environmental Sustainability
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between global commodity price returns and country-level environmental performance. Using a panel of 46 developed and emerging economies over the period 2003-2022, we combine annual commodity futures returns with country-level environmental indicators constructed from firm-level environmental scores. We document a robust negative relationship between commodity returns and subsequent environmental performance. The effect is particularly strong for energy and metals commodities and is more pronounced in developed economies. Channel analysis shows that commodity price increases are associated with higher energy intensity and greater dependence on natural resource rents, both of which are associated with environmental deterioration. Our findings remain robust across alternative specifications, dynamic panel models, instrumental variable estimation, and the use of carbon intensity as an alternative environmental measure. Overall, the results suggest that commodity returns are associated with significant environmental pressures by encouraging resource- and energy-intensive economic activity.

title: Foreign Sovereign Debt Holdings and Financial Instability: The "Venturi Effect" in Macro-Finance

detail.abstract: This article introduces the Venturi Effect (VE) in macro-finance. In fluid dynamics, the VE describes the acceleration of flow through a constricted channel, where constriction generates a static pressure drop that drives higher fluid velocity. By analogy, in macro-finance the VE is the amplification of the the speed at which exchange rates and reserves adjust (“velocity of dissipation”) by the force of investors offloading sovereign liabilities (“portfolio pressure”), which may occur when a shock hits a sovereign economy whose residual domestic capacity of debt absorption is critically compressed (“constricted channel”). This is case where, under certain conditons, human rational behavior produces a mechanical effect. The article develops the theory explaning the VE in macro-finance and finds preliminary supportive evidence. A panel of 15 emerging market economies over 2000Q1–2024Q4 shows that the mechanism activates only above an elevated debt-to-GDP regime, estimated at approximately 70 percent in the baseline specification. The article discusses the implications of the VE for debt sustainability analysis.
