detail.abstract:
This study assessed the environmental, economic, and socio-cultural impacts of the Kambingan Festival in Tuy, Batangas, Philippines, by comparing the perceptions of its two primary stakeholder groups: goat farmers and tourism stakeholders.            Grounded in Stakeholder Theory, the Triple Bottom Line (TBL), and the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework, the study employed a quantitative comparative design with 90 purposively selected respondents (62 goat farmers, 28 tourism stakeholders) using a structured questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.970, Content Validity Index = 0.92). 
     Results revealed strong consensus across both groups on positive environmental and economic impacts (*p* = 0.45, *d* = 0.16; *p* = 0.15, *d* = 0.32). However, a statistically significant difference emerged in socio-cultural perceptions (*p* = 0.04, *d* = 0.45, 95% CI [0.01, 0.89]), with goat farmers (Mean = 3.40, SD = 0.37) holding a more positive view than tourism stakeholders (Mean = 3.23, SD = 0.38). Qualitative feedback from 28 respondents corroborated these findings, revealing themes of cultural pride, economic seasonality, and environmental concerns. 
    This study provides empirical evidence on stakeholder perception gaps in agricultural festivals, demonstrating that cultural proximity significantly influences how festival impacts are experienced and valued. The findings offer actionable insights for inclusive festival governance in resource-constrained rural contexts.

title: When Data Centers Arrive: Data Center Development and Local Housing Markets
affiliations: , Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University, ,  and San Diego State University

detail.title: When Data Centers Arrive: Data Center Development and Local Housing Markets
detail.abstract: In this paper we study the impact of data center development on local economic outcomes, especially the local housing market. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design that exploits variation in data center announcement and construction timing, we find that data center development leads to slower growth in local housing prices. Further analysis shows that data center operations increase electricity consumption and prices. In addition, we find little evidence of improvements in employment, establishment formation, or property tax revenue. Consistent with these disamenities, we find a shift toward more shares of lower-income households in these communities after data center establishment. Lastly, we document a significant increase in spreads on utility municipal bonds issued by localities with new data centers. Our findings suggest that data centers may create noticeable negative externalities for their host communities.

title: Spinoffs with(out) Coworkers: Retaining the Founding Team
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE) and Koc University

detail.title: Spinoffs with(out) Coworkers: Retaining the Founding Team
detail.abstract: Employee spinoffs are typically team-founded, yet theory models departure as bargaining with a single innovator. We model an incumbent, restricted to shortterm contracts, whose innovative employee can recruit a complementary coworker, so the firm bargains against a latent founding team. A better match raises retention costs but not the implementation cutoff. The firm nonetheless shelves projects a planner would develop and, under strong complementarity, over-implements defensively. Private entrepreneurial utility generates equilibrium spinoffs: the firm buys out the coworker at low complementarity and concedes the team at high. This regime switch can flip the coworker's pay from back-loaded to front-loaded.

title: Pricing the Cost of Compliance: Equity Reactions to Mandatory ESG Disclosure in a Frontier Market

detail.title: Pricing the Cost of Compliance: Equity Reactions to Mandatory ESG Disclosure in a Frontier Market
detail.abstract: Mandatory ESG disclosure regulation imposes compliance costs that vary systematically across firms with their level of prior ESG infrastructure. This paper develops a compliance cost framework yielding three central predictions, together with an auxiliary prediction on return volatility, and examines them around the November 2021 introduction of the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) ESG Disclosures Guidance Manual. Using 60 NSE listed firms and hand-collected annual reports (2010 to 2024), I construct firm-level ESG disclosure scores via fine-tuned RoBERTa transformer models, one per pillar. Cumulative abnormal returns are estimated with the market model and tested using the Boehmer, Masumeci, and Poulsen (1991) standardized statistic with the Kolari and Pynnönen (2010) cross-sectional correlation adjustment. The average market reaction is negative but statistically weak, so the central evidence is cross-sectional. Firms with stronger pre-existing ESG communication earn markedly higher abnormal returns, approximately 2.8 percentage points per standard deviation of the disclosure score, an effect concentrated in the Environmental pillar, the domain in which firms enter least prepared and in which the mandate imposes its most demanding data-collection burdens. The effect does not vary detectably with firm size or sectoral exposure, and is not accompanied by any change in post-shock return volatility. This absence of a volatility response locates the result in the differential cost of regulatory adaptation rather than in reduced information asymmetry. The findings inform the design of mandatory disclosure frameworks in frontier capital markets where the compliance burden varies systematically with firm preparedness.

title: Beyond De-risking: Strategic Dependence as a Geopolitical Externality

detail.title: Beyond De-risking: Strategic Dependence as a Geopolitical Externality
detail.abstract:
Economic security has become a central concern in contemporary political economy, yet existing debates often focus on identifying vulnerabilities rather than explaining why strategically significant dependencies emerge and persist. This paper argues that strategic dependence should be understood as a geopolitical externality. Firms organize production and sourcing decisions according to private incentives that reward efficiency, specialization, and cost reduction, but some of the resulting risks are borne by consumers, governments, critical infrastructures, and society more broadly. Markets may therefore generate more strategic dependence than is socially optimal. 
     Drawing on the economics of externalities, the paper conceptualizes strategic dependence as a form of geopolitical market failure and reframes economic security as a problem of governing interdependence rather than reducing it. It develops a Strategic Dependence Index based on concentration, substitutability, and systemic impact, and applies the framework to rare-earth supply chains and advanced semiconductors. The analysis shows how strategically significant dependencies can be distinguished from ordinary commercial interdependence and identifies conditions under which public intervention may be justified.

title:
Governing Artificial Intelligence in Finance: 
Strategies for Balancing Sustainable Development, Innovation, Risk, and Competitiveness
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Faculty of Law

detail.title:
Governing Artificial Intelligence in Finance: 
Strategies for Balancing Sustainable Development, Innovation, Risk, and Competitiveness
detail.abstract:
The rapid development and increasing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are transforming finance. In many respects, the financial sector has led AI use (in some cases, for over two decades), not least in the context of trading and risk-management activities. Financial institutions are accelerating AI adoption to increase operational efficiency, improve risk management, and enhance their business activities. In terms of risk management, regulatory compliance, and supervisory monitoring, AI is already being widely used by both industry and regulators, improving the soundness and safety of financial markets. However, the increasing use of AI exposes the financial sector to a range of challenges and risks. 
In this paper, we analyse approaches to AI governance in finance. Following an analysis of the use of AI in finance, we first present a new taxonomy of governance and regulatory approaches based on a framework of five main elements: strategy, approach, scope, framework, and technology, derived from analysis of evolving practices across the world. Second, we develop a new analytical framework and taxonomy for the major categories of AI risk and governance across five main risk areas: macro risks, micro or sectoral risks, infrastructure risks, malicious actor and behaviour risks, and culture and human capital risks. We conclude the paper by framing the core elements of strategic approaches in terms of the development and governance of AI in finance, based on these twin taxonomies, focusing on strategy, infrastructure, regulatory approaches, the use of technology for regulatory and supervisory purposes, and the importance of developing the wider ecosystem.

title: Breadth, Depth, and Coalition Stability in Complementary Oligopoly
affiliations: Agricultural University of Athens and Drexel University

detail.title: Breadth, Depth, and Coalition Stability in Complementary Oligopoly
detail.abstract: We study when coordination among complementors is self-enforcing and price-reducing. Unlike one-dimensional complementor models, we allow each complementary component to contain rival firms, so coordination can vary both across components and within components. This creates two distinct margins: breadth across components and depth within components. Breadth internalizes cross-component spillovers, while depth weakens within-component competition and changes participation incentives. We show that stable price-reducing coordination, when it exists, preserves full breadth and adjusts depth. Strong complementarities support full-depth coordination; weak complementarities support minimal-depth coordination; and intermediate symmetric depths can restore stability only away from the endpoints of the complementarity range. Stable intermediate symmetric-depth coordination, however, need not be price-reducing. Partial-breadth or asymmetric-depth architectures do not provide stable alternatives in the market structures examined. The analysis shows that coalition size alone is insufficient to predict stability or price effects: what matters is how participation is distributed across complementary and rivalrous positions. The theory therefore provides guidance for designing coordination that internalizes complementarities while preserving enough within-component rivalry to keep prices low.

detail.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has automated the design of deep learning models but traditionally requires massive computational resources, often measured in thousands of GPU-days. In this paper, we propose a frugal and memetic NAS framework designed to democratize architecture design on consumer-grade hardware. Our approach combines the global macro-search capabilities of an autoregressive Transformer controller, trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL), with the local micro-exploitation of an Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) algorithm. To prevent premature convergence during the RL phase, we introduce a dynamic entropy mechanism that forces topological exploration upon detection of performance stagnation. Evaluated on a standard GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3060), our hybrid method effectively resolves the "cold-start" problem inherent in metaheuristics. By algorithmically penalizing network depth, our framework actively mitigates model bloat: on the CIFAR-10 dataset, it discovers an efficient architecture reaching 84.85% accuracy with only ∼174,000 parameters-significantly smaller than standard baselines like ResNet-20-in 3 hours of search time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the framework's flexibility by applying it to credit card fraud detection, directly optimizing the F1-Score on highly imbalanced tabular data to reach a F1-Score of 0.71 with a compact network of ∼4,600 parameters. These results suggest that our approach can yield tailored, accessible, and highly parameter-efficient deep learning models suitable for edge deployment.

title: From Fear to Meaning: A Generative efficiency Model of Work Effort
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics, , University of Pavia, LUMSA University and University of Perugia - Department of Economics

detail.title: From Fear to Meaning: A Generative efficiency Model of Work Effort
detail.abstract: Why do workers exert effort in environments where monitoring is imperfect and sanctions are weak? The standard efficiency wage framework explains effort as a response to extrinsic incentives where higher wages discourage shirking by increasing the cost of job loss. In this paper, we propose and test an alternative mechanism based on intrinsic motivation, which we term generative efficiency. Using survey data and structural equation modeling, we show that workplace participation does not directly affect productivity, measured as the absence of quiet quitting. Instead, participation operates indirectly by enhancing workers' well-being, which in turn significantly increase effort and reduce opportunistic behavior. We also find that participation reduces turnover intentions through its impact on the perceived meaningfulness of work. Our results suggest that effort can be sustained even in the absence of strong monitoring or wage premia, through internalized motivations linked to participation and meaning. This provides an extension to the efficiency wage literature by identifying a non-pecuniary pathway to efficiency that relies on intrinsic rather than disciplinary mechanisms. These findings have important implications for both theory and practice, highlighting the role of participatory governance and workplace meaning as substitutes for traditional incentive schemes.

This paper introduces Bounded Wealth Theory (BWT), an economic framework that proposes a mathematical ceiling on an individual’s wealth accumulation practices. It reveals a sharing mechanism applied to wealth growth above the defined ceiling. The framework further discloses a distribution model for the resulting fund. BWT addresses three problems that existing frameworks have failed to overcome. First, the immeasurable compounding of wealth inequality identified by Piketty (2014), for which no enforcement procedures have been formally articulated. Second, the self-sustaining revenue source to keep UBI (Universal Basic Income) alive. Third, the welfare payments that discourage people from working. The BWT framework introduces five formal rules on caped wealth beyond a ceiling. First, the wealth ceiling (W*) is defined as 10,000 times national GDP per capita. The maths has been derived on the grounds of total working days in one’s complete career. Second, a sharing rate formula using an exponential wealth saturation function. Third, an Extraction Score (E) that quantifies the total wealth captured vs. the wealth created. Fourth, a three-tier distribution model called Graduated Conditional Universalism (GCU), and fifth, three mathematically defined equilibrium conditions that push forward the theory’s success criteria. An empirical simulation for India (2024), using data from the World Bank, Credit Suisse/UBS, and Hurun, estimates that BWT could raise about ₹19.76 lakh crore ($237 billion) annually from around 167,000 individuals. The average payment to the poorest individual would exceed the $2.15/day poverty line. This could potentially lift many of India’s 129 million extremely poor people out of poverty. The analysis uses transparent assumptions, with all data sources and limitations clearly stated.

title: Political Persuasion under Strategic Fact-Checking
affiliations: University of Cyprus, , University of Cyprus and School of Economics, University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Political Persuasion under Strategic Fact-Checking
detail.abstract: We study political persuasion when communication is disciplined by an endogenous, imperfect fact-checker in an electorate with heterogeneous voters. A strategic Persuader designs a communication policy to influence public beliefs, anticipating a Checker who can audit realized messages. Audits attempt to refute messages by checking for inconsistency and succeed only probabilistically. This imperfection creates a certification channel: when an audit does not refute a message, voters update in the message's favor. Certification reshapes the Checker's incentives. Although auditing can screen out misleading claims, it can also backfire by legitimizing surviving claims and persuading otherwise skeptical voters. We characterize equilibrium auditing and communication, identifying conditions under which the Checker strategically abstains to avoid such certification-induced backfires. Heterogeneous voter skepticism is central to this mechanism, as the Persuader trades off broad persuasion against preserving support among easier-topersuade voters. The Persuader optimally exploits the Checker's reluctance by injecting calibrated noise at the boundary where the Checker is just indifferent to auditing. We extend the model to partial commitment and show that our equilibrium results are robust to sufficiently strong commitment power.

title: LLMs and Economic History: A Comment on Ferrara (2026)
affiliations: Department of Economics, Stellenbosch University

detail.title: LLMs and Economic History: A Comment on Ferrara (2026)
detail.abstract: Ferrara (2026) provides economic historians with a detailed guide to large language models, organised around an iterative workflow for working with them. Its worked examples concentrate on the middle of the research process: turning a source into a validated variable and checking that the variable measures what it claims to. I argue that this is where the technology changes the discipline least, because it is the stage the discipline already knew how to perform, at high cost. The larger effects, and the new scarcities, occur at the two ends of the research production function – the chain of steps from question to published paper – with judgement in the choice of question and source at one end, and the choice of narrative, not its prose, in communicating the result at the other; and in a coordination layer between them. I set out this reframing, propose specific uses at the stages the guide does not cover, and identify four concerns it underweights: recursive contamination of the historical record, a validation paradox, unequal access and congestion in how research is evaluated. The central claim is that the binding constraint in economic history is moving from production to judgement.

detail.abstract: How do you convince someone of a claim they cannot check? Many economic questions that decide elections-whether immigrants take jobs, whether automation will destroy them-have answers distant in time, diffuse in cause, and unobservable from ordinary life. Like the listener to a time traveller, the citizen cannot test them and falls back on a prior; which prior fills the vacuum turns on whether elites have made the issue partisan. Holding a survey item fixed and measuring tribalization independently from a century of congressional speech, we find the Republican-Democrat gap on whether immigrants take jobs widening from zero in 1996 to thirty-three points in 2024, driven almost entirely by the out-group converging on the experts, until the fact sorts nearly as hard by party as the policy preference beside it. The sorting is sharpest among the most knowledgeable-the signature of motivated reasoning, not ignorance-and the same asymmetric capture reappears on a fact from outside economics entirely, disbelief that humans evolved. Facts, not only preferences, undergo issue evolution, and on contested claims more information sharpens the divide rather than closing it.

title:
Beyond Punishment
A Neurobiological and Philosophical Foundationfor the Evolution of Justice

detail.title:
Beyond Punishment
A Neurobiological and Philosophical Foundationfor the Evolution of Justice
detail.abstract:
The measure of a civilization is not the severity of its punishments, but the depth of its capacity to heal."-İrfan Boko  
This book challenges the foundational logic of punitive justice by situating criminal behavior within a neurobiological and philosophical framework. Drawing on neuroscience, ontology, and systems theory, it argues that punishment as currently practiced is not a rational response to harm but a culturally inherited reflex — one that fails both the individual and society. The author introduces the Boko Neuro-Justice (BNJ) framework, which reconceptualizes crime not as moral transgression deserving retribution, but as a systemic signal of developmental failure, neurological constraint, and structural inequality. Each chapter develops a layered argument: from the architecture of the brain and the formation of selfhood, through the social and political dimensions of justice, toward a transformative model grounded in neurocognitive realism and ethical responsibility. The book proposes that the evolution of justice requires moving beyond punishment toward a system capable of understanding, repairing, and ultimately preventing harm at its root. Written in three languages — English, Turkish, and French — this trilingual work reflects the author's commitment to making transformative ideas accessible across linguistic and cultural boundaries.

title: Concentration at the Audit-free Ceiling: First-Time Issuers and the Regulation Crowdfunding Audited-financials Threshold
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Concentration at the Audit-free Ceiling: First-Time Issuers and the Regulation Crowdfunding Audited-financials Threshold
detail.abstract: A September 2022 rule requires first-time Regulation Crowdfunding (Reg CF) issuers to file audited rather than reviewed financial statements once the offering cap exceeds $1,235,000. After the rule, first-time issuers concentrate at the audit-free ceiling. The concentration is absent before the rule, is much larger than at nearby roundnumber placebo thresholds, and is not matched by repeat issuers at the same dollar value. Repeat issuers instead concentrate at their own $618,000 audit threshold. The evidence points to a response to the audited-financials cutoff rather than a general preference for round numbers or a broad 2021 market effect. The result remains after removing portals with high exact-threshold templating. The estimated 1 excess-bunching share is 0.108 outside the high-templating portals and 0.318 in the full sample. The first estimate is interpreted as a conservative lower bound on issuer-side bunching, while the second includes portal templating. The design estimates the bunching response at the audit threshold; it does not recover a structural dollar cost of compliance.

title: "Paradox of Digital Literacy and Cybercrime in the Education Sector"
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: "Paradox of Digital Literacy and Cybercrime in the Education Sector"
detail.abstract: This paper argues that India’s digital turn in education has produced a paradox: the same expansion of digital literacy and infrastructure that democratises learning has also amplified the scale, sophistication and frequency of cybercrime against and from within the education sector. It points out the cyber deficiencies in the education sector to understand why the sector is one of the most attacked ones in India. Further, it analyses the paradoxical impact by drawing on anecdotal incidents and proposes practical and aspirational solutions.

title: Transfer Learning for Change-point Problems: A GBC Markov-embedded Approach
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Warwick - Department of Statistics

detail.title: Transfer Learning for Change-point Problems: A GBC Markov-embedded Approach
detail.abstract: We develop a framework unifying three lines of research on change-point problems: the Bayesian treatment of Smith [1975] and the Markov embedding of Chib [1998]; the minimax theory of change-point localization and online detection; and structured nonparametric estimation by trend ltering. The connection has two parts. First, Chib's left-to-right hidden Markov embedding is a prior whose maximum-a-posteriori segmentation coincides with the ℓ 0-penalized least-squares estimator of the minimax literature; the geometric segment durations are an exponential prior on spacing, and a globallocal (horseshoe) prior on rst dierences is its continuous relaxation, which contains Bayesian trend ltering as a special case. Second, we use Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) as the inference engine: the segmentation posterior is represented as a transport map from a uniform base measure, learned once by a deep quantile network on simulated data, so that inference at a new series is a single forward pass. This amortized representation is, we argue, the natural vehicle for transfer learning: a generator trained on an abundant source domain transfers a shared change-point structure to a data-scarce target domain, while domain-specic segment parameters are re-estimated. We prove posterior contraction at the minimax localization rate, Bayes-factor consistency for the number of change points, and a BerkSanov concentration theorem showing that under model misspecication the posterior converges to the KullbackLeibler projection at an exponential rate; we bound the generative approximation error, establish an oracle inequality that delineates positive from negative transfer, and give an anytime-valid e-process calibration of the online forward lter, which we relate to particle lters and to the continuous-time Shiryaev problem. Four simulation studieson transfer learning, amortized posterior calibration, ℓ 0 solvers, and robustness under misspecication support the theory.

title: Predictive Martingale Inference without Mixing: Consistency, Local Asymptotic Normality, and Deviation Principles

detail.title: Predictive Martingale Inference without Mixing: Consistency, Local Asymptotic Normality, and Deviation Principles
detail.abstract: We give a unified account of predictive Bayesian inference in which the engine is the martingale structure of a sequence of one-step-ahead predictive distributions, not a mixing or ergodicity hypothesis on the data. For conditionally identically distributed sequences-whose future observations are identically, though not independently, distributed given the pastthe predictives converge almost surely and uniformly to a random limit, the de Finetti directing measure, by Doob's theorem alone; we record this and a generalisation requiring only that each predictive coordinate be a bounded martingale. We then trace the same martingale-difference principle through three asymptotic regimes governed by a single local information object: a local asymptotic normality (LAN) expansion whose central sequence is a martingale and whose limit is normal (well-specified, ergodic) or mixed normal (non-ergodic, exchangeable); a moderate deviation principle (MDP) interpolating between the LAN and large-deviation scales; and a Sanov / largedeviation principle whose rate function is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. A predictive limit theorem collects these regimes and shows that the curvature H * and score variance  at the Kullback-Leibler projection control all of them, with the MDP quadratic rate equal both to the Hessian of the Sanov rate and to the inverse asymptotic covariance. The framework subsumes the recursive quasi-Bayes constructions of Hahn-Martin-Walker and Fong-Holmes-Walker, the prequential consistency of Skouras-Dawid and Sinha Roy-Everitt-Robert-Dutta, the tilted de Finetti theorem of Polson-Zantedeschi, the moderate-deviation calibration of Bayesian testing of Datta-Polson-Sokolov-Zantedeschi, and the stochastic-approximation analyses of predictive recursion and online EM. title: The Relaxed Bayesian Investor: Optimal Stock Liquidation under Drift Uncertainty, Gap, Default and Volatility Risk

detail.title: The Relaxed Bayesian Investor: Optimal Stock Liquidation under Drift Uncertainty, Gap, Default and Volatility Risk
detail.abstract: Mijatović et al. (2026) solve two symmetric stock-liquidation problems built on the lifetime supremum of a defaultable asset driven by a spectrally negative Lévy process. Their optimal rules are a pair of thresholds on the drift µ that partition the parameter space into sell now, hold to default, and an intermediate drawdown-barrier regime. We take the thresholds at face value and confront them with the one fact that makes them hard to use: µ is the only quantity in the model that cannot be estimated. The asymmetry is a theorem of high-frequency econometrics (Aït-Sahalia and Jacod, 2014): the diffusion coefficient is recovered at rate √ n from intraday data, the drift only at rate √ T in calendar span, with irreducible standard error σ/ √ T. Following Rogers' relaxed-investor program and the Bayesian premium analysis of Jobert et al. (2006), we recast liquidation as filtering and stopping: µ carries a prior and is learned from the path, σ is known. Three results follow. The problem stays Markovian in the posterior (m t , v t) and the drawdown, so the thresholds survive under µ → m t and σ 2 → σ 2 + 2v t /q; uncertainty widens the barrier region and sells sooner. A relaxed Bayesian investor who reviews every h loses only 1 4 σ 4 h π * 2 (1-π *) 2 per unit time, orders of magnitude below the cost of drift uncertainty. And the predictive law of the supremum is a posterior mixture with a strictly heavier tail than its plug-in counterpart, so plug-in calibration understates drawdown risk. We give efficient estimators for every parameter, a generative-Bayes recipe for the non-conjugate jump and tempered-stable cases, and an empirical analysis of the NASDAQ Composite. T 1 {τ ≥T } .

title: Market Expectations in the Cross-Section of Leading Present Values

detail.title: Market Expectations in the Cross-Section of Leading Present Values
detail.abstract: We revisit the cross-sectional present-value framework of Kelly and Pruitt (2013) and show that it remains robust once heterogeneous information diffusion is taken into account. We propose a LASSO-PLS approach that uses LASSO to identify real-time information leaders, followed by factor extraction via partial least squares. By filtering out stale signals from slow-moving assets, our method restores out-of-sample market return predictability, improving the monthly R 2 oos to 1.1% over 1930-2024, while remaining robust across portfolio granularities, sample splits, and alternative specifications. Our results demonstrate how incorporating economically motivated market structure can enhance the reliability of supervised learning methods in asset pricing.

title: Breadth Momentum and Hidden Markov Regime Detection: A Composite Signal for Tactical Equity Allocation

detail.title: Breadth Momentum and Hidden Markov Regime Detection: A Composite Signal for Tactical Equity Allocation
detail.abstract: We apply a composite regime gate to a tactical allocation strategy on a universe of 19 country equity exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The composite is constructed by combining two regime detectors, the breadth-momentum signal and a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show that the two signals are complementary rather than redundant. Breadth is a cross-sectional measure of how broadly the universe is participating, while HMM is a time-series measure of the statistical state of the basket. Each signal alone produces many false positive bear flags, while the combination of two signals agrees at the major regime transitions of the backtested period. We use 4 equity-based features and 2 rate-based features. The defensive leg rotates between long-duration Treasuries (TLT) and cash. Over the period from January 2004 to December 2025, the composite strategy delivers a Sharpe ratio of 0.72 and a maximum drawdown of-23.1%, compared to 0.53 and-58.0% for the equal-weighted basket, 0.46 and-57.4% for MSCI EAFE, and 0.77 and-50.8% for SPY buy-and-hold. The composite strategy more than halves the maximum drawdown of the passive benchmarks and exceeds SPY's compound annual growth rate by 1.5%.

detail.abstract: Antonio Genovesi's Lezioni di commercio has usually been read as a theory of pubblica felicità, with fede pubblica treated as a moral precondition for civil economy. This article proposes a more limited and historically constrained reconstruction. It does not claim that Genovesi formulated a modern social-scientific theory of trust production. Rather, it argues that the Lezioni provides conceptual resources for an anticipatory framework in which public trust is formed through reciprocal assistance, conserved and extended by intermediate institutions, and amplified, but not originated, by commerce. On this reading, pubblica felicità is less an independently specified goal than the civil outcome and diagnostic indicator of a social order in which these mechanisms function. The article reorders, rather than rejects, existing interpretations: Bruni and Zamagni rightly identify the normative centrality of reciprocity and public happiness; Robertson and Reinert rightly locate Genovesi within the reform ambitions of Naples; Putnam empirically demonstrates the association between civic life and trust; Coleman specifies some network conditions of obligation and enforcement; North identifies the indispensability of informal constraints. Genovesi's contribution, reconstructed here, is to make visible the formative and reproductive processes that these literatures often leave incompletely specified. The article therefore positions civil economy not as a fully articulated modern theory, but as a historically specific proto-theory of trust production whose reconstructible ordering remains useful for contemporary debates on social capital, institutional transplantation, and the non-state foundations of commercial society.

title: Finite-Horizon Portfolio Choice, Labor Supply, and Early Retirement under Borrowing Constraints

detail.title: Finite-Horizon Portfolio Choice, Labor Supply, and Early Retirement under Borrowing Constraints
detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon optimal consumption and portfolio problem with labor supply flexibility and an irreversible early retirement option under a borrowing constraint. The agent chooses consumption, risky investment, and leisure before retirement, while after retirement labor income disappears and leisure is fixed at its maximal level. Preferences are described by a Cobb-Douglas utility, and wealth must remain nonnegative. Using a dual martingale method, we transform the primal problem into a zero-sum stoppersingular-controller game. The associated dual value is characterized by a min-max parabolic variational inequality with obstacle and gradient constraints. We show that the maximal strong solution of the resulting variational inequality is the unique admissible strong solution whose gradientconstrained free boundary, namely the binding boundary, is monotone increasing in calendar time. A verification argument then identifies this strong solution with the value of the stopper-singularcontroller game, and duality recovers the optimal retirement, consumption, leisure, and portfolio policies. The numerical analysis recovers the value function and optimal policies, and illustrates how labor supply flexibility affects consumption, portfolio choice, and retirement timing under borrowing constraints.

detail.title: Geoeconomics and trade
detail.abstract: We study the role of geoeconomics in shaping globalisation and trade policy. We first review the evolution of world trade since the end of World War II, highlighting the drivers of globalisation and its economic consequences. We then synthesise recent research on geoeconomics, which analyses how countries use trade policy as a tool to pursue geopolitical objectives. Against this background, we argue that the gradual shift in geoeconomic power from the United States toward China since the 2000s has been driving a fragmentation in world trade along geopolitical lines. We provide conceptual policy recommendations for the European Union to navigate an environment characterised by intensifying geopolitical competition.

title: GBC for Graphical Models: the Dual Geometry of CEGs and MDMs

detail.title: GBC for Graphical Models: the Dual Geometry of CEGs and MDMs

keywords: 62-08. Keywords And Phrases. Chain Event Graphs

detail.abstract: Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) is a likelihood free, simulation driven inference engine. It writes a posterior as a transport map θ = H(τ, S(y)) that pushes base noise τ ∼ U(0, 1)d forward to the posterior, and it learns H from prior predictive draws with a deep quantile network, conditioning only on a summary statistic S(y). Its central open question is which statistic to use. We answer it for two of the most flexible graphical model classes: Chain Event Graphs (CEGs), for discrete processes that unfold asymmetrically, and Multiregression Dynamic Models (MDMs), for multivariate time series with a contemporaneous causal architecture. Both, we show, carry a single dually flat information geometry. A staged tree or CEG is a discrete log linear (toric) model whose atomic probabilities are monomials in the floret parameters, so its staging hypotheses are affine in the natural coordinates and cut out e flat submanifolds. An MDM is a system of conditional Gaussian dynamic linear models glued by a contemporaneous directed acyclic graph, so each conditional filter transports a Gaussian belief whose moments are the dual coordinates while the graph imposes m flat constraints. Our main structural result is that in both classes the minimal sufficient statistic is the mixture (expectation) coordinate of the dual geometry, namely stage pooled floret counts for a CEG and predictive moments for an MDM, and this is exactly the statistic on which GBC must condition; a noise outsourcing argument then shows that the conditional transport map exists and is fixed by that statistic. The geometry therefore selects the GBC summary rather than leaving it to taste. We prove the supporting results, give one GBC algorithm covering both classes with a maximum expected utility decision layer, and validate the method on a staged CEG against the exact Dirichlet posterior, on a two node MDM against exact Kalman filtering, and on a non conjugate logistic floret against a gold standard sampler. Two empirical studies show the method at scale: a hierarchical, non conjugate staged tree fitted to the Titanic data, and a stochastic volatility dynamic network of four European equity indices, on which the GBC ensemble transport filter recovers the latent volatility that the conjugate Kalman recursion cannot, while an amortized GBC map estimates the volatility hyperparameters of this non exponential family model from a geometry selected second order summary

detail.abstract: I extend the cross-sectional channel between earnings-announcement timing and postannouncement returns documented by Bagnoli et al. (2002) from the first moment (the within-firm directional deviation of the announcement delay) to the second moment (the within-firm time-series variance of the delay). For each firm-quarter (𝑖, 𝑞), let Δ 𝑖,𝑞 denote the announcement delay, defined as the calendar-day difference between the firm's quarterly earnings-announcement date and its fiscal quarter-end. The signal of interest, 𝑉 𝑖,𝑡 , is the standard deviation of Δ 𝑖,𝑞 over the eight quarters ending at 𝑡. On a Russell 3000 panel of 620{,}290 firm-quarter observations spanning 1999-2024 from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) and Compustat, the long-short portfolio that goes long the lowest-quintile 𝑉 firms within the Fama-French 12-industry monthly cross-section and short the highest quintile is sign-correct in 12 of 12 in-sample cells and in 11 of 12 hold-out cells (2017-2024). Four of twelve cells survive a family-wise Bonferroni correction at the 5% level in-sample; zero of twelve do so on the eight-year hold-out. The equal-weighted composite of the four primary cells, vol-matched to the in-sample maximum-Sharpe tangent combination of the Fama and French (2015) five-factor and Carhart (1997) momentum factors (annualized volatility 3.9%), delivers a Newey-West HAC-corrected annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.01 in-sample and 0.82 on the hold-out net of a 20-basis-point monthly round-trip transaction cost, against the tangent benchmark's 1.05 and 1.01. The cadence-variance signal is mechanistically separated from post-earnings-announcement drift: replacing the next-trading-day forward-window start with a one-week delay strengthens rather than weakens the result in all four primary cells. The within-firm directional deviation signal proposed by Chambers and Penman (1984) fails the same battery on the same panel under both symmetric and asymmetric encodings, indicating that the within-firm-deviation channel has decayed post-publication while the variance channel survives. The contribution is methodological: a moment extension of an established anchor, a parallel failed replication of the nearest prior signal, and mechanism-separation evidence ruling out the most natural alternative explanation.

title: Sleepless Nights, Safer Roads? Night-time Air Alerts and Behavioural Risk Avoidance

detail.title: Sleepless Nights, Safer Roads? Night-time Air Alerts and Behavioural Risk Avoidance
detail.abstract: Do salient threats make people take more or less risk? I study this question using wartime air alerts in Ukraine, a recurring shock that is threatening, disruptive, and often occurs at night. Combining time-stamped alert records with daily administrative traffic-accident data from Lviv, I find that each additional hour of overnight alert exposure is associated with about 10 percent fewer next-day accidents. The decline is concentrated in afternoon and evening travel, weekends, central areas, and accident categories linked to risky driving, while fatigue-related accidents do not increase. These patterns are consistent with behavioural risk avoidance: after a salient threat, people appear to reduce or retime discretionary travel and drive more cautiously. Evidence from thirteen other Ukrainian cities suggests that this response is strongest where alerts are relatively rare and weaker where alerts are routine. Salient threats can therefore reduce risky behaviour, but the response appears to depend on continued salience.

title: The Environment of Social Institutions: Measuring the Informational and Behavioural Infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Environment of Social Institutions: Measuring the Informational and Behavioural Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Institutional analysis has long treated the informational environment as a neutral backdrop-something institutions exist "within" but do not shape. This article argues that the medium through which signals propagate is itself a constitutive feature of institutional life, and that prescriptive communications (norms) operate on a plane analytically distinct from the behavioral clusters (institutions) they are assumed to produce. Drawing on Shannon's information theory, Rapoport's systems subjectivism, and empirical research spanning algorithmic governance, cross-cultural communication, and regulatory compliance, the article constructs a fully specified conceptual architecture for the informational dimension of institutional analysis. It defines a signal's internal anatomy (source, carrier, form, timestamp), proposes four measurable field-level parameters (density, propagation speed, access asymmetry, entropy), and formalizes the norm as a meta-signal-an interpretative code that exists in the information field alongside ordinary descriptive signals. The measurable divergence between the normative layer (what agents are told they ought to do) and the behavioral layer (what they actually do) is formalized as institutional anomie, a diagnostic variable grounded in Durkheim's original formulation and rendered operationally precise through modern computational methods-including the Jensen-Shannon divergence and total variation distance. Each parameter and construct is illustrated with examples drawn from digital platforms, cross-cultural settings, and contemporary regulatory environments. The result is a framework that treats the information field not as a passive container but as an active, configurable dimension of institutional analysis-one that can be measured, compared, and experimentally manipulated.

title: Contaminated Capital: Brownfield Grants, Entrepreneurship, and Place-Based Redistribution
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Finance Area, Harbert College of Business, Auburn University and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Contaminated Capital: Brownfield Grants, Entrepreneurship, and Place-Based Redistribution
detail.abstract: We study whether environmental cleanup incentives operate as effective place-based redistribution by transforming contaminated land into productive capital for local entrepreneurs. We link the universe of grant applicants to the Environmental Protection Agency’s Brownfields Program with business credit records, firm outcomes, property tax parcels, mortgage activity, and rental market data. Exploiting discontinuities in cleanup grant scores via a stacked dynamic regression discontinuity design, as well as EPA funding expansions in 2018 and 2022, we find that cleanup grants increase local firm entry, survival, employment, and business credit access, with complementary effects on parcel liquidity and mortgage credit that suggest remediation improves the collateral value of formerly contaminated land. These effects are concentrated within three miles of remediated sites and persist after construction activity ends, suggesting that remediation does more than generate temporary cleanup demand. Treatment effects are strongest in places with more severe pre-existing contamination, industrial decline, and credit frictions, and the gains accrue primarily to local owners and entrepreneurs. Environmental remediation incentives therefore increase aggregate local growth while redistributing investment toward historically capital-starved places through flypaper effects, mitigating the misallocation problem traditionally associated with place-based subsidy programs.

detail.abstract: The paper documents models used to analyse the interactions and trade-offs between price and financial stability at the European Central Bank. The paper describes a simple conceptual framework to think about the short- and medium-term trade-offs between price and financial stability. Short-term trade-offs arise whenever current inflationary pressure is high, but the financial system is experiencing stress. Medium-term trade-offs arise whenever current inflationary pressure is low, but risk is building up in the financial system. We document four main sets of models used to quantify trade-offs: time series models, balance sheet models, credit risk models and DSGE models with banking and financial frictions.

detail.abstract: Post-harvest loss (PHL) in Sub-Saharan Africa is routinely cited at 20 to 40 percent of perishable output, yet this aggregate figure obscures the relative weight of its causes and has driven two decades of investment toward on-farm storage while transport, the link connecting every other stage of the chain, has remained comparatively under-examined. This short communication disaggregates published PHL evidence by cause and supply-chain stage, drawing on national household surveys, Zimbabwean tomatochain diagnostics, and regional value-chain studies, to estimate the share of loss attributable specifically to transport failure. Across the reviewed evidence, transport-linked factors, including delayed pickup, vehicle unavailability, poor road quality, and improper in-transit handling, account for a substantial and frequently underestimated portion of physical and quality loss in perishable horticulture, in several cases rivalling or exceeding storage-related loss. Operational data from digital freight-matching platforms serving informal African produce markets corroborate the literature by showing that reductions in farmer waiting time for transport correspond with measurable reductions in reported spoilage. We argue that PHL reduction strategies that treat transport as exogenous infrastructure, rather than as a coordination failure amenable to digital intervention, will continue to under-deliver. Policy and investment should be rebalanced toward demand-responsive, technology-enabled transport coordination for last-mile produce movement.

title: Who Pays for Growth? Evidence from Data Centers and the Grid
affiliations: Sanford School of Public Policy, Duke University , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, North Carolina State University and North Carolina State University

detail.title: Who Pays for Growth? Evidence from Data Centers and the Grid

declarations.funderStatement: Zhenxuan Wang gratefully acknowledges funding support from the Institute for Humane Studies (grant no. IHS020420) for data purchase.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving rapid growth in electricity demand through the expansion of data centers. Meeting this demand requires complementary infrastructure investment, but who pays for that investment depends on the institutions that finance, regulate, and allocate its costs. We study this question by linking facility-level data on data center entry to utility-level data on retail electricity prices, infrastructure investment, operational outcomes, and regulatory rate case proceedings across the United States. Data center entry between 2010 and 2024 increases average retail electricity prices by 2.7%, with effects of 2.1% for residential customers, 2.8% for commercial customers, and 4.2% for industrial customers. These effects are concentrated among investor-owned utilities, where average retail prices rise by 5.6%, while effects are much smaller among publicly-owned utilities and absent among cooperatives. Price increases are also larger in states with deregulated electricity generation. To explain these patterns, we examine utility investment, operations, and rate case outcomes. Data center entry induces real infrastructure and operational responses, including construction work in progress, generation investment, transmission spending, and larger authorized rate bases. But pass-through depends on regulatory environment: vertically integrated utilities in regulated states appear to absorb load growth partly through improved utilization, while utilities in deregulated states exhibit more active cost recovery and greater exposure to system constraints. The results show that the incidence of infrastructure-intensive technological change depends not only on the technology itself, but also on the institutions governing complementary infrastructure investment and cost recovery.

title: Taxing Generative AI: Evidence from Chicago

detail.title: Taxing Generative AI: Evidence from Chicago
detail.abstract: I estimate three empirical objects using variation from a new tax on generative AI: passthrough, demand elasticity, and incidence across the income distribution. To my knowledge, none has been estimated in the consumer market for generative AI. Using transaction-level data from 97 million debit and credit cards, I first establish that a 9% tax induced a price increase of 8.06%, i.e. near full pass-through. Second, 13 months after the tax, ChatGPT subscriptions in Chicago were approximately 25.9% below a synthetic control, implying a demand elasticity of -3.2. Third, while ChatGPT subscribers are much richer than average, a tax on generative AI is not progressive as a share of income. The income gradient in subscriptions is not steep enough to offset the fact that the tax is a flat dollar amount. Finally, combining these estimates in a sufficient statistics formula, I find an optimal tax rate on ChatGPT far below Chicago's current rate of 15%.

title: Local Spillovers of Startup Innovation
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Hollo School of Real Estate, University of Richmond and University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Local Spillovers of Startup Innovation
detail.abstract: When startups innovate, does the surrounding area prosper? Exploiting quasi-random assignment of patent examiners with varying leniency, we show that patent grants to startups increase nearby annualized real estate returns by 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points for residential properties and 0.5 to 0.9 percentage points for commercial properties and vacant land. Effects are largest for the first successful startup in an area and decline with additional successes. We also find that patent-granted startups spur nearby patenting, establishments, and jobs. Yet these real effects emerge only over the following decade, while real estate return premia appear immediately.

title: Liberty Global and the Revival of Economic Substance
affiliations: University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: Liberty Global and the Revival of Economic Substance
detail.abstract: On April 21 the Tenth Circuit issued its longawaited opinion in Liberty Global. 1 By a 2-1 majority, the panel upheld the decision of the district court that a tax shelter used by Liberty Global had to be disregarded under the economic substance doctrine (ESD). This decision is the third victory of the government in ESD cases, following Patel and Otay. 2 But it is the most significant because it strikes a decisive blow against tax shelters built on a literal application of the statutory text but ignore Congress’s purpose in enacting that text. Patel established that the ESD can be relevant to tax shelter cases even if the shelters follow the text of the statute, and Otay held that a transaction that had a valid overall business purpose can still fail the ESD if that purpose did not require an elaborate tax-motivated structure. Liberty Global goes beyond these cases by holding that a tax shelter that complies with the text of the code can be disregarded because it deviates from Congress’s purpose in enacting that text. This is a welcome departure from the narrow textualism followed by the Tax Court in Varian.

title: A Socioeconomic Analysis of AI Agents and the Restructuring of the Knowledge Labor Market

detail.title: A Socioeconomic Analysis of AI Agents and the Restructuring of the Knowledge Labor Market
detail.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents is fundamentally reshaping the socioeconomic structure of knowledge-based industries. This paper examines the impact of these technologies on labor market dynamics, specifically focusing on the generational tension between senior and junior professionals. Utilizing a mixed-methods research design that combines macroeconomic technology adoption data with a qualitative analysis of vanguard industry case studies, we analyze how the automation of complex cognitive workflows alters the traditional talent pipeline. The findings reveal the emergence of "Synthetic Seniority": junior workers experience an immediate amplification of their operational output but lack the critical judgment required to audit subtle algorithmic failures. Concurrently, senior professionals who fail to adapt to the governance of multi-agent systems face accelerated obsolescence due to the economic non-viability of manual execution timelines. We conclude that AI agents do not generate a linear path toward technological unemployment; instead, they trigger a structural fragmentation of the labor market, shifting economic value away from technical execution and toward strategic human judgment and risk management. This shift underscores an urgent need to reconfigure corporate training frameworks and school-to-work transition models.

detail.abstract: We analyze sectoral resilience for wage increase by constructing a multi-ratio composite index using the 2023 CPS ASEC data. The Unemployment Ratio measures labor market slack, with a 3% unemployment rate as a baseline. Sectors meeting this rate are assigned a ratio of 1, while sectors with higher or lower unemployment rates are adjusted proportionally. The Wage Ratio evaluates sectors based on their median wage levels, using the national median wage as a baseline, with adjustments made for sectors with above or below median wages. Further breakdowns include the Educational Wage Ratios and Regional Wage Ratios, which assess how education and regional differences influence wage dynamics across sectors and within the same sector. A formula that combines the Unemployment Ratio, the Educational Wage Ratio and the Regional Wage Ratio produces the multi-ratio composite index to assess sectoral resilience in a more granular fashion. Scores above 1 indicate a sector's capacity to manage wage increases effectively, while scores below 1 highlight potential pressure points that may require cost-saving measures. The multi-ratio composite index provides business leaders with valuable insights into strategic decision-making in a rapidly changing economic landscape.

detail.abstract: This study analyzed the implementation gaps in disaster risk reduction (DRR) in educational institutions in Metro Manila. It focused on key areas such as resource allocation, capacity building, infrastructure, and preparedness measures, including drills and emergency kits. The study used a qualitative approach with elements of mixed methods, combining documentary analysis and data presented through reference tables. Data were collected from secondary sources such as government publications and related studies. Quantitative data from selected literature were summarized in tables to support the analysis. The findings showed that while schools demonstrate moderate preparedness, gaps still exist in resources, training, and infrastructure, affecting the overall effectiveness of DRR programs.

detail.title: Women’s Rights in Afghanistan under Taliban rule- A Human Rights Perspective
detail.abstract: The rights of women all around the globe from time immemorial has been in jeopardy more so in certain geographical regions than others and it has worsened with time. Women’s rights have been stolen, their freedom curtailed beyond reason, and their whole entity reduced to a mere animal existence. Though violations of rights and crimes against women are prevalent across the world, their intensity and prevalence have been excessive in certain states. The laws, rules and customs based on religion created by the powers that be, have all contributed to oppress women further. It is pertinent to mention that this study does not aim to diminish religion or is not against any specific religion or customs, but it only seeks to point out the shortcomings of the humans or leaders in interpreting and enforcing such norms for individual benefit and with the ulterior motive of suppressing one gender. This study is limited only to women rights in Afghanistan subsequent to the rule by the Taliban. It focuses on how the Taliban regime tends to affect millions of women’s rights and freedom in Afghanistan, and the role of international law in promoting women's rights. This study seeks to analyse the lives of women in Afghanistan before and after Taliban rule, and through that it sheds limelight on how women are treated even in the 21st century, as property of men and are suffering a worse fate than an animal.

title: Subjective Expectations and Inequalities in Human Capital Across the Early Life Course
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Subjective Expectations and Inequalities in Human Capital Across the Early Life Course
detail.abstract: Inequalities in human capital emerge early in life and persist across both low-and high-income countries alike. Understanding the mechanisms behind these disparities is essential for designing effective policy responses. Heterogeneity in parental choice plays an important role. This article examines how subjective expectations data can be used to identify the sources of heterogeneity in parental choices and investments that shape children's human capital throughout the early life course. Drawing on evidence from multiple applications, I show how eliciting subjective expectations in surveys-and combining them with observed choices-can help disentangle the relative roles of preferences, beliefs, and constraints in shaping investment behavior. The findings reveal that the dominant mechanisms vary across contexts, highlighting the value of expectations data in guiding context-specific policy interventions.

title: The Erosion of Labor-Based Comparative Advantage: Artificial Intelligence and Development Regime Transition
affiliations: The University of Manchester and University of Southampton

detail.title: The Erosion of Labor-Based Comparative Advantage: Artificial Intelligence and Development Regime Transition
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology capable of transforming productivity, innovation, and economic organization across a wide range of sectors. While existing research has primarily focused on the implications of AI for employment, wages, and productivity, its consequences for structural transformation and comparative advantage remain insufficiently understood. This paper develops a theoretical framework to examine how AI may reshape the traditional development mechanism that links labor abundance, low wages, manufacturing competitiveness, and industrialization. Building on the Lewis-Kuznets-Chenery tradition of structural transformation, the paper argues that AI progressively weakens the labor-cost channel that has historically enabled laborabundant economies to industrialize through manufacturing-led growth. A formal model is developed in which AI substitutes for labor in production while simultaneously reducing the responsiveness of competitiveness to wage differentials. Extending conventional structural transformation models, the framework incorporates task-level heterogeneity, sectoral variation in AI exposure, capability accumulation, endogenous AI adoption, and services-led development pathways. The analysis demonstrates that increasing AI adoption lowers manufacturing labor demand, diminishes the competitiveness value of low wages, weakens labor reallocation from agriculture to modern sectors, and slows the traditional structural transformation process. However, these effects are shown to be uneven across industries and tasks, depending on the extent to which production activities are susceptible to automation. The paper introduces the concepts of the erosion of laborbased comparative advantage, task-based comparative advantage, the structural transformation trap, and capability-based comparative advantage. The model predicts a transition from a labor-based development regime, in which competitiveness derives primarily from favourable factor endowments, to a capability-based development regime, in which competitiveness depends increasingly on technological capability, human capital, digital infrastructure, institutional quality, and the ability to adopt and complement AI technologies. Simulation analysis illustrates how AI progressively weakens the traditional relationship between wages, industrial expansion, and structural transformation while increasing the importance of capability accumulation. More broadly, the analysis suggests that AI may transform not only employment and production but also the fundamental mechanisms through which economic development occurs.

title: The Vestal of Pension-Age True Crime: Oksana Zabuzhko, Cultural Narcissism, and the Gender Industry of Ukrainian Literary Nationalism A Critical Polemic in Literary Studies, Psychoanalysis, and Cultural Theory
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Vestal of Pension-Age True Crime: Oksana Zabuzhko, Cultural Narcissism, and the Gender Industry of Ukrainian Literary Nationalism A Critical Polemic in Literary Studies, Psychoanalysis, and Cultural Theory
detail.abstract: There is something profoundly symptomatic — in the strict clinical sense of that word — about the scene that opens our inquiry. A Ukrainian writer of significant reputation, Oksana Zabuzhko, opens her Facebook feed at some indeterminate hour of the wartime morning, and, before she can register whether Crimea has become an island or what new territory in Russia is ablaze, she is assaulted — assaulted, mark you, not merely bothered — by discussion of a television personality who confessed to childhood cruelty toward animals. What follows is not a paragraph, or even a measured essay; what follows is a twelve-hundred-word Facebook performance, an act of prophetic lamentation over "the loss of cultural code," in which the tortured sparrows of nineteenth-century Ukrainian peasant literature are conscripted into the war of public morality, with Dostoevsky (Russian) condemned in the dock and Panas Myrnyi (Ukrainian) crowned in absentia. The audience applauds with 7,900 emoji-laden reactions. The prophet has delivered. The cultural code has been invoked.

title: False Confidence in Machine-Learning Asset Pricing
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: False Confidence in Machine-Learning Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper studies when machine-learning return forecasts are calibrated on average yet overconfident in the states where portfolios take risk. Design/methodology/approach: The analysis applies conformalized quantile forecasts to the Chen-Zimmermann/OpenAP panel of 212 monthly stock characteristics in annual out-of-sample tests from 1982 through 2023. Findings: Ninety percent conformal intervals achieve near-marginal coverage, while highidiosyncratic-volatility and market-regime cells remain undercovered. A false-confidence score, defined as directional forecast confidence scaled by the positive undercoverage gap of the calibration group, predicts future forecast failure and produces a LinearQR conformal-FC signal with a 1.527 Sharpe ratio and 12.2 percent FF5+UMD alpha. Originality: The paper connects conformal prediction, conditional forecast reliability, and assetpricing portfolio performance by showing that a model's own calibration history is an economically priced state variable.

title: Vertical Mergers, Double Marginalization, and Foreclosure
affiliations: University of Miami Herbert Business School and University of Florida

detail.title: Vertical Mergers, Double Marginalization, and Foreclosure
detail.abstract: We analyze vertical mergers in markets where both the upstream and downstream sectors are characterized by a dominant firm and a competitive fringe. We show that adding a competitive fringe at each stage-while preserving the successive monopoly structure of Spengler (1950)-is sufficient to generate the full range of anticompetitive mechanisms identified in the post-Chicago literature. The premerger equilibrium exhibits double marginalization arising from the sequential exercise of market power. Elimination of double marginalization provides an efficiency rationale for vertical integration. The merger creates incentives for input foreclosure, customer foreclosure, and competitive fringe exit. We characterize five post-merger equilibria and show that the downstream fringe may exit the market without any active foreclosure conduct, as a consequence of the efficiency-driven price reduction of the integrated firm. Implications for antitrust policy under Section 7 of the Clayton Act are derived. The EDM efficiency defense and the nonpredatory exit harm are driven by the same parameter, creating an inherent tension in vertical merger review.

title: When Do Anomalies Deserve Capital? Macro-Regime Memory and Dynamic Cross-Sectional Factor Allocation
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: When Do Anomalies Deserve Capital? Macro-Regime Memory and Dynamic Cross-Sectional Factor Allocation
detail.abstract: This paper studies when characteristic-based return predictors deserve capital. A broad anomaly panel is organized into economic families, and a macro-regime memory allocator assigns capital across those families under an annual walk-forward protocol. The lead allocation rule earns 2.13 percent per month, with a Newey-West t-statistic of 9.21 and an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.51. The same family allocation structure improves the full 212-signal hierarchy by 0.0197 monthly information-coefficient points relative to static aggregation, with a t-statistic of 6.25. The model's answer is concentrated: Continuation and Valuation absorb most capital and account for nearly all allocation performance, while the other families operate as state-contingent exposures. The sharpest mechanism is Liquidity/Limits by market trend. The Liquidity/Limits family earns 1.41 percent per month in low-trend states and reverses to-1.79 percent in high-trend states, with the low-minus-high premium strongest outside the deepestcapacity stocks. The findings show that the economic value of anomalies is not fixed characteristic by characteristic; it is state dependent, organized by anomaly family, and shaped by macro conditions and arbitrage capacity.
