title: Affordable Care Act Retrenchment
affiliations: University of Miami - School of Law

detail.title: Affordable Care Act Retrenchment

declarations.ethicsApproval: The IRB determined this study meets the criteria for an exemption as described in Federal Regulation 45 CFR 46.104.

detail.abstract: The "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" (OBBBA) is poised to make the largest cuts in federal support for health insurance coverage in United States history. Yet this law is both poorly understood and rife with uncertainty. This Article tells the story of how the OBBBA will undermine the 2010 Affordable Care Act and reduce access to health care, how Congressional Republicans enacted the law, how state officials are struggling to implement the law, and what the law means for the future of the safety net. It draws on a series of in-depth interviews with 34 state government officials, health care nonprofit officials, for-profit lobbyists, representatives of health care industry groups, and other health care experts. It explains how the OBBBA will impose a dizzying array of new administrative and financial burdens on enrollees in Medicaid and the ACA Marketplaces, curtail health insurance coverage for legal immigrants, and shift the burden of funding the Medicaid program from the federal government to the states. It outlines the different legislative strategies and factors that led to the enactment of the law, which defies the conventional wisdom that social programs are nearly impossible to dismantle. It finds that state policymakers, who are charged with implementing many of the provisions in the OBBBA, are pessimistic about their ability to mitigate coverage losses and face various constraints in doing so. And it finds that, although there remains significant uncertainty as to whether the changes wrought by the OBBBA will endure or be scaled back in the long run, the law is likely to have fiscal ripple effects at the state and local levels that will lead to further cuts to Medicaid.

title: Dialectic of Excise Taxation of Tobacco Products in Ukraine: Eurointegration Aspect
affiliations: , State Tax University, State Tax University and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Dialectic of Excise Taxation of Tobacco Products in Ukraine: Eurointegration Aspect
detail.abstract: The paper reveals the scientific approaches to the transformation of the excise taxation of tobacco products in order to achieve the objectives of fiscal consolidation and the fulfilment of the requirements of the Association Agreement with the EU. The tendencies of development of mechanisms of taxation of excise taxes on tobacco products in the EU countries in the context of new challenges and threats are analysed, and special attention was paid to the practice of raising the level of taxation of these excisable goods in certain EU countries. Problems in the realisation of the fiscal and regulatory potential of excise taxation of tobacco products in Ukraine are revealed. The directions of reformation of excise taxation of tobacco products in Ukraine are grounded, taking into account the requirements of EU directives and European experience.

title: Signatures of Financial Markets
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Signatures of Financial Markets
detail.abstract: A track record is a stream: returns arriving in time, each beside a state of the market. Performance evaluation runs almost entirely on aggregates, the Sharpe ratio, the information ratio, Jensen's alpha, which summarise the return distribution and throw away order. We model a strategy as a multivariate path and apply the signature transform of rough-path theory, a reparametrisation-invariant graded feature set that records how performance and market stress interact through time with no parametric likelihood. A strategy's law is identifiable from its expected signature up to tree-like equivalence; style drift becomes a signature-kernel twosample test; and detection of state-dependent performance becomes anytime-valid, a signature conformance score turned into an e-process whose error is controlled at every sample size at once by Ville's inequality, with the null conditioned on the past so that volatility clustering and momentum do not break it. The discriminating coordinate is the signature's Lévy area, which measures whether returns rise exactly when the market turns hard, the antisymmetric lead-lag that the timing regressions of Treynor and Mazuy and of Henriksson and Merton discard. We prove that the Sharpe ratio, the information ratio, and every statistic of the return multiset are invariant under reordering returns in time, so a fund that aligns its reported gains with market states, the Madoff signature, matches an honest profile on every aggregate yet is exposed by the area. We are careful about what the area certifies: state-dependent convexity, shared by genuine timing, mechanical optionality, and reported-return fraud, with netting against a convexity benchmark as the attribution step. In a study calibrated to NASDAQ volatility the e-process holds exact type-I control, power rises with timing strength and record length, and a first-order growth law predicts detection time.

title: Global Current Account Monitor: Regime Anchors and Exchange Rate Repricing Signals
affiliations: Laval University, Faculté des Sciences Sociales, Département d'Économique, Students

detail.title: Global Current Account Monitor: Regime Anchors and Exchange Rate Repricing Signals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The sole author declares no competing financial or institutional interests.

detail.abstract:
This macro note monitors current account regimes across 16 sovereigns and regional aggregates using IMF World Economic Outlook data (April 2026), extracting exchange rate repricing signals through a non-parametric distributional framework. The 50 % Highest Density Region (HDR) anchors each sovereign's structural external financing gravity in realised outcomes rather than theoretical sustainability benchmarks. 
Breach of the HDR lower bound — signalling that the external liability position is expanding beyond the structural range — elevates the sovereign risk premium ψt, transmitting into exchange rate repricing through distinct regime contingent channels: continuous spot adjustment under floating regimes, and reserve depletion culminating in forced devaluation under fixed and pegged regimes.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Strategic Communication, and Allocation

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Strategic Communication, and Allocation
detail.abstract: The paper studies strategic communication in allocation decisions. A receiver decides whether to allocate an object, such as a job, admission slot, grant, or contract, to an informed sender. The sender privately knows whether allocation would be desirable or undesirable for the receiver and privately chooses between two communication tests: a direct test or an AI-assisted test. The receiver observes a signal realization and a report about test use, forms beliefs, and decides whether to allocate. In equilibrium, AI-use declarations are uninformative cheap talk. AI matters instead through signal generation and the receiver's interpretation of signal realizations. The paper characterizes pure-strategy equilibria and derives welfarerelevant comparative statics: posterior dispersion improves the receiver's screening payoff, while a sender benefits when AI makes her communication more persuasive. The paper then studies which AI tests arise in equilibrium and how they affect welfare. AI that improves high-value senders' ability to produce credible signals supports certification, whereas AI that improves low-value senders' ability to resemble high-value senders supports imitation. If AI can only repackage information already contained in the direct test, then it cannot generate selective certification: certification requires new information, while imitation and pooling can arise from repackaging alone.

title: The Dynamics of Ample Reserves
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: The Dynamics of Ample Reserves

keywords.keywords: monetary policy; liquid deposits; ample reserves; policy rate

detail.abstract: How monetary policy is implemented can have significant implications for the dynamics of the central bank's balance sheet. If liquid deposits increase the demand for reserves (Lopez-Salido and Vissing-Jorgensen 2025), then the "ample" level of reserves needed to close the spread between the policy rate and interest on reserves is itself a function of liquid deposits. The supply of reserves will continue to normalize after first reaching ample levels and until liquid deposits return to trend as well. Furthermore, if the supply of reserves encourages deposit creation (Acharya et al. 2024), then a feedback loop arises that can amplify the persistence of elevated deposits and even lead to explosive dynamics. An off-the-shelf calibration exercise finds that even modest amounts of intrinsic deposit persistence could trigger explosive dynamics. Attenuating the response of ample reserves to deposits removes the risk of instability at a modest cost in terms of rate deviations. Simulations with stable roots show that reserves first reach ample earlier and at a higher level than expected by the demand of reserves alone. However, the supply of reserves may decrease further thereafter, at least relative to trend, as liquid deposits remain elevated in the transition period. * The author would like to thank the Wharton Finance department for its hospitality, as well as James Clouse and audiences at the University of Miami and University of Houston for their feedback. The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia or the Federal Reserve System.

title: Screening with Product Mismatch
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Screening with Product Mismatch
detail.abstract: A monopolist sells a product line whose variants are horizontally differentiated from the buyers' perspective but ordered by production cost. Buyers privately know their ideal product, and willingness to pay may be correlated with horizontal need. The seller screens buyers through product mismatch, and what she must screen determines whether mismatch creates or reduces information rent. When buyers differ only in horizontal need, mismatch creates rent: the seller induces less mismatch, assigning served buyers products closer to their ideals than under the first best. When willingness to pay is correlated with horizontal need, mismatch instead reduces rent: the seller induces more mismatch, sells the basic product to buyers whose efficient products are advanced variants while excluding buyers better matched to it, and stronger horizontal differentiation can expand coverage and raise profit. Because mismatch is type-specific, optimal allocations are determined by individual rationality rather than by incentive compatibility alone.

title: Human Capital as an Informal Environmental Institution: Higher Education Expansion and Regional Carbon Intensity in China
affiliations: Xiamen University, Xiamen University, Xiamen University and Xiamen University

detail.title: Human Capital as an Informal Environmental Institution: Higher Education Expansion and Regional Carbon Intensity in China
detail.abstract: While formal environmental regulations are extensively studied, the role of human capital as an informal institutional constraint in carbon mitigation remains largely underexplored. Utilizing a comprehensive city-year panel dataset in China, this paper examines the effect of Higher education expansion on regional carbon emission intensity. Employing a two-way fixed effects model alongside an instrumental variable approach based on the 1952 nationwide college restructuring, we find that higher education expansion significantly and robustly reduces regional carbon intensity. Mechanism analysis reveal that this effect operates through a sequential process of regional green transformation: higher education expansion first reshapes green preferences on the demand side by enhancing public green awareness and generating bottom-up social pressure; this demand-side pressure then stimulates green technological innovation on the production side; and the resulting accumulation of green capabilities further facilitates industrial structure upgrading on the development side. Further analysis documents an institutional substitution effect: the emission-reduction effect of higher education expansion is more pronounced in cities where local government environmental attention is relatively weak. These findings suggest that higher education expansion can function not only as a source of human capital, but also as an informal environmental institution that supports regional low-carbon transition.

title: ESG and Financial Performance in Public and Private Companies: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: University of Regensburg - Department of Finance,  and Fundação Dom Cabral

detail.title: ESG and Financial Performance in Public and Private Companies: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: Using detailed, questionnaire-based ESG data embedded in a broader corporate ranking for 156 public and 317 private Brazilian companies from 2017 to 2023, we examine the relationship between ownership structure, financial performance, and ESG performance. Panel regressions and propensity score matching reveal that public companies have lower ESG scores than private companies due to weaker governance. The gap is most pronounced among large companies with low leverage, high liquidity, and low capital intensity. Transitions from public to private ownership are associated with improved ESG scores. Prior profitability is positively linked to ESG scores, particularly in brown industries and among companies with weaker financial constraints, consistent with financial slack theory. Family ownership is positively associated with profitability, especially in private companies. A difference-in-differences design around an ESG disclosure regulation shows that ESG scores of public companies significantly increased after implementation. Our findings highlight the pivotal roles of ownership structure, financial slack, and disclosure mandates in shaping ESG performance in emerging markets.

keywords: Algorithmic Familiarity (AI-Mediated Entity Familiarity) Algorithmic Familiarity

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper draws primarily on peerreviewed theoretical literature in psychology, consumer behavior, marketing, information systems, and human-AI interaction. This literature is used to ground the proposed mechanisms: mere exposure, cognitive fluency, the Illusory Truth Effect, availability, trust in automation, automation bias, cognitive offloading, and social proof. Non-peerreviewed or emerging working papers are discussed only when they define adjacent constructs, such as AI availability, and are not treated as empirical validation of Algorithmic Familiarity. The paper uses Algorithmic Familiarity as the shorthand name of the construct. Its more precise technical meaning is AI-mediated entity familiarity. The construct does not refer to users' familiarity with algorithms, artificial intelligence systems, or chatbots. It refers instead to familiarity with external entities, such as brands, products, concepts, institutions, tools, destinations, experts, or options, that may emerge through repeated exposure to those entities within AI-generated outputs. In short: Familiarity with AI refers to the user's knowledge of the technological system. Algorithmic Familiarity refers to the user's familiarity with entities repeatedly surfaced by the AI system. This distinction is important because the term familiarity is already used in adjacent literatures. Research on algorithmic advice often uses algorithm familiarity to mean a user's familiarity with algorithms. Research on chatbot adoption uses chatbot familiarity to mean prior experience with chatbot interfaces. Recent research on AI availability focuses on the probability that a brand is surfaced by generative AI systems. Algorithmic Familiarity is related to these literatures, but it addresses a different level of analysis: the cognitive internalization of entities after repeated AI-mediated exposure.

title: Responsibility Locking and Corrective Effectiveness in Action Domains: A Structural Theory of Closure and Correction

detail.title: Responsibility Locking and Corrective Effectiveness in Action Domains: A Structural Theory of Closure and Correction
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a structural theory of effective correction in action domains, focusing on the interplay between responsibility locking and corrective effectiveness. Building on WP1’s formulation of responsibility locking and error correction, its primary contribution is to formalize responsibility closure and corrective sequence as a combined R–CE structure. Existing theories, including property rights, contract, organizational accountability, and market discipline, address related mechanisms in specific domains but do not usually specify how consequences return to responsibility nodes across heterogeneous action domains.

Responsibility locking is decomposed into three components: R1, responsibility entry; R2, attribution return; and R3, consequence settlement. Corrective effectiveness is decomposed into four sequential stages: recognition, calibration, formulation, and execution. Recognition identifies relevant constraints or deviations; calibration aligns action with the objective under constraints; formulation constructs a workable corrective scheme; execution carries the scheme into action with continuity, coordination, and feedback. Effective correction requires both responsibility closure and a functioning corrective sequence.

The framework explains why observable activity, procedures, attribution, or execution alone may appear corrective yet fail structurally. It provides a basis for analyzing failures in markets, organizations, public administration, infrastructure, and conflict, and offers the theoretical foundation for later operational failure analysis of action-domain breakdowns.

Keywords: Action Domain Structural Theory; Responsibility Locking; Responsibility Closure; Corrective Effectiveness; Action–Consequence Responsibility; Attribution Return; Consequence Settlement; Calibration; Open-Loop Adjustment; Failure Analysis

title: The Asymmetric Green Transition: Global Value Chains, Fixed Adoption Costs, and Firm-Level Carbon Productivity
affiliations: Chungnam National University and Villanova University

detail.title: The Asymmetric Green Transition: Global Value Chains, Fixed Adoption Costs, and Firm-Level Carbon Productivity
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether global value chain (GVC) participation improves firm-level carbon productivity and why the effects differ by firm size. We develop a heterogeneous-firm model in which firms face fixed costs of adopting abatement capacity. Backward GVC participation can raise domestic carbon productivity by reducing domestic processing per unit of value added, while the effect of forward participation is theoretically ambiguous. We test these predictions using Korean manufacturing firms subject to the emission trading system during 2011-2021, combining firm-level emissions and financial data with industry-level GVC measures. To ensure empirical rigor, our design examines baseline dynamics via system GMM estimation, establishes primary causal identification through a shift-share instrument approach, and implements alternative specifications for exhaustive sensitivity checks. The results show that backward GVC participation is associated with higher carbon productivity mainly among large firms. Small and medium-sized enterprises show little response to GVC exposure or emission trading system (ETS) dummies, consistent with fixed costs limiting green adjustment. Further exploration of possible reasons behind this pattern suggests that large firms' gains are associated with both cost-driven sourcing from developing partners and technology-related links to advanced-economy partners, especially when financial constraints are weaker.

title: Transport Supply and Car Use: Evidence from Population-Wide Panel Data
affiliations: Swedish National Road and Transport Research Institute and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Transport Supply and Car Use: Evidence from Population-Wide Panel Data
detail.abstract: We estimate how changes in transport supply affect vehicle kilometres travelled (VKT) and thereby transport energy demand. Specifically, we examine how changes in generalized travel times by car, generalized travel times by other modes (public transit, walking, and cycling), and destination density affect individual VKT. The analysis uses Swedish register panel data for 1998, 2005, and 2017, matched to historically reconstructed transport networks and destination distributions. We exploit within-individual first differences and use an instrumental-variable strategy based on changes around individuals’ initial residential locations to separate changes in transport conditions from changes induced by residential relocation. The results show that pooled cross-sectional models substantially overstate the effects. Moreover, the IV estimates are substantially smaller than the first-difference estimates, indicating that endogenous residential relocation and preference shifts may affect both experienced travel conditions and car use. Improvements in generalized travel times by other modes reduce VKT, but the implied effects are modest: a one-standard-deviation improvement reduces annual VKT by about 183 km, corresponding to 2.3% of mean VKT, in the preferred IV specification. The effects of changes in car generalized travel times and destination density are less robust.

title: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the estimation of causal treatment effects on demand when treatment is randomly assigned but prices adjust in response to treatment. We show that regressions of demand on treatment or on treatment and price lead to biased estimates of the direct treatment effect. The bias in both cases depends on the correlation of price with treatment and points in the same direction. In most cases including an endogenous price control reduces bias but does not remove it. We show how to test whether bias from an endogenous price response arises and how to recover an unbiased direct treatment effect using a price instrument. We apply our approach to the estimation of feature advertising effects across several product categories using supermarket scanner data and show that the bias when not instrumenting price can be substantial.

reference: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming
title: Student Preference for Size of Colleges and Universities
affiliations: University at Albany (SUNY), Independent, Independent and Independent

detail.title: Student Preference for Size of Colleges and Universities

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Since 2011, most sectors of institutions of higher education have lost enrollment, with losses ranging from 9% to 35%, depending on overall size. The exception are the very large institutions, which have seen a growth in enrollment of more than three-quarters of a million students during that period. Exactly why students are gravitating to these larger institutions is less clear, although a simple preference for larger colleges and universities may be the driver. This report examines the results of a survey of nearly 1,500 prospective students carried out in July 2025 in partnership with Hanover Research regarding their preference for size of college or university. The results were segmented by age, region, education level, and degree type. Respondents were an even mix of traditional (expectant or recent high school graduates) and nontraditional (older students years removed from completing high school) and distributed equally across the four regions of the United States (Northeast, South, Midwest, and West) who were seeking either an undergraduate or a graduate degree, were 16-55 years old, and were interested in enrolling in a higher education institution within the following two years.

title: Exposed but Not Adopted: A Codifiability Index for Generative AI Adoption

detail.title: Exposed but Not Adopted: A Codifiability Index for Generative AI Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests in relation to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants or animals; it analyzes publicly available occupational task descriptions and aggregate AI-usage data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Generative AI's economic impact is uneven across tasks and sectors, and how that impact is distributed, who gains, which work transforms, and how knowledge and control are reorganized, is fundamentally a political-economy question. This paper argues that the structure of that distribution is governed by codifiability: whether the knowledge a task requires can be represented in symbolic, communicable, and reproducible form. It introduces a task-level Codifiability Index that scores O*NET tasks on symbolic representability, physical causality dependence, somatic knowledge requirement, and collective coordination intensity. In a 100-task pilot merged with public AI-usage and task-level exposure data, the index predicts whether a task has observed usage on the extensive margin and captures variation related to, but not identical with, capability-based exposure. The index makes a political-economy claim measurable: because generative AI operates on already-codified knowledge, unequal codification capacity becomes unequal AI capacity, concentrating adoption in firms and sectors that can document production while leaving tacit, embodied, and collectively coordinated work behind. The paper develops the implications for labor (codification as control, dual precarity), capital allocation, and AI policy. The evidence is preliminary, but the contribution is a knowledge-structure measure, distinct from AI exposure, capability, and usage, that makes the distributional and institutional consequences of AI adoption empirically tractable.

title: Asians in the Arab World: Labor Migration and Public Policy
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Asians in the Arab World: Labor Migration and Public Policy
detail.abstract: Ten years after the first oil price rises were declared in 1973 the countries of the Middle East were still struggling to understand the implications of these momentous events. Economic changes induced by events of 1973 created a dynamic process that fundamentally changed both the view of, and the reality in, the Arab world. The economic development of the region is critically tied to manpower requirements; many of the bottlenecks and constraints on economic growth stem directly from the flow of labor across national boundaries. The appearance of increasing numbers of South and East Asian workers in the Arab Gulf represents the most important recent change in the labor markets of the region.

title: Beyond Industry 4.0: Physics-Informed Autonomous Semiconductor Manufacturing and the Emergence of AI-Native Semiconductor Enterprises

detail.title: Beyond Industry 4.0: Physics-Informed Autonomous Semiconductor Manufacturing and the Emergence of AI-Native Semiconductor Enterprises
detail.abstract: The semiconductor industry is entering an era of unprecedented manufacturing complexity driven by advanced process nodes, heterogeneous integration, shrinking process margins, and increasingly stringent defect-control requirements. While Industry 4.0 initiatives have accelerated the adoption of smart manufacturing technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, cyber-physical systems, and predictive analytics, current semiconductor manufacturing systems remain largely fragmented, reactive, and heavily dependent on empirical process optimization. In particular, existing AI implementations in semiconductor manufacturing are frequently constrained by black-box architectures, limited physical interpretability, and weak generalization capabilities across process conditions and manufacturing platforms. This paper proposes a conceptual framework termed Physics-Informed Autonomous Semiconductor Manufacturing (PIASM), which integrates physics-informed AI, digital twins, multi-modal sensing, scientific machine learning, and autonomous decision architectures into a unified semiconductor manufacturing intelligence system. The framework extends beyond conventional Industry 4.0 paradigms by introducing closedloop adaptive manufacturing intelligence capable of combining real-time manufacturing data with physical process knowledge, defect physics, thermo-fluid dynamics, and predictive optimization. The proposed architecture consists of four integrated layers: manufacturing systems and multi-modal sensing and metrology, physics engines, AI intelligence systems and digital twins, and autonomous decisionmaking mechanisms. This proposed framework is illustrated with examples from crystal growth, defect engineering to product marketing and applications. The paper further discusses the strategic, organizational, and geopolitical implications of autonomous semiconductor manufacturing, including AI-native manufacturing capabilities, human-AI collaboration, semiconductor supply-chain resilience, and sustainable intelligent manufacturing. The study contributes to the emerging discourse on next-generation manufacturing systems by positioning semiconductor manufacturing as a pioneering domain for autonomous scientific intelligence systems integrating physics, AI, and industrial decision-making.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Public land-grant Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) face persistent resource constraints, enrollment pressures, funding volatility, and stakeholder complexity. Existing governance models emphasize funding and performance but under-specify the role of institutional trust as a strategic capacity. This paper applies the Convergent University Framework—developed in Working Papers 1 and 2—to the leadership environment of 1890 land-grant institutions.

Research Question: How might institutional trust, constituent alignment, and governance quality influence organizational resilience within public land-grant HBCUs under resource constraints?

Central Argument: Institutional trust functions as a strategic governance asset that can amplify the impact of available resources, buffer against shocks, and influence the sustainability of performance—not as a substitute for funding but as a complementary capacity.

Case Context: The paper draws on a pilot inventory of 25 administrative initiatives executed at South Carolina State University, an 1890 land-grant HBCU, to illustrate the framework's descriptive applicability. No causal or validation claims are made.

Contributions: The paper provides (1) a trust-centered vocabulary for discussing governance challenges in resource-constrained HBCU environments; (2) a risk-based analysis linking trust capital to institutional resilience; (3) a conceptual diagnostic tool—the Trust Risk Exposure Matrix (TREM); and (4) stakeholder-specific implications for presidents, boards, policymakers, and 1890 institutions.

detail.abstract:
This master thesis investigates the relationship between brand image and consumer perception in the luxury watch industry using Rolex as a primary case study. The research traces the historical evolution of luxury watch branding contrasting its traditional roots with the transformative influences of digitisation and the emergence of online resale markets.


Interviews with three distinct demographics—Rolex owners, those aspiring to own a Rolex and owners of other luxury watch brands (Audemars Piguet and Patek Philippe)—provided a comprehensive understanding of the brand’s perception in the digital age. These discussions illuminated the multifaceted influences shaping brand loyalty, aspirations and the nuanced dynamics of the luxury watch market in the digital era. Implementing brand strategies within this evolving framework presents both challenges and opportunities.


Given the insights from this research, it is crucial to understand the intricate factors associated with brand image, societal influences, digital transformation and economic implications to craft effective branding strategies. The research methodology encompassed interviewing participants from these three demographics offering a holistic view of individual brand perceptions and broader industry trends. The findings underscore that Rolex’s brand image, bolstered by its heritage, strategic branding and adept navigation of digitisation and resale markets, significantly influences consumer perceptions. The results suggest a strong correlation between brand image and consumer loyalty with potential implications for market positioning and future branding strategies in the luxury watch sector amidst rapid digital transformation.

detail.abstract: AI algorithms can analyze vast amounts of data quickly and accurately, leading to insights and predictions that can drive decisionmaking and improve processes. As AI continues to advance, it has the potential to revolutionize world history, industries and transform the way we live and work. However, the economic nuances of African societies have led to algorithmic bias. Historically, algorithmic bias arises when an AI system produces systematically discriminatory outcomes due to flawed assumptions or biases in the training data used during machine learning. Therefore, there is a need for the development of algorithms that are tailored to the specific needs and characteristics of African populations. Additionally, there is a need for greater transparency and accountability in the development and deployment of AI systems to ensure that they do not perpetuate biases or discrimination in credit scoring. By addressing these challenges, Africa can harness the full potential of algorithm driven solutions. By incorporating African native-centric algorithms into artificial intelligence (AI) systems, the aim  is to decolonize ethical issues that have often been overlooked in mainstream AI development for credit scoring. The research adopts a philosophical method of analysis. The integration of African native-centric algorithms can help address biases and promote more equitable outcomes in AI applications. By incorporating local perspectives and values into algorithm design, policymakers can ensure that AI technologies are more culturally sensitive and responsive to the needs of diverse populations. This approach can also help build trust and acceptance of AI systems among communities in Nigeria and beyond. However, the incorporation of African native-centric algorithms in the development of AI algorithms is challenged by cultural individualism. User-centric interface design in the management of data and computations is necessary to train and accommodate cultural values. Despite these challenges, the study concludes that incorporating African worldviews in AI algorithms has the potential to enhance effectiveness and the development of indigenous knowledge in the global AI race.

title: Delegating Innovation: Sequential and Parallel Search Under Competition
affiliations: Business School, National University of Singapore, National University of Singapore (NUS) and

detail.title: Delegating Innovation: Sequential and Parallel Search Under Competition
detail.abstract: Concept generation plays a critical role in the success of new product development (NPD) projects by identifying products or services that address unmet customer needs. Given the inherent uncertainty and complexity of the innovation landscape, it is essential for firms to search broadly across the space of possible concepts to enhance the likelihood of discovering a winning idea. In practice, sequential and parallel search strategies represent two fundamental approaches to concept generation: sequential search develops and evaluates one concept at a time, stopping once a promising idea is found, while parallel search explores multiple concepts simultaneously before selecting the best. This paper considers a setting where a buying firm delegates the search process to multiple suppliers. In such a competitive, multi-agent setting, should the buyer prefer suppliers to adopt sequential or parallel search strategies? By embedding a classical search model into a contest framework, we show that the buyer prefers sequential search when either (i) the unit search cost is high or (ii) the maximum number of evaluation opportunities is large. In these cases, sequential search confers two advantages: an informational benefit that allows suppliers to adapt using performance feedback (a "quality effect"), and an incentive benefit that encourages suppliers to search more extensively (a "quantity effect"). When neither condition holds, parallel search is preferred. Solving the buyer's optimal design problem further shows that the optimal supplier base always features restricted entry, limiting participation to as few as two suppliers. We also study an extension in which the firm incurs costs when evaluating submitted samples.

detail.abstract:
The rapid evolution of digital finance is transforming the architecture of modern banking by reshaping how financial institutions acquire information, evaluate borrowers, manage credit risk, and deliver financial services. Beyond improving operational efficiency, digital financial technologies are redefining the informational foundations of financial intermediation, creating new opportunities for risk management while simultaneously introducing new sources of systemic complexity. Despite the growing prominence of digital finance in banking research, its implications for banking stability remain theoretically fragmented, with limited consensus regarding the mechanisms through which digital transformation influences the resilience of banking systems.

This paper addresses this gap by developing an integrated conceptual framework that explains how Digital Finance Intensity (DFI) contributes to Banking Stability (BSI) through organizational and institutional mechanisms. Drawing upon Financial Intermediation Theory, Information Economics, the Risk-Taking Channel of Finance, and Complex Systems Theory, the proposed framework identifies Credit Risk Management Quality (CRMQ) as the principal organizational mechanism through which DFI is translated into more effective risk governance and, ultimately, greater BSI. The framework further proposes that Open Banking Intensity (OBI) moderates this relationship by enhancing data accessibility, interoperability, and information sharing across the banking ecosystem, thereby strengthening the effectiveness of DFI in improving CRMQ.

The paper contributes to the emerging literature in several important ways. First, it integrates previously disconnected research streams on digital finance, credit risk management, Open Banking, and banking stability into a unified theoretical model. Second, it advances CRMQ as the key mediating mechanism linking DFI with BSI, thereby providing a clearer explanation of the organizational processes underlying digital transformation in banking. Third, it conceptualizes OBI as an institutional condition that shapes the effectiveness of DFI, emphasizing that the benefits of digital finance depend not only on technological adoption but also on the surrounding regulatory and data-sharing environment. Finally, the study establishes a coherent analytical foundation that supports future empirical investigation of digital finance within European banking systems.

As a conceptual working paper, this study does not present empirical evidence or statistical estimation. Instead, it develops a theoretically grounded and empirically testable framework that can inform subsequent research employing bank-level panel data, composite indicators, and advanced econometric techniques including Fixed Effects models, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM) to examine the proposed relationships. In doing so, the paper serves as the theoretical foundation for a broader empirical research agenda on the role of digital finance in promoting banking stability within the evolving European financial landscape.

title: Pre-Implementation Organisational Readiness for AI- Strategic Antecedents of AI Adoption
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Pre-Implementation Organisational Readiness for AI- Strategic Antecedents of AI Adoption
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a strategic priority for organisations seeking to improve productivity, strengthen decision-making and create sustainable competitive advantage. Despite increased investment, many organisations continue to struggle to move from successful pilot projects to organisation-wide AI adoption. Existing research has largely explained these challenges through technological capability, data quality, governance, leadership and change management. While these perspectives have substantially advanced understanding of AI implementation, they generally assume that implementation begins when organisations decide to deploy AI technologies. This paper argues that this assumption overlooks an earlier organisational phase during which implementation capability is progressively created.

Drawing upon recent literature in AI implementation and Strategic Human Resource Management (SHRM), this paper introduces Pre-Implementation Organisational Readiness (PIOR) as an organisational capability developed before AI deployment through recruitment and onboarding. Rather than treating these activities as supporting human resource functions, the paper positions them as strategic antecedents that shape workforce capability before implementation formally begins. An illustrative executive example demonstrates how implementation challenges frequently originate from organisational capability rather than technological capability. The paper concludes by proposing PIOR as a complementary capability to technology readiness and identifies directions for future empirical research.

detail.abstract: Cross-model Presence Consistency (CPC)-the stability of a brand's surfacing across a reference panel of large language models-is the Consistency component of the AI Availability Score (AIAS™), a proposed third brand-growth system alongside mental and physical availability. A prior coefficient-of-variation operationalization (CV-CPC) was falsified as a consistency instrument: because the coefficient of variation of a low-rate count couples to its mean (CV ≈ 1/ √ mean), CV-CPC reparametrized recall level rather than measuring consistency (pooled |𝜌(CV-CPC, 𝜇)| = 0.77). title: Intervention, Hierarchy, and Agency in Bolivia

detail.title: Intervention, Hierarchy, and Agency in Bolivia
detail.abstract: This article evaluates the evidentiary architecture of the abridged edition of A Century of U.S. Intervention in Bolivia, coordinated by Juan Ramón Quintana and introduced by Néstor Kohan. The strategy combines an auditable inventory of thirty-five propositions, an explicit evidentiary rubric, a structured comparison of eight episodes, source criticism, and causal process tests. The analysis distinguishes presence, influence, pressure, coercive intervention, covert action, complicity, operational direction, and institutional, structural, and productive forms of power. Primary documents and specialized scholarship corroborate creditor control, diplomatic protection of Standard Oil, conditionality imposed on the National Revolution, clandestine political and labor programs, counterinsurgency cooperation, complicity in the operation against Ernesto Guevara, and covert funding of opponents of Juan José Torres. Support weakens when the book moves from bounded mechanisms to a homogeneous U.S. will, a monocausal explanation of underdevelopment, or demonstrated direction of every coup and every domestic opposition movement. The article proposes a model of conditioned interventionism: external resources produce effects through material vulnerability, domestic coalitions, institutional openings, and bureaucratic coordination, and may be neutralized by resistance, state capacity, or international alternatives. The conclusion is not equidistant: recurrent intervention is strongly documented; causal omnipotence is not. Disaggregation strengthens, rather than weakens, the critique of bilateral hierarchy.

detail.abstract:
Does resource scarcity increase intra-household conflict? While a large literature links rainfall shocks and violence in rural economies, less is known about the social consequences of infrastructure-driven scarcity in urban settings. This paper examines the causal effect of urban water rationing on domestic violence using a natural experiment from Bogotá, Colombia. In response to the 2023–2024 El Niño episode, the city implemented rotating 24-hour water service suspensions across fixed hydraulic service zones, generating sharp spatial and temporal variation in water access.

I exploit this variation using a boundary-specific spatial regression discontinuity design that compares domestic violence incidents in neighbourhoods located immediately across hydraulic service boundaries on the same day. The analysis combines georeferenced administrative records from Bogotá’s emergency response system with detailed information on rationing schedules and network topology.

Across more than 20,000 incidents and 15 treatment-control boundaries, I find no evidence that temporary water rationing increases reported domestic violence. Estimated effects are small, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and robust to alternative specifications and placebo tests. These findings contrast with evidence from rural settings, where water scarcity often operates through income shocks and has been linked to heightened intimate partner violence. The results suggest that short, predictable interruptions to urban water service do not generate comparable social spillovers and provide new evidence on the social consequences of climate-related water management in cities.

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping contemporary communication by participating not only in the production and circulation of information but also in the interpretation through which meaning is constructed. While existing scholarship has extensively examined generative AI in relation to automation, governance, ethics, bias, and organisational adoption, comparatively less attention has been devoted to explaining how AI reorganises communication as a process of collective interpretation. This article addresses that theoretical gap by extending David Cecchetto’s (2022) account of the afterlife of data towards what is conceptualised as the afterlife of AI.

Adopting a conceptual theory-building approach, the article develops an integrated communication-theoretical framework comprising interpretive infrastructures, communicative overreliance, and synthetic consensus. Interpretive infrastructures describe the communicative environments within which AI-generated explanations, summaries, and recommendations increasingly mediate human interpretation. Communicative overreliance explains how interpretive labour is progressively redistributed across human and computational actors, while synthetic consensus identifies one possible communicative consequence in which shared reliance upon AI-mediated interpretation influences the formation of collective agreement. The framework further argues that although interpretation increasingly becomes collaborative, communicative accountability remains fundamentally human and institutional.

The article contributes to communication theory by demonstrating that generative AI represents a historical transition from infrastructures that primarily organise information to infrastructures that increasingly organise interpretation itself. By repositioning AI as an emerging communicative condition rather than merely a technological tool, the framework extends existing scholarship on digital mediation and provides a conceptual foundation for future research on interpretation, communicative authority, consensus, and accountability in increasingly AI-mediated environments.

detail.abstract: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has increasingly represented an essential component of economic growth in developing countries, particularly in Africa's economic landscape. As one of Africa’s largest economies, Nigeria has in spite of major setbacks continued to attract significant investor interest in sectors such as energy, telecommunication, fintech and manufacturing. However, foreign participation also attract certain risks which investors generally consider with respect to the degree of protection offered by national laws. FDI in Nigeria is thus regulated by various statutory frameworks towards providing equal opportunities for both foreign investors and local players alike to thrive. This essay seeks to provide insight into the legal protection of foreign investors in Nigeria. It begins with an overview of FDI and its impact within the Nigerian context. The essay then proceeds to examine the various legal frameworks for foreign direct investment in light of investors’ protection, as well as the challenges needed to be addressed. It further provides recommendations to strengthen Nigeria’s legal architecture for protecting existing and prospective investors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how state-dependent dividend restrictions (taxes and bans) and capital requirements influence a bank's optimal capital buffers accumulation and risk-taking decisions. In the model, the bank distributes dividends and issues costly equity to maximise shareholder value, while its loans generate stochastic income under time-varying macroeconomic conditions. We solve the bank's stochastic control problem and derive the distribution of its capital buffers in closed form. We find that imposing dividend restrictions in bad macroeconomic states generates an intertemporal trade-off, as it encourages capital buffers accumulation in those states but promotes dividend payouts in the good ones. Furthermore, we show that the policy can undermine financial stability by reducing the bank’s value and weakening its incentives to recapitalise in all states. Coordinating dividend taxes with counter-cyclical capital requirements can mitigate value losses and ease the trade-off, but it also exacerbates disincentives for recapitalisation. Finally, we show that when the bank can (optimally) reduce its risky loans in bad states, capital buffers generated through dividend restrictions mitigate the contraction by dampening its precautionary motive against costly recapitalisation.

title: The Mathematics of Diversification Growth, Information, and Learning
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Mathematics of Diversification Growth, Information, and Learning
detail.abstract: The mean-variance rule  that de Finetti (1940) and Markowitz (1952) bequeathed us presupposes that a covariance matrix exists and is the correct summary of risk. Real returns are heavy tailed, skewed, and non-stationary, so the second moment is at best an approximation and at worst undefined. This paper develops a theory of diversification that never assumes a covariance structure. The organising object is the growth-optimal (log-optimal) portfolio b * = arg max b E[log(b ⊤ R)], which requires only an integrable log return. Four moment-free statements follow. First, rebalancing earns a nonnegative excess growth rate that is a Jensen gap, of which the Fernholz covariance formula is the second-order shadow. Second, the value of diversifying information equals a mutual information, and the growth rate relative to any benchmark equals a Kullback-Leibler divergence, linking diversification to Sanov large deviations and to the de Finetti-Sanov-Bayes triangle. Third, Cover's universal portfolio attains the growth of the best rebalanced portfolio in hindsight, adversarially and without any distributional assumption, and is itself a de Finetti mixture. Fourth, replacing the covariance hypothesis with exchangeability yields a Bayesian predictive theory of diversification in which heavy tails are induced rather than assumed, and fractional Kelly is exactly posterior shrinkage. A Bellman-Kalaba adaptive-control formulation makes learning explicit: with log utility the value function separates, the myopic policy is Bayesian Kelly, and the residual is an exploration premium. The archetype throughout is the horse race, a diversification problem defined entirely by probabilities and prices, in which Benter (1994) built a profitable operation, and whose bet selection is the water-filling of Cover and Thomas. A worked normal-conjugate example, and the turtle-trading position-sizing rule of Polson and Sokolov (2026), show the theory operating without a covariance matrix ever being formed. We also recover de Finetti's and Markowitz's efficient frontier as dual sweeps of a single water level.

detail.title: Liberalizing Discrimination Law
detail.abstract:
Abstract

Liberalizing Discrimination Law (2025) by Daniel Freeman and Alex Morton examines the evolution of anti-discrimination legislation in the United Kingdom and argues that the Equality Act 2010 has expanded beyond its original purpose of preventing direct discrimination. The authors contend that contemporary approaches, particularly those addressing indirect discrimination and seeking to equalize outcomes between groups, undermine the liberal principle of treating individuals equally before the law. They argue that policies based on group identities can create division, distort incentives, and fail to assist genuinely disadvantaged individuals. The paper advocates a return to a more limited framework focused solely on prohibiting direct discrimination, recommending the repeal of provisions concerning indirect discrimination, positive action, and wider equality duties. According to the authors, such reforms would establish a stronger and more genuinely liberal anti-discrimination regime centered on individual rights rather than group outcomes.

title: Bangladesh–New Zealand Bilateral Trade Relations: A Comparative Analysis of Trade, Culture, Policy, and Market Entry Strategies

detail.title: Bangladesh–New Zealand Bilateral Trade Relations: A Comparative Analysis of Trade, Culture, Policy, and Market Entry Strategies
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the bilateral trade relationship between Bangladesh and New Zealand in terms of international business, comparative advantage, cultural differences, government policy and market entry strategy. Despite their contrasting positions in the global economy – Bangladesh as a labour intensive manufacturing exporter and New Zealand as a resource based, high income exporter – the two countries have significant structural economic complementarities that offer scope for deeper commercial engagement.

The research takes into account political, legal, economic and cultural background of the respective countries, especially Hofstede’s cultural dimensions, foreign direct investment (FDI), trade policies, digital commerce, sustainability practices and international business risks. The results show that the bilateral trade is concentrated in a narrow range of products, mainly Bangladeshi ready-made garments and New Zealand dairy products, while investment flows, joint ventures and institutional cooperation remain limited.

The study has identified ready-made garments, pharmaceuticals, information and communication technology (ICT) services, agro-processing and renewable energy as the most promising sectors for future collaboration. It also contends that cultural differences in power distance and individualism are important in the negotiation processes, partnership development and market-entry decisions. In view of the present economic and political environment, a phased market-entry strategy of exporting, licensing and later joint ventures is found to be more suitable than direct equity investment.

The paper finds that notwithstanding the limited scale of existing trade, the Bangladesh–New Zealand relationship is endowed with significant untapped potential. In the coming years, the economic engagement between the two countries can be substantially improved by strengthening institutional cooperation, promoting investment partnerships, improving digital trade infrastructure and pursuing a formal bilateral trade framework.
